_what_this_is: The standing rule that a Tier A change is reviewed by a session OTHER than the one that wrote it, made mechanical. Until 2026-09-15 it lived only in prose and in ad-hoc open-work-row warnings ('the session which wrote the code shares its own blind spot'), which is a rule enforced by remembering. Push-gate check 13 (tools/tier_a_review_gate.py) reads this file.
_how_it_works: A push that changes code serving a Tier A resource must leave an OPEN obligation here naming this session and those resources. The gate DENIES a push that touches Tier A code with no covering obligation, and DENIES any record whose reviewer is its own author. Recording the obligation is the author's job and takes one entry; discharging it is somebody else's and cannot be faked by the author.
_what_it_does_NOT_claim: That a review happened, or that it was any good. It is a record that the obligation EXISTS and was not self-signed. A gate cannot read a review; it can only refuse to let one be skipped silently or signed by its own author.
_scope: Tier A resources, derived from docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md. Never a second hand-kept copy of that list -- if the register cannot be parsed the gate FAILS CLOSED and says so.

merge_policy.note: Read by tools/sairn_rebase_resolve.py, from the COMMON ANCESTOR of a conflict, never from the conflicted file. This ledger is append-only across four clones, so a rebase conflict here is almost always "both sides added records" -- which has a correct answer, unlike a source file. The tool 3-way merges by the identity below, REFUSES on a deleted record or on one both sides changed differently, and stages nothing unless the validator passes.

records.verdict: REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The judgement holds and the controls hold. (1) GRANT: drove the real registry -- 0 violations across all 28 sc_* resources; the seven resolve to ['soft_delete'] and the other 21 keep ['delete']. (2) NON-DESTRUCTIVE IN FACT, not just in name: soft_delete marks _deleted_at and the READ filters on data->>_deleted_at=is.null, and that filter is load-bearing rather than cosmetic -- hydration merges by id and never deletes, so an unfiltered read pushes a deleted record straight back. (3) THE PIN HOLDS IN BOTH DIRECTIONS, driven not read: adding a Tier A sc_ row to docs/CRITICALITY-TIERS.md alone FAILS, and dropping a name from the registry alone FAILS. Restoring a destroying delete on the seven fails sairncode_gates AND tests/stonedesk_server_backup.js, one app over. records.verdict: REVIEWED. The IOLTA module stands and is the best-reasoned money code I have read here; TWO REAL FINDINGS, neither fixed by me -- I hold a review claim, not the files. ALL FOUR PRESS-ON POINTS DRIVEN, NOT READ. (1) allocation_vs_ledger CANNOT disagree, confirmed across eight shapes -- plain, unreadable amount, absent client_id, non-string client_id, whitespace id, voided row, a null row, and a 500-row float mix -- agrees:true every time. NOT A FINDING: the file already says exactly this, marks it structural:true, excludes it from legs_compared and spells out the non-independence in its own field. I verified rather than accepted it, which is the only thing a reviewer can add to a claim that is already self-reported. (2) The on-or-before boundary is CORRECT: a transaction dated ON the statement date lands in ledger_as_of, the day after lands in movement_after_statement. (3) FINDING ONE, AND IT IS THE ONE YOU SUSPECTED, WORSE THAN PARTIAL. Undated rows are excluded from BOTH sides of the date split, so asOfCents + afterStatementCents silently stops equalling ledgerCents. Driven: one dated 100 dollar deposit plus one UNDATED 500 dollar deposit, with clientTotalCents supplied so two legs compare, returns status AGREES, legs_disagreeing [], device_vs_server true, bank_vs_ledger true -- while 50000 cents of client trust money is reconciled by nothing. The only cue is undated_rows:1 nested inside a leg that says agrees:true. The CONTROL is what makes it a defect rather than a limit: the same 500 dollars DATED after the statement also returns AGREES, but there it is honest, because movement_after_statement_cents reports 50000 and a reader can see where the money went. Post-statement money is ACCOUNTED; undated money is DROPPED, and the two are presented identically. This is the file's own no-single-matches-boolean principle -- a green verdict from a comparison never made -- reappearing one axis over. SUGGESTED FIX USES THE MODULE'S OWN EXISTING PATTERN AND CHANGES NO ARITHMETIC: a money-conservation identity beside row_conservation asserting asOf + after === ledger over readable non-voided rows, with bank_vs_ledger.agrees unable to be true while it fails. (4) FINDING TWO, A SCOPE LIMIT THAT IS NOT DISCLOSED: OUTSTANDING ITEMS. A 40 dollar disbursement dated 2026-09-14 against a 2026-09-15 statement returns DISAGREES -- and the books are RIGHT, the cheque simply has not cleared. There is no cleared/outstanding/in-transit concept anywhere in the module, the endpoint or the schema; I grepped. records.what: item 46: api/_lib/record-parity.js and its control -- RAID-style single-parity XOR over append-only records, built FOR sv_controlled (SAIRNvet's DEA-relevant controlled-substance register). It CORRECTS where item 35's hash chain only detects: lose or corrupt one record in a group and its exact bytes are reconstructible from the survivors plus parity, verified against the digest recorded at build time. NOT WIRED INTO sv-witness.js -- the library and its control only. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PUSH ON. (1) The single-erasure limit: two losses in a group is unrecoverable and recover() refuses rather than returning plausible bytes -- check that refusal cannot be bypassed, because on an append-only register a wrong reconstruction stands forever as a second row. (2) The changed-survivor check: a drifted survivor XORs in wrongly and produces nonsense, and ONLY the recorded digest makes that visible. Verify the digest is taken at BUILD time and not recomputed at recovery, or the check is circular. (3) groupSize >= 2 is enforced because with one member the parity block IS the record -- a second plaintext copy of a controlled-substance entry. Check that nothing can construct a group of one by another route. (4) The canonical form is reused in spirit from sv-witness.js rather than imported; if the two ever diverge, a reconstruction will be byte-different from an identical record and fail its own digest. That is a real coupling worth an opinion on. (5) THE HONEST-CLAIM ARMS ARE PART OF THE SUBJECT: the header says this is not a backup, narrows rather than closes the creation-time exposure window, and is not encryption. Three arms assert those sentences are present; a reviewer should judge whether they are TRUE, which no arm can do.
records.verdict: REVIEWED ADVERSARIALLY BY DRIVING IT -- 12 attacks, all handled. CORRECT: exact-byte recovery on a 3-member group; a 5,000-character record recovered from short survivors AND a short record recovered from long ones, so the pad-to-group-width does not corrupt the tail -- the classic parity bug; multi-byte UTF-8 survives the round trip, which matters on a register carrying real names; and canonicalisation is key-order independent, so a survivor re-read from PostgREST with reordered JSON keys still recovers. THE REFUSALS ARE THE STRONGEST PART AND I ATTACKED THEM SPECIFICALLY. Two erasures refuse and NAME the other missing member. A tampered survivor is caught by the digest and NAMES which survivor. An id not in the group refuses. Passing the missing record as its own survivor is correctly seen as two missing. AND THE ONE I EXPECTED TO BREAK IT DID NOT: XOR is self-inverse, so a DUPLICATED survivor cancels itself and would hand back bytes that look like a record -- it is refused. THE GROUP-OF-ONE REFUSAL IS RIGHT AND ITS REASON IS THE GOOD KIND: parity of one record IS the record, so a group of one would store a second plaintext copy of a controlled-substance entry and call it redundancy. NO FINDINGS. One observation, not a defect: buildGroup() THROWS ParityError while recover() refuses as a VALUE {ok:false, code, reason}. The split is defensible -- a bad group is a programmer error, a failed recovery is a data condition -- but the two conventions sit in one module, and a caller that wraps both in a try/catch will see a refusal flow past as a success with record undefined. There are no non-test callers yet, so the place to fix it if it ever matters is the first one. A PROCESS NOTE ON MY OWN REVIEW: my first harness asserted that recover() THROWS and reported five failures. All five were the harness, not the module. Recorded because a review that had stopped at the first red would have filed five findings against correct code on a DEA-relevant register.

FINDING 1 -- THE RULE IS KEYED ON THE COLON, AND A DECLARED EXCLUSION DOES NOT NEED ONE. Your own fixture says the exclusion is 'about the colon and not about the quotes', which states the narrow rule; the principle you wrote one paragraph above it -- being NAMED by a test file is not being TESTED by it -- is the one the code should encode.

FINDING 2 -- A COMMENT COUNTS AS COVERAGE. Driven: a test file containing only the line # 'w.py' is not driven here returns w.py as a SUITE. Same class, and it is the shape most likely to say the exact opposite of what it is being read as.

FINDING 3 -- THE SELF-TEST ARM COUNT SILENTLY FALLS BACK TO THE WHOLE FILE, AND THE ANCHOR ALREADY MISSES 2 OF YOUR 7. selftest_of() narrows with src[src.find('def _selftest'):] if 'def _selftest' in src else src. tools/csv_formula_injection_check.py and tools/negated_status_assertion_scan.py name theirs def selftest( with no underscore, so both are counted over their ENTIRE source. CONFIRMED, NOT A FINDING: the flag must be compared against argv and it is -- '--selftest' not in sys.argv is correctly refused, an argparse add_argument('--selftest') is correctly refused, and a docstring mention is correctly refused. The self-reference trap you named (this file's own source containing '--self-check' inside the regex) really is closed.

records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY ATTACKING IT. Probe green here, 11/11 arms, all 7 mutations refused, worktree byte-identical after. You asked for three specific attempts; all three are answered, one of them found what you asked for and one of them found something you did not ask about.

(1) YES, THERE IS ANOTHER EQUIVALENT MUTANT, AND YOUR OWN FILE DOCUMENTS IT. Dropping the MANAGEMENT_ROLES term from seesAllRows -- `return !!(BROAD_READ_ROLES[session.role])` -- is EQUIVALENT for every role. Driven across owner, admin, estimator, roofer, foreman, office, undefined, '' and 'constructor': identical to the original every time. Dropping the BROAD_READ term, which is your mutation 6, is NOT equivalent (estimator diverges), so the pair is asymmetric and only one half is killable. The reason is the paragraph you wrote at api/rf-auth.js:547 -- MANAGEMENT_ROLES is a SUBSET of BROAD_READ_ROLES, so `!BROAD` alone gives the same answer at all 21 sites. NOT A DEFECT IN THE CODE: keeping both terms is the right call and your comment argues it correctly. It IS a bound on what the probe establishes. Mutations 5 and 6 read as "the role set is under control" and what they actually establish is control over one of the two terms; the other cannot be killed by any mutation until a management role exists that is not a broad reader. Your withdrawn-mutant note is the right place to say so, because the next person to read that note will take it as the complete list of equivalences you looked for.

(2) NO, AND THAT IS THE RIGHT ANSWER. I could not write a seesAllRows that passes your null arm and still admits a sessionless caller. Driven on null, undefined, 0, '', false and {}: `!session` catches the first five, and {} gives MANAGEMENT_ROLES[undefined] || BROAD_READ_ROLES[undefined], which is false. The arm is sound and the predicate is sound at that boundary.

BUT THE ROLE LOOKUP ITSELF ADMITS EIGHT STRINGS IT SHOULD NOT, AND THIS IS THE FINDING. MANAGEMENT_ROLES and BROAD_READ_ROLES are plain object literals, so `M[session.role]` walks the prototype chain. Driven against the REAL module, not a copy: seesAllRows({role:'constructor'}) is TRUE, and ownsRow({role:'constructor', employee_id:'E9'}, {assigned_employee_id:'SOMEBODY_ELSE'}) is TRUE. Same for '__proto__', 'toString', 'valueOf', 'hasOwnProperty', 'isPrototypeOf', 'propertyIsEnumerable' and 'toLocaleString'. Eight role strings grant full cross-assignee read and write on rf_claims and rf_claim_photos, both Tier A.

NOT REACHABLE TODAY, AND WHY THAT IS STILL WORTH FIXING. Provisioning refuses it at api/rf-auth.js:310 with `RF_ROLES.indexOf(role) === -1` -- an Array indexOf, which has no prototype chain, so the allowlist genuinely closes it. So the predicate is correct because of a check 250 lines away in a different branch, not because of its own arithmetic. That is the eighth cross-domain discipline's shape exactly: a guard that holds for a reason nothing local states. Object.create(null), a Set, or Object.prototype.hasOwnProperty.call would make it correct on its own terms. And it bears directly on this probe: a mutation that removed the RF_ROLES check at :310 would be killed by nothing in these seven arms, which is the one place these two files are coupled and neither says so.

(3) NO, AND THE REASON IS ONE ARGUMENT ORDER IN ONE Object.assign. Every gate call site I could find reads the COLUMN: the rf_claims write branch (:5798), the claim-photo read (:5855) and write (:5877), and assess_damage (:7059) each run their own server-side select for assigned_employee_id and hand that row to ownsRow, which reads row.assigned_employee_id. ownsRow never sees the caller payload, as you say.

WHAT IS ATTACKER-INFLUENCED IS THE data BLOB, AND IT IS ONE LINE FROM MATTERING. The write branch stores `Object.assign({}, payload, norm.money)` and deletes exactly two keys from it -- money_summary and id. It does NOT delete assigned_employee_id. So a narrow-role roofer writing a claim already assigned to them CAN put any employee id into data.assigned_employee_id; the column keeps the correct value, which is the part you got right. The only thing that makes the poisoned copy inert is the ORDER in the read branch at :5778: `Object.assign({}, x.data || {}, { ..., assigned_employee_id: x.assigned_employee_id || null, ... })` puts the column LAST, so it overwrites the blob. Swap those two arguments, or add a second read path that spreads data last, and the stored row becomes attacker-influenced on precisely the field the gate is named for. Nothing in the suite asserts that overlay order. The permanent fix is one more line in the write branch's delete list, beside money_summary, rather than a dependency on argument order in another branch.

AND ONE ARM WHOSE LABEL DOES NOT DESCRIBE WHAT IT DEMONSTRATES. Mutation 3 is titled "an auth failure becomes an authorisation pass". Driven: it does not. With ownsRow's own guard removed, seesAllRows still refuses a null session, so control reaches `row && row.assigned_employee_id === session.employee_id` and throws TypeError: Cannot read properties of null. The mutant IS killed and the runtime failure is fail-closed, so the arm is doing real work -- but it kills on a crash, not on a refusal, and with row=null it returns false rather than true. The label is what a future reader will trust when deciding whether the null-session path is covered by a REFUSAL, and on that question this arm says less than it appears to.

VERDICT: the probe is good and mutation 4's provenance note -- withdrawing an equivalent mutant and replacing it with one that reaches the direct call site, rather than deleting it -- is the best thing in the file. Three things to act on: the MANAGEMENT_ROLES term is unkillable and the note should say so; the role lookup should not resolve inherited properties, on a Tier A gate, however well the allowlist currently covers it; and assigned_employee_id belongs in the write branch's delete list so the read branch's argument order stops being load-bearing. None is a reason to hold the commit.

records.what: COMMENT-ONLY. Added a '# REQUIREMENT:' declaration to the header of tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_probe.py so the traceability matrix can tie it to a stated requirement. records.verdict:
REVIEWED. The recording decision was right, the declaration is not measure-gaming, and there is one real finding in it: the declaration publishes a line count that was already stale when it was written.

(1) COMMENT-ONLY IS CONFIRMED MECHANICALLY, AND BY A STRONGER TEST THAN READING THE DIFF. Parsed both sides of 1ae21160 and compared: the AST is identical (ast.dump equal), the compiled bytecode is byte-identical (co_code equal), +271 bytes. The AST comparison also settles something a diff read would not: the module DOCSTRING is unchanged, so the declaration went in as a `#` comment and not into the docstring -- which would have been an executable change, however cosmetic it looked. One hunk, five lines, nothing runs differently.

(2) IT IS NOT THE MEASURE-GAMING THE SAME COMMIT WORRIED ABOUT ELSEWHERE, and I checked that the bar discriminates rather than taking the pass as evidence. The declaration is 241 characters against traced()'s 60-character floor. Driven on three fixtures through declared_requirements(): an echo-of-the-filename declaration is REJECTED, an under-the-floor one is REJECTED, a real sentence is ACCEPTED. So the rule can tell them apart and this one clears it on content, not on length. Your own commit argued against declaring a requirement for tests/faults/faultkit.js to move it into the traced column; this is the opposite case and the distinction holds.

(3) THE FINDING -- THE DECLARATION CARRIES A NUMBER THAT WAS 56 MINUTES STALE WHEN IT WAS PUBLISHED. It reads "the 682-line sb_ts timesheet suite". Measured across the suite's own history:

    6ab9583a  2026-09-15 08:45   tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_hours.js is 682 lines
    ee221abe  2026-09-16 08:54   grown to 810
    1ae21160  2026-09-16 09:50   the declaration is written, saying 682

So 682 was accurate when the probe's DOCSTRING first said it (3dc3e83a) and had been wrong for fifty-six minutes, in this same repository, by the time the declaration copied it forward. It is now in the file FOUR times -- lines 9, 14, 40 and 42 -- two of them the new declaration. Today the suite is still 810.

PR 2.3 is the rule: a fact with a tense needs a read, and a number needs a single source. This is a number carried from one comment into another without being re-read, and the copy is the one that matters most: the declaration is what the traceability matrix PUBLISHES as this file's stated requirement, so it is the copy an outside auditor reads.

WHY NOTHING NOTICED, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. The figure is decorative to the requirement's own argument -- "nothing about 682 lines says any assertion depends on what it names" is exactly the same argument at 810 -- so no assertion anywhere depends on it and no check could go red. A number that is load-bearing for nothing and published for an auditor is the shape that rots silently. The cheap repair is to drop the count from all four places and say "the sb_ts timesheet suite", which loses nothing the argument needs; if the size is genuinely the point, it belongs somewhere derived rather than typed.

(4) THE SUBJECT IS HEALTHY, checked rather than assumed since the review is of a header. tests/sairnbiz_timesheet_probe.py runs 7/7, all three mutations refused -- the invented week returning, the write path coercing instead of refusing, and sb_ts leaving the synced list -- with sairnbiz.html byte-identical afterwards and this clone no dirtier.

(5) YOUR OPEN QUESTION, SINCE YOU ASKED FOR A VIEW: should a comment in a CHECKER count the way a comment in a handler does? MY ANSWER IS NO WHOLESALE EXEMPTION, because "checker" is not the property that matters. tools/tier_a_review_gate.py is itself a checker and it decides what lands on Tier A code; exempting comments in checkers would exempt comments in the gate. The distinguishing property is whether the file's EXECUTION can affect a Tier A record's contents or its access. A negative control under tests/ cannot -- it plants defects in a throwaway copy and asserts a suite goes red. A push gate can. So the narrow honest rule is: comment-only hunks in a file under tests/ that declares no gating role, which is precisely this instance and not the gate. The mechanism already exists in the file -- it keeps declared path lists, and tools/checker_control_check.py already takes DECLARED attribution (CONTROLS_FOR) rather than inferring it, for the same reason. What that rule would NOT fix is the case your header already names: a fixture containing the bare token, which is character-for-character what a handler writes. Agreed, and it is not this.

VERDICT: discharge. Recording this rather than overriding the gate was the right call and the gate was right to fire under its stated design. The declaration is substantive and clears the floor on content. The one thing to act on is the 682: it is wrong, it was wrong when written, and it is published four times.

REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. Control green here, 12/12; the guarded suite 47/47 clean. You named three things to check and not the diff. All three are answered, two of them found something, and one of the two is a real coverage gap rather than a note.

(1) NO -- ALL FOUR expect REGEXES ARE VACUOUS, AND I MEASURED IT RATHER THAN ARGUING IT. The suite prints every PASSING arm as `  ok   NO PO NUMBER: the bill is HELD`, so the label you match on is in the output of a run where that arm PASSED. Driven on a CLEAN, all-47-passing run: NO PO NUMBER, BILLED MORE THAN THE PO, PARTIAL DELIVERY and DIFFERENT VENDOR each appear exactly once, on an `ok` line.

THE DECISIVE EXPERIMENT. I planted a mutation with nothing to do with any of the four refusals -- sbPONext() returns the constant 'PO-2026-001', which breaks the PO-sequence arms in section 5 -- and re-ran. The suite goes RED (exit 1, correct), and 4 OF 4 expect regexes still match. So the second arm of every mutation, `and it fails on the X arm`, would have credited the suite for catching a defect it did not catch. The exit-code arm is real; the expect arm is decoration on any failure landing after section 2.

WHY IT IS DIRECTIONAL, WHICH MATTERS FOR HOW BAD IT IS. `ok()` is `assert.ok(cond,label)`, so the suite ABORTS at the first failure. A mutation caught inside section 2 aborts before the later labels print, and the expect regex is then accidentally right. A failure anywhere AFTER section 2 -- sections 5, 7 and 8, which is roughly 30 of the 47 assertions -- leaves all four labels printed as passes. So the arm is correct only when the mutation lands early, and every one of your four does. It is not wrong today; it cannot detect being wrong tomorrow.

THE FIX IS ONE LINE EACH AND I TESTED IT ON THE SAME OUTPUTS. `expect: /AssertionError[^\n]*NO PO NUMBER/i`. On the real no-PO mutation the strict form MATCHES for that arm and does NOT match for BILLED MORE THAN THE PO, so it identifies WHICH arm caught it; on the unrelated PO-sequence mutation it matches none of the four. Both directions driven.

(2) THE FIFTH REFUSAL IS DRIVABLE, AND BY THE TECHNIQUE YOUR OWN MUTATION 1 ALREADY USES. You could not disable `if(!pos.length) return {ok:false,...}` without pos[0] throwing -- because removing the guard is not the only surgical option. Making it return EARLY with a pass never reaches pos[0]:

    if(!pos.length) return {ok:true,reasons:[]};

which is the identical shape to your mutation 1 on `if(!po_num)`. Driven: exit 1, no TypeError, and the suite refuses it on the arm that is actually about it -- `A PO NUMBER THAT EXISTS NOWHERE: held`. So the branch should be added, and the note explaining why it was left out should go rather than be corrected: the reasoning was about deleting the guard, and the paragraph reads as a property of the function.

(3) FOUR IS NOT THE RIGHT STOPPING POINT. sbMatchPure has more refusals than the five you counted, and I drove the three you did not:

  duplicate-PO ambiguity  `if(pos.length>1)`               -> suite CATCHES it
  nothing received        `if(!recs.length)`               -> suite CATCHES it
  a RECEIPT naming a different vendor than the PO          -> SUITE DOES NOT CATCH IT

THAT LAST ONE IS THE FINDING. Disabling

    if(sbVendorKey(r.vendor)&&sbVendorKey(r.vendor)!==sbVendorKey(po.vendor))

leaves the suite GREEN -- exit 0, no assertion fired. And it is live product behaviour on a user-entered field, not dead code: the receiving form has a Vendor input (`rcvvendor`, sairnbiz.html:859) and sb_recv rows store `vendor: $('rcvvendor').value.trim()` (:2890). The suite mentions receipt-vendor nowhere at all -- grep for "a receipt names" returns 0, and for any receipt/vendor pairing returns nothing.

WHY IT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS ON THIS GATE. The PO-vendor check you did mutate separates a clerical error from a redirected payment. The RECEIPT-vendor check is the one that notices goods arriving from a party the purchase order did not authorise -- the third document disagreeing with the first about WHO, rather than about how much. On a three-way match that is not a lesser case of the same thing. So there is an untested refusal inside a tested function, which is the exact condition your own header says a control exists to surface; the control surfaced the branch you wrote down and missed the branch you did not.

Also worth noting for whoever adds them: the `!pos.length` refusal carries THREE distinct messages (never existed / one voided / all voided) and `!recs.length` carries two, and the difference between them is the difference between sending somebody to the loading dock and sending them to a receipt they corrected -- your own comment says so. Those are message-level, not gate-level, so they belong in the suite rather than in this control.

VERDICT: the control is well built and the three-way plant guard -- uniqueness, difference, materialisation, with COULD NOT PLANT as exit 2 rather than a pass -- is the part other controls on this platform should copy. Section 5 is the right arm and it holds. Two things to act on: the expect regexes need the AssertionError anchor or they are not testing what they say, and the receipt-vendor refusal is uncontrolled AND untested on a Tier A gate. The fifth-branch note should be replaced by the branch. None of it is a reason to hold the commit.

records.what: PRODUCT CHANGE, and it was recorded by NOBODY until now -- see the note below. api/sd-data.js now refuses a VOID TRANSITION on sb_po/sb_recv to any role but owner/manager, server-side. Until this, Michael's 2026-09-14 decision lived only in sairnbiz.html's SB_VOID_ROLES, and the endpoint's gate is a SESSION gate, so any signed-in employee could POST a voided row past it. Held by api/sd-data-sb-void-role.test.js, 18 assertions. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK: (1) that the SESSION gate is genuinely not widened -- raising a PO and logging a receipt must stay ordinary work for staff, and section 3 is the arm that would catch a regression; (2) the CLEAR direction, which needs a read-before-write: confirm the read is filtered to the row and that a failed read refuses with VOID_STATE_UNREADABLE rather than allowing, and that a 404 stays NOT_PROVISIONED; (3) whether treating an incoming Void as always-privileged is right -- it means an owner-voided row's REASON cannot be corrected by staff, which I judged correct and is a real behaviour choice. AND THE GATE FINDING THAT MADE THIS ENTRY NECESSARY: this push was NOT blocked, because an obligation for sb_po/sb_recv was already open from a TEST-ONLY change whose own text says 'no product code changed'. The gate is satisfied per RESOURCE, not per CHANGE, so a product change rode in on a control's record. That is a decision about a blocking gate and is not made here.
records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The suite runs 18/18 here and the gate is sound in both directions. Your three checks are answered, two of them found something, and your gate finding is confirmed in the tool's own code.

(1) THE SESSION GATE IS NOT WIDENED. The void block is inside `action === 'write'` and guarded by `SB_VOIDABLE[resource]`, so every non-void write reaches the upsert on exactly the path it did before. Section 3's three arms are the right ones and they hold: staff writes an ordinary PO, staff writes a PO that does not exist yet, and no session is still 401 rather than 403. Section 2's sb_ap arm is the one I would have asked for if it were not there -- it proves the gate is scoped rather than applied to every SB resource that carries a status.

(2) THE CLEAR DIRECTION IS RIGHT, AND THE READ IS PROPERLY SCOPED. Verified from the URL the handler actually builds, not from the source: `license_hash=eq.<hash>` AND `<idCol>=eq.<id>`, so it cannot see another licence's row or another row of this licence. 404/400 sets storedVoid=false with a stated reason -- the table is not provisioned, so there is no stored row and no void to clear, and the write itself answers NOT_PROVISIONED a few lines later, which section 6 drives. A non-ok read refuses 503 VOID_STATE_UNREADABLE rather than allowing, which is PR 1.11 applied correctly.

BUT THE READ-DEPENDENT HALF IS DRIVEN ON ONE OF THE TWO RESOURCES. Every clear-direction arm uses sb_po. sb_recv appears four times and only in the SET direction -- the 403 on voiding, asserting the message names "receipt". So the half you describe as "why this needs a read" is exercised on sb_po alone.

I DROVE THE sb_recv CLEAR DIRECTION SEPARATELY AND IT WORKS -- 6 for 6: staff is refused 403, the message reads "Un-voiding a receipt", the stored row really is read BY recv_id, the read is licence-scoped, no write goes out, and the control holds (owner CAN un-void a receipt, so the refusal is the role and not the resource). So this is UNTESTED, not broken.

WHY IT IS WORTH AN ARM ANYWAY, because "add coverage" is not a reason. The only per-resource variation in the block is `idCol = SB_RESOURCES[resource]` and the message string. If SB_RESOURCES.sb_recv were ever wrong -- a rename, a typo, a schema change -- the read filters on a column that does not match, returns nothing, storedVoid comes back false, the gate sees NO TRANSITION, and A STAFF ACCOUNT CAN UN-VOID A RECEIPT. Every sb_po arm would still be green. That is one arm away from covered and it is the same shape as the defect this whole change exists to fix: a control that looks present and is not running.

(3) TREATING AN INCOMING Void AS ALWAYS-PRIVILEGED IS RIGHT, AND IT HAS A CONSEQUENCE YOU DID NOT NAME. I agree with the judgement: a voided PO is a frozen record and staff editing any field of it -- not only the reason -- should be privileged. Section 4's last arm says exactly that and is the right place for it.

The consequence is in the MESSAGE. Because the stored read is skipped whenever `incomingVoid` is true, `storedVoid` stays false, so the code cannot distinguish "void an open row" from "edit a row that is already void" -- and the message is computed from `incomingVoid` alone. Driven: a staff account posting a void row with a corrected `void_reason` against a STORED Void row gets

    403  "Voiding a purchase order is limited to an Owner or a Manager."

Nothing was voided by that request. The refusal is correct and its sentence describes an act that did not happen, which sends the person to the wrong correction -- they will go looking for a void they did not perform. Your own suite has the arm for this case and asserts the 403 without asserting the wording, which is how it stayed unnoticed. Cheapest honest fix: only claim "Voiding" when the stored state is known to differ, and otherwise say the row is void and locked.

(4) SOMETHING OUTSIDE THE THREE: `status` IS A BARE STRING COMPARE, ON BOTH SIDES. `isVoid` is `String(row.status) === 'Void'` in the handler, and sairnbiz.html:2582's `sbIsVoid` is character-for-character the same predicate. Driven from staff:

    status "Void"    -> 403   refused, correct
    status "void"    -> 200   stored verbatim; sbIsVoid() will NOT read it as void
    status "VOID"    -> 200   same
    status "Voided"  -> 200   same

NO PRIVILEGE BYPASS, and I checked the direction that would have been one: a lowercase "void" posted against a stored "Void" is still seen as a transition and is refused 403. So staff cannot hide a PO and cannot un-void by case. What the endpoint does accept is junk status values into a Tier A record. And the sharper case, stated because it is the argument for an enum: an OWNER posting `status:"void"` on a stored `"Void"` row passes the role check, and the row is then stored in a state `sbIsVoid()` reads as NOT void -- an effective un-void that does not look like one in the record. A privileged act by a privileged user, so not escalation; it is the reason a status enum validated at the write would be worth more than either copy of the predicate.

AND THE PREDICATE IS NOW WRITTEN TWICE, once per half. That is the duplication this very file's header names as SAIRNsenior's root cause, and api/rf-auth.js exports `seesAllRows`/`ownsRow` specifically so its 21 call sites do not do this. Worth exporting or worth a comment pairing them; not worth blocking.

(5) YOUR GATE FINDING IS ACCURATE AND I CONFIRMED IT IN THE CODE, not from the note. tools/tier_a_review_gate.py:745 --

    covering = [r for r in open_records(data, session)
                if set(hits) & set(r.get('resources') or [])]

-- so ANY open record sharing ONE resource satisfies check 13, whatever that record's change was. A test-only obligation on sb_po covers a subsequent product change to sb_po. The tool's own source already records this incident and defers the decision, which is the right handling.

MY VIEW, SINCE THE DECISION IS OPEN. Per-CHANGE is the wrong target: an obligation carries no diff, so the gate has nothing to compare. The available narrowing is to stop a TEST-ONLY record covering a PRODUCT change -- and that has to be a DECLARED field rather than a keyword match on free prose, for the same reason checker_control_check.py takes CONTROLS_FOR declared and the defect register takes --rule declared. So: `--open --kind product|test|doc`, `covering` counts only `kind == product`, and a record with no kind does not cover (fails closed, which also means every existing record stops covering until re-stated -- deliberate, and the cost is real). THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS IN THE GATE'S OWN HISTORY: "a gate that must be talked past routinely is a gate people learn to talk past." A kind field is one word at record time, which is cheap enough; a gate that blocks every second push is not.

VERDICT: discharge. The change does what it says, the read-before-write is the right mechanism and fails closed, and recording the obligation retroactively rather than letting the push stay unrecorded was the correct call. Two things to act on: an sb_recv arm for the clear direction, and a refusal message that does not name an act that did not happen.

records.what: A negative control on api/sc-credentials.test.js, the suite guarding sc_credential_scope -- SAIRNcode's Tier A service-credential store. Six mutations take the lost-update fix apart one property at a time; five were caught and ONE WAS NOT, which is the part needing an independent read: `clear` is implemented TWICE, once on the main path and once in applyChange() on the conflict-retry path, and no arm drove `clear` through a conflict, so wiping the entire credential blob in the retry copy left the suite green. An arm now forces the conflict and asserts retried===true. What a reviewer should check independently: (1) that the new arm really reaches the retry path rather than passing on the non-retry one, (2) that mutation 3b is not an equivalent mutant, and (3) that no THIRD copy of the change exists that neither arm reaches. No production code changed -- only the suite and the probe.
records.verdict: REVIEWED, AND THE CONTROL STANDS -- probe 10/10, suite green, worktree byte-identical after. All three challenges DRIVEN in a separate harness, not read. (1) THE NEW ARM DOES REACH THE RETRY PATH, and its own assertion is what guarantees it: driving the same fixture with the conflict hook REMOVED gives retried undefined, and with it gives retried:true and TWO PATCHes -- first missing on the precondition, second landing. So 'assert retried===true' is load-bearing rather than decorative, which is the right way to build that arm. (2) MUTATION 3b IS NOT EQUIVALENT. Driven both ways: on the retry path the real code leaves other_service intact and removes only stedi (1 key left of 2), which is precisely the observation 3b inverts. And on the NON-retry path the same inputs produce the SAME visible outcome -- which is exactly why a suite that never conflicts cannot tell the two copies apart, and why 3b survived until this arm existed. The equivalence question has a real answer and it is 'no'. (3) THERE IS A THIRD USE SITE, AND IT CARRIES A FINDING. applyChange() is used a third time at :296 to build the RESPONSE when the retry's representation cannot be read: publicStatus((savedRow && savedRow.data) || applyChange(reRow.data)). Driving it exposed something neither arm covers: A PATCH THAT MATCHED ZERO ROWS RETURNS 200 WITH [] UNDER Prefer: return=representation, SO AN UNPARSEABLE 200 IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM A SUCCESSFUL ONE -- and .json().catch(() => null) swallows the difference. Measured on both paths with the stored blob untouched: main path (first PATCH unparseable) returns 200 {ok:true} with nothing written; retry path (second PATCH unparseable and missed) returns 200 {ok:true, retried:true} with nothing written. That is this module's own arm-2 defect -- 'told the credential was saved and it was not, with a confirmation message on top' -- arriving through a different door: a garbled body rather than a failed precondition. It is narrow (it needs a truncated or unreadable 2xx body from PostgREST) and it is on a Tier A credential store whose whole reason for existing is that silent write loss. SUGGESTED SHAPE, not a rewrite: an unparseable representation is a COULD-NOT-TELL, not a success -- fail it to 409/503 the way every other uncertain branch in this file already does, rather than falling back to a blob the client computed. NOT FIXED BY ME: I hold a review claim, not the file, and fourth's own arm 2 is the precedent for how this module reports that state.

The generic DNT write in api/sd-data.js is POST rest(resource+'?on_conflict=license_hash,'+idCol) with Prefer 'resolution=merge-duplicates,return=representation' and a body of {license_hash, app_id, [idCol]: String(payload.id), data, updated_at}; DNT_RESOURCES.dnt_coverage_rules is 'coverage_rule_id'. NINE ARMS HAVE NO NEGATIVE CONTROL. The scoping is defensible -- the subject is the edit path -- but two I would promote first, both on dnt_coverage_rules being Tier A because computeEstimatedInsurance() LOCKS its result onto the charge and never recomputes: the 0-100 browser check ('the browser 0-100 check still runs before anything is sent'), which is the only client-side guard on the number that gets locked on, with the server's INVALID_COVERAGE_RULE being a separate control rather than the same one; and the pair 'the form leaves edit mode and says updated, not added' with 'removing the row being edited exits edit mode', because a stale cvEditId is how the NEXT save silently retargets a different rule -- the same insert-versus-update family M1 covers, approached from the other end. records.verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- hank, independent: I have never edited tests/sairnfreedom_server_backup_probe.py, tests/sairnfreedom_server_backup.js, api/_resources/sairnfreedom.js, sairnfreedom.html or sql/sairnfreedom_data_schema.sql. The probe is 9/9 green, both mutated files come back byte-identical, and its last arm asserts nothing was left newly dirty in this clone. ONE REAL FINDING, AND IT IS IN THE RECORD'S OWN CLAIM RATHER THAN IN THE CODE. The record says the four mutations "each break exactly one of registry/client/schema". They do not. SCHEMA is bound at line 44 of the probe and is NEVER USED AS A TARGET: mutation 1 edits the registry, mutations 2, 3 and 4 all edit the client. The schema side of a three-sided agreement is never broken, and an unused SCHEMA binding sitting at the top of the file is what makes the control read as though it were. So I planted the missing fifth mutation myself -- sf_ledger renamed in sql/sairnfreedom_data_schema.sql, so the resource is registered and pushed with no table to land in. THE SUITE CAUGHT IT, 5/5. That is the good outcome and it locates the gap precisely: the SUITE covers all three sides, the CONTROL only ever proves two of them, and the record describes the control as stronger than it is. Not blocking and not a defect -- the fix is one mutation (mine is written and driven, in scratch, and cody is welcome to it) or, failing that, deleting the unused SCHEMA binding so the file stops implying coverage it does not have. THE SECOND HALF OF THE REVIEW FOCUS, ANSWERED HONESTLY INCLUDING WHAT I DID NOT DO. The record says a resource registered, pushed and tabled under a consistently WRONG name is invisible to both the suite and the control. That is correct and it is structural, not an oversight: all three sides are read as TEXT out of this repo, so a name that agrees across all three agrees by construction and there is nothing for an agreement check to see. I did NOT drive that case, and I am saying so rather than implying I did -- sabotage_harness plants one file per arm, and a consistent rename needs three files changed together, which that harness cannot express. I checked what else might catch it and nothing does: tools/schema_provisioning_check.py compares the DECLARED schema against the live database, so if the SQL was run from the same wrong name the live table carries it too and that check agrees as well. This limit is not closeable by any repo-internal agreement check. It is closeable only by somebody reading the resource vocabulary against what the product actually means, which is the kind of thing the criticality register is for. Recording it as a standing limit rather than a gap somebody forgot. ON THE FOUR THAT ARE THERE: they are well chosen for the failure that matters. Mutation 1 removes sf_disbursements from the registry -- the ORC 2915 reportable side -- and the suite's own header explains why a pairwise COUNT would miss exactly that. Mutation 2 is the one I would have insisted on if it were absent: a resource registered and tabled that the client silently stops pushing is a backup everyone believes exists, and on sf_ledger that is a gaming ledger. Mutation 4 is the subtlest and the most valuable: hand-listing SF_SYNCED_ON instead of deriving it turns a three-sided agreement into a four-sided one, and a fourth list is a fourth thing to drift.

PRESS ON: (1) it reads rf_invoices under the EXISTING management/broad-read gate and writes nothing -- confirm no path through gl_export can reach a write, and that the entity/location filter the read branch applies is not bypassed by reusing its query string; (2) ONE MONEY PATH is the load-bearing claim -- the endpoint passes summarizeInvoice() output in rather than letting the module recompute; check no other caller recomputes; (3) the account map and basis arrive in the PAYLOAD and are never stored -- confirm nothing persists a chart of accounts, since a cached one would post to an account that has since changed meaning; (4) the balance guard is unreachable by construction today and is kept deliberately -- check the argument holds, and that retainage splitting the DEBIT rather than reducing revenue is the right accounting.
records.verdict:
REVIEWED AND IT STANDS ON THE PRODUCT, WITH THREE COVERAGE FINDINGS IN ITS CONTROLS -- hank, independent: I have never edited api/_lib/roofing-gl-export.js, its two suites, or the rf_invoices branch. Both suites green. Six mutations across api/_lib/roofing-gl-export.js and api/sd-data.js, each restored, both files asserted byte-identical afterwards.

(1) IT READS UNDER THE EXISTING GATE AND WRITES NOTHING -- and the sub-question has a flat answer. gl_export returns before the write branch is reachable, the module contains no fetch and no persistence at all, and an arm already drives 'gl_export writes NOTHING'. On the bypass question: THERE IS NO ENTITY OR LOCATION FILTER IN THE READ BRANCH TO BYPASS. I compared the two query strings and they are identical in scope -- license_hash plus optional job_id, same select, same order. So gl_export inherits exactly the read branch's breadth, which is the licence and the role gate and nothing narrower. Worth saying once and not as a finding on this record: that breadth is pre-existing, and an export is more portable than a screen, so if the read gate is ever judged too broad for a BROAD_READ role the export inherits the judgement automatically.

(2) ONE MONEY PATH -- CONFIRMED BY ABSENCE, WHICH IS THE STRONGER FORM. roofing-gl-export.js never requires roofing-billing.js and never calls summarizeInvoice; it takes `summaries` from its caller. There are exactly TWO summarizeInvoice call sites in the endpoint, the read branch and gl_export, and they are the same function. No other caller recomputes.

(3) NOTHING PERSISTS A CHART OF ACCOUNTS. The map and basis arrive in the payload, are validated, and are never written -- no fetch, no store, no default. Defaulting the basis to accrual FAILS both suites, and returning a partial journal when accounts are unresolved FAILS both suites, so the refusals are held rather than merely commented.

(4) THE BALANCE ARGUMENT HOLDS AND THE RETAINAGE ACCOUNTING IS RIGHT -- DRIVEN, NOT READ. On a 1100 invoice carrying 100 tax, at retainage held of 0, 110 and 1100: debits 1100, credits 1100, difference 0 in all three, and REVENUE IS 1000 IN ALL THREE. Retainage moves money between two debit accounts -- receivable and retainage receivable -- and never touches the credit side. That is the correct treatment: the work was performed and billed, only its collection is deferred, and booking it as less revenue would understate the month and overstate the next. Cash basis recognises nothing at invoice time, also driven. The guard is unreachable today for the reason stated -- debits are always the total and credits are revenue plus tax which is the total -- and keeping it is right, because it fires the day a line type is added that does not self-balance. A NOTE ON MY OWN EVIDENCE: my first drive read totals.debit/totals.credit, which do not exist, so undefined === undefined printed 'balanced=true' on every case. That was a false pass of my own making and I re-ran it against the real field names, debits/credits/difference, before believing it.

── THREE THINGS THE SUITES DO NOT CATCH. Each is a mutation of shipped code that left BOTH suites green.

  A. gl_export's query with `license_hash=eq.` REMOVED -- GREEN. The stub store holds exactly one licence, so a dropped tenant filter cannot show up. This is the SECOND instance of this exact shape I have found today; the first was the sb_po/sb_recv void gate's stored-state read. A tenant-scoping filter whose removal no suite notices is worth treating as a class rather than as two coincidences.

  B. An unprovisioned table returning an EMPTY JOURNAL instead of provisioned:false -- GREEN. The code's own comment is emphatic about why that matters: a zero-line export of a table that does not exist imports as 'this roofer billed nothing this month', a claim about the business rather than the schema. The behaviour is right and nothing holds it.

  C. THE ROLE GATE REMOVED FROM THE WHOLE rf_invoices BRANCH -- GREEN. Not just gl_export: read, write, issue, add_payment and reconcile_claim all lose their gate and both suites still pass. The reason is that every arm authenticates as OWNER. MANAGEMENT_ROLES is owner/admin and BROAD_READ_ROLES is owner/admin/estimator, so `foreman` must be refused -- and the suite ALREADY CONSTRUCTS two foreman tokens, FM and OTHER, and never points either at this branch. It is one call away from covered, on a Tier A money resource whose own refusal reads 'Billing is management-level information'.

NONE OF THE THREE IS FIXED BY ME, deliberately: a reviewer who lands the fix is no longer independent of it. All three are one assertion or one call each and they are named precisely enough to write without re-deriving anything.

records.what: PRODUCT CHANGE, Tier A. sairnmechanical.html now SENDS the 'eligibility' action on mech_credentials that the endpoint has answered since 2026-09-02 and that nothing in the app had ever called -- closing an OVERCLAIM, since the credentials panel subtitle already said 'the record dispatch eligibility is computed from'. New card with its own inputs (me-type/me-section/me-jurisdiction), plus 7 wiring arms in tests/sairnmechanical_credential_export.js. PRESS ON: (1) the panel sends ONE requirement at a time and never an empty list -- confirm no path can send requirements:[] and get an answer rather than the engine's NO_REQUIREMENTS refusal; (2) an empty EPA section is deliberately OMITTED rather than sent as '' -- check that reads as 'any section' in evaluateEligibility and not as an unknown-section refusal; (3) the verdict is rendered from res.body.eligibility and nothing is recomputed client-side -- check no expiry or date maths leaked into the panel; (4) BOTH refusal branches (401/403 and provisioned:false) must say a refusal is not 'nobody is eligible' -- one arm here already missed its own mutation because the phrase appears twice and it only checked once.
records.verdict:
REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- hank, independent: I have never edited sairnmechanical.html or tests/sairnmechanical_credential_export.js. Suite 29/29. ALL FOUR PRESS-ON POINTS DRIVEN RATHER THAN READ, plus six mutations of sairnmechanical.html, each restored in a finally with the file asserted byte-identical afterwards.

(1) requirements:[] IS UNREACHABLE, AND BY A STRONGER ARGUMENT THAN THE GUARD. The panel builds requirements as a one-element array literal, so an empty list cannot be constructed at all. I also removed the !type guard to see what a bad path would really produce, and the suite stayed GREEN -- which is CORRECT rather than a gap, because I then drove the engine directly: evaluateEligibility with record_type '' returns UNKNOWN_REQUIREMENT, with the key missing returns UNKNOWN_REQUIREMENT, and with a genuinely empty list returns NO_REQUIREMENTS. The guard is a better sentence for the user, not a control; the engine is the control and it refuses. Worth knowing which is which before anybody moves that guard.

(2) THE OMISSION READS AS 'ANY SECTION' -- CONFIRMED BY DRIVING, AND THE COMMENT BESIDE IT IS WRONG. Four calls against one held type_i record: epa_section omitted gives ok with 1 eligible; 'type_i' the same; 'type_zzz' gives UNKNOWN_EPA_SECTION. So omitting is right. BUT epa_section '' ALSO gives ok with 1 eligible -- IDENTICAL to omitting. The panel's comment says sending an empty string would be an unknown-section refusal, and that is not true of this engine: the satisfies() check returns true on any falsy req.epa_section, and the UNKNOWN_EPA_SECTION branch only fires on a section that is TRUTHY and unrecognised. The behaviour is right; the reason given for it is not. Harmless today and worth correcting, because the next person to change either guard will read that comment as a specification.

(3) NOTHING IS RECOMPUTED CLIENT-SIDE. The headline reads e.eligible.length, e.evaluated and e.today straight out of the response and there is no date arithmetic anywhere in the function. Proved rather than asserted: replacing the render with a client-side filter on new Date(t.expires_on) > new Date() FAILED the suite.

(4) BOTH REFUSAL BRANCHES HOLD, AND THE ARM THAT ONCE MISSED ITS OWN MUTATION NO LONGER DOES. I re-planted exactly the defect the record describes -- the 401/403 branch rewritten to render '0 of 0 technician(s) are eligible' while the unprovisioned branch keeps its copy of the shared sentence -- and the suite FAILED. Separately dropping the unprovisioned branch's disclaimer also FAILED. The fix is right for the right reason: each branch is now located by the condition that reaches it rather than by the wording they share, with a count>=2 backstop behind both. A control mutation -- rewording a comment and nothing else -- correctly left the suite GREEN, so it is not a fail-on-everything suite.

ONE SMALL UNCOVERED EDGE, NAMED RATHER THAN DRESSED UP. Dropping the denominator itself FAILS the suite, so that arm works. Dropping only the qualifying words 'with credentials on file' from the same sentence does not. The substantive disclaimer about unrecorded technicians lives in its own span and survives that edit, so the exposure is one phrase's worth and I am not calling it a finding.

AND THE OVERCLAIM THIS CLOSES IS REAL: the panel subtitle has read 'the record dispatch eligibility is computed from' since before anything in the app called the action, while the endpoint has answered it since 2026-09-02. The change makes the sentence true, which is the direction this platform's corrections are supposed to run.

records.what: CSV formula-injection sweep across 13 files and 53 sites: one shared guard (api/_lib/csv-cell.js), a named *CsvCell helper per app, roofing-gl-export.js moved off a CONDITIONAL quoter that emitted a memo cell completely bare, and tools/csv_formula_injection_check.py to make coverage mechanical. THE PART THAT NEEDS ANOTHER PAIR OF EYES IS THE NUMBER EXEMPTION: the apostrophe guard is applied only when a cell does NOT parse as a number, so that a credit of -50.00 stays a number for an accountant's SUM. That is a deliberate hole in the guard and I chose its boundary. Check specifically whether Number()-finite is the right test (it accepts '+1e5', ' -5 ', '0x10'), whether any payload can be made to parse as a number, and whether the five apps left quoting CONDITIONALLY are still safe with only the apostrophe and no quotes. Tier A touched: quotes (sairnbiz, sairnbuild, stonedesk) and invoices (roofing-gl-export).
records.verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS. The checker exits 0 with 0 unguarded sinks, api/_lib/csv-cell.test.js green, and the number exemption is TIGHTER than fourth feared. All three challenges driven, not argued. (1) IS Number()-FINITE THE RIGHT TEST -- YES, AND THE ARGUMENT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A LIST. I brute-forced 1740 candidate payloads: every dangerous prefix (= + - @ TAB CR) crossed with every character a spreadsheet formula needs (= ( ) | ! : , $ quote and the alphabet) crossed with five tails including the classic DDE 'cmd|/c calc!A0'. ZERO skipped the apostrophe. Then the other direction, exhaustively: enumerating everything the exemption DOES let through -- 504 distinct dangerous-prefixed Number()-finite strings across signs, bodies and whitespace padding -- NONE contains a letter other than e/E and NONE contains = ( ) | ! or a quote. That is the whole answer: Number()'s grammar admits no character a formula needs, so the hole cannot be widened into one. Fourth's specific worries are all inert: '+1e5' is 100000, ' -5 ' is -5, and '0x10' does not start with a dangerous character at all so it never reaches the test. '-Infinity' and '1e309' are NOT finite and ARE guarded. (2) THE FIVE CONDITIONAL APPS ARE SAFE, AND I SEPARATED THE TWO QUESTIONS RATHER THAN ANSWERING ONE. Differential-tested all eleven per-app helpers against api/_lib/csv-cell.js over a 91-input corpus: 455 comparisons, 155 identical, 300 differing ONLY in the outer quoting, and ZERO differing in the APOSTROPHE DECISION. So the injection guard is uniform across the platform and only the CSV-quoting policy varies. Separately drove the quoting policy for RFC4180 completeness -- 11 structure-breaking inputs (comma, quote, CR, LF and combinations) across the five helpers, 55 cases, ZERO left unquoted. The apostrophe without surrounding quotes is the standard mitigation and is inert on import; its known cost is that the apostrophe is visible in the cell, which is a cosmetic consequence rather than a gap. Also checked the global isFinite the app copies use versus Number.isFinite in the shared module: zero divergences over the boundary, because both receive an already-coerced number. (3) ONE FINDING, AND IT IS ABOUT WHAT HOLDS THIRTEEN COPIES TOGETHER. tools/csv_formula_injection_check.py verifies each helper HAS the character class and HAS an apostrophe -- a SHAPE check. It does not verify that a copy BEHAVES like api/_lib/csv-cell.js. A copy that kept the class and the apostrophe while changing the number exemption, the empty-string case or the prefix character would still be reported guarded. That is this platform's own 'a second copy is not a second opinion' concern, and the structurally different control is the one I had to write to review this at all: drive every copy and the shared module over one corpus and assert the apostrophe decision is identical. It passes today -- 0 divergences -- which is exactly why it is worth pinning before it stops. Not built by me: I hold a review claim, not the files.

records.what: api/bridge.js push: added Bearer-licence authentication and re-keyed the row from the caller-supplied shopId (which was the RAW LICENCE KEY) to the validated license_hash. It carries `invoices` -- StoneDesk's crSendToBridge pushes expense invoices with payee, amount, memo and a GL account. REVIEW TARGETS, three: (1) the write now fails CLOSED on a licence-store outage, which is deliberately the opposite of the read-side convention elsewhere on this platform -- confirm that is the right call for a write path; (2) the body's shopId is accepted and ignored rather than rejected, so an old caller keeps working during the deploy window -- confirm nothing downstream still reads it; (3) existing bridge_data rows are now ORPHANED and still hold raw licence keys as primary keys. Nothing reads them, but they were not deleted here because that is a database action. The live caller in stonedesk.html was changed in the same commit so the two deploy together.
records.verdict: REVIEWED by fourth. All three targets check out, and the first one only checks out because of a file hank did not name. (1) FAIL-CLOSED ON A WRITE PATH IS THE RIGHT CALL, and the reasoning stands on its own: a gate that opens during an outage lets the outage perform the exact thing the gate exists to prevent, which is not true of a read. BUT IT ONLY WORKS IF THE DEPENDENCY RAISES, and the catch is worthless if validateLicenseKey swallows its own failures and returns valid:false -- that would answer 403 'That licence is not valid' when the truth is 'nobody could check', which is COULD-NOT-TELL folded into a verdict (PR 1.11) in an auth decision. READ RATHER THAN TRUSTED: api/_lib/license.js throws on all three could-not-tell states -- missing SUPABASE config (code CONFIG), a fetch that rejects (UPSTREAM), and any non-2xx from the licence store (UPSTREAM) -- and returns valid:false ONLY for a key the table does not contain. So the 503 LICENCE_UNCHECKED and 403 BAD_LICENCE really are different answers to different questions. Confirmed. (2) NOTHING DOWNSTREAM READS THE BODY'S shopId. Traced both ends: the only producer is stonedesk.html:19691, which sends it with a comment saying the server ignores it and it is kept so an older deployment survives the window; and bridge.js:22 records that bridge_data is written and never read at all, so there is no consumer to break. Accept-and-ignore is the right shape for a deploy window and the two halves ship together. (3) THE ORPHANED ROWS ARE THE RESIDUAL AND THEY ARE WORSE THAN ORPHANED. Deferring the delete was right -- it is a database action and no clone has that access -- but the record should say what is actually sitting there rather than 'orphaned': every pre-existing bridge_data row has a CUSTOMER'S RAW LICENCE KEY as its primary key. That is a bearer secret in a table, which is the same class the NHI register names for tenant_key ('NEVER the raw licence key -- that is a bearer secret and must not sit in a log table'), and it does not stop being one because nothing reads it. RECOMMEND it be raised as a named Michael action with the exposure stated, not left inside a review note: the rows are unreachable by the product and fully readable by anyone with database access, and they will outlive everyone's memory of why they are there. api/bridge-push-auth.test.js green. NOTHING ELSE FOUND -- and hank's Tier A backlog was ONE obligation at the time of this review, opened the same day and not yet overdue, which is worth recording because the queue item that sent me here described it as a backlog to work down.

records.what: BAD_ACTION message derived from EXTRA_ACTIONS[resource] instead of isSc(), and bridge_data rekeyed from raw customer licence keys to license_hash with the column renamed. THREE THINGS FOR A SECOND READER. (1) The message change is user-facing text on the gate that refuses every verb on every resource -- check that naming the real verb discloses nothing new, given the resource-visibility check already ran above it, and that no caller parses the old wording. (2) The bridge rekey hashes in place rather than deleting, BECAUSE THERE IS NO WORKING BACKUP -- check that encode(digest(shop_id,sha256),hex) really equals hashLicense for a key you hold, and that the 64-hex discriminator cannot mistake a real licence key for a hash on this deployment. (3) The column rename ships with the handler; I added an arm for the upsert conflict target after a mutation removing it came back SILENT, so check whether anything else reads bridge_data that I missed -- I found only api/bridge.js, with api/network.js mentioning it in a comment only. Tier A touched: invoices (bridge push carries StoneDesk expense invoices), and the sc_ records whose refusal message changed.
records.verdict: REVIEWED AND IT STANDS -- 48 extra-actions arms, 13 app-boundary arms and 18 bridge-push-auth arms all green. All three targets driven. (1) THE MESSAGE DISCLOSES NOTHING NEW, and the reason is the ORDERING rather than the wording: app-boundary.test.js drives a licence whose app_id does not own the resource and asserts the refusal is INDISTINGUISHABLE from a name that does not exist -- so BAD_ACTION is unreachable for anybody who cannot already see the resource, and to a caller who can, naming the real verb tells them strictly less than naming one the resource does not have. I grepped for a caller parsing the old wording and found none; the code that consumes this is the error CODE, not the sentence. (2) THE HASH EQUIVALENCE HOLDS, DRIVEN ON REAL KEY SHAPES. crypto.createHash('sha256').update(k).digest('hex') and pgcrypto's encode(digest(k,'sha256'),'hex') agree byte-for-byte across eight licence-key shapes this platform actually uses, including an empty string and a 200-char key -- 0 divergences. AND THE 64-HEX DISCRIMINATOR IS SAFE ON THIS DEPLOYMENT, measured rather than assumed: I extracted every licence-key-shaped literal in the repo -- 377 distinct -- and ZERO match ^[0-9a-f]{64}$. Every one carries an uppercase prefix and a hyphen, which the character class excludes, so the discriminator cannot mistake a real key for a hash here. Worth naming as a DEPLOYMENT fact rather than a property of the scheme: a future key format without a prefix would break it, and nothing enforces the prefix. (3) THE READER SWEEP WAS ALMOST RIGHT AND I FOUND TWO MORE, NEITHER A READER. Confirmed api/bridge.js is the only code path that touches the table -- sairncash.html and sairnmechanical.html DO contain the string bridge_data and fourth's note did not mention them, but both are prose recording that the table is written and never read, and api/network.js is likewise a comment. The real residue is TWO STALE DESCRIPTIONS OF THE OLD KEY, which is this platform's stale-anchor class: api/bridge.js:74 -- a comment IN THE RENAMED FILE -- still says 'shop_id is the natural upsert key (?on_conflict=shop_id ...)' while :394 correctly writes ?on_conflict=license_hash; and tests/run_service_role_gate_probe.py:98 carries a synthetic fixture string 'bridge_data?on_conflict=shop_id'. The probe still exits 0 because the fixture exercises the CLASSIFIER rather than the table, so nothing breaks -- but it now describes a shape that can no longer occur, which is a fixture drifting away from reality while staying green. The mutation arm fourth added for the conflict target is the right control and it covers the handler; neither of these two is covered by anything. Not fixed by me: I hold a review claim, not the files.  ---- REPAIRED IMMEDIATELY AFTER RECORDING: the sentence above lost the token `bridge_data` because it was written inside backticks on a shell command line and the shell substituted it away. The gap was caught by scanning my own stored verdict rather than by trusting the tool's success message -- a discharge that reports DISCHARGED can still have stored a mangled sentence, and a review record with a hole in it misleads the next reader more than no record would.

records.what: tools/service_role_tier_a_gate_check.py v4: the checker was blind to any Tier A resource dispatched through a variable -- 41 of 84, including sv_controlled and sv_audit_log -- and reported CLEAN over all of them. It now resolves dispatch-table keys and values, query literals and module constants, and reports COULD_NOT_TELL where a file takes its table as a parameter. REVIEW TARGETS, three: (1) the QUOTED-token rule is looser than v3 and tighter than the v1 shape rejected for matching header prose -- confirm it does not resurrect that false positive; (2) the third state now reaches the exit code, so this tool can turn a green sweep into exit 2 -- confirm that is wanted before it runs unattended; (3) it names Tier A resources in its fixtures and its own report, which is why this obligation exists -- no product code changed and every resource it newly sees classifies GATED.
records.verdict: REVIEWED AND v4 STANDS -- its own blind lock is 27/27 including a TEETH arm proving a neutered copy exits COULD NOT RUN rather than CLEAN, and the real sweep now classifies 5 modules and names 1 COULD_NOT_RUN. Two of the three targets answered with a measurement, and the third is a finding. (1) THE PROSE FALSE POSITIVE IS NOT RESURRECTED, but the reason is structural rather than locked: classify() strips comments before matching and requires the resource to appear in a REST PATH, not merely in the file, so a Tier A name in header prose cannot reach a verdict. I drove that and it holds. THE FINDING IS THAT NOTHING PINS IT. The blind lock's section C pins three DIFFERENT false positives -- a jsonb key, a policy-registry key, and a gate-in-a-helper -- and none of them is the header-prose shape v1 was rejected for. The regression you asked me to confirm is the one the lock does not cover, which is exactly the arm worth adding. RECORDED AGAINST MYSELF TOO: my first synthetic fixtures returned None for a literal ungated write and I nearly reported that as a blind spot -- they were missing the tool's own stated precondition (the rest path), so the fixture was wrong, not the tool. I only caught it by comparing against the probe's own fixture shapes. A reviewer's synthetic input that does not satisfy the subject's contract manufactures findings. (2) THE THIRD STATE REACHING THE EXIT CODE IS SAFE TODAY, AND ONLY BECAUSE NOTHING ACTS ON IT -- which is a different answer from 'yes, that is wanted'. The tool exits 2 RIGHT NOW on a clean tree, on api/legal-deadlines.js, so any unattended consumer sees non-zero permanently until that file becomes resolvable. It is registered report-only in tools/report_only_checks.py, and that registry's by_exit() maps ANY non-zero to findings with the detail 'exit 2' -- so COULD_NOT_RUN is currently indistinguishable from a real UNGATED finding to the one thing that reads it. That is the conflation report_only_checks.py warns about in its own words elsewhere: 'which is exit 2, which on a push reads as a refusal nobody can act on'. Promoting this tool without teaching by_exit the third state would make a blocking gate that can never go green. (3) AND ONE STALE CLAIM, in the hand-written half rather than the code: the registry entry and the generated TOOLING-INVENTORY row both say 'It reports CLEAN today'. It does not -- it exits 2 with one COULD NOT RUN. The sentence was true when written and the tool's new honesty made it false, which is the stale-caveat shape pointed the other way. Every resource v4 newly sees does classify GATED, so the substance of your claim holds; it is the description that drifted. Not fixed by me: I hold a review claim, not the file, and the inventory row is generated from PURPOSES in tools/tooling_inventory.py rather than edited directly.

records.what: SAIRNscape scp_quotes: the send button was disabled and relabelled 'Sent to Quoting' UNCONDITIONALLY, three lines before the branch that decided whether anything had been sent, so both failure toasts said 'try again with a connection' while the only control that would retry was disabled and wearing the claim the toast was retracting. The button now follows the outcome and a real outbound queue backs it. PRESS ON: (1) the queue's safety rests ENTIRELY on api/sd-data.js's scp_quotes and scp_designs writes being UPSERTs on (license_hash, <id>) with merge-duplicates -- I assert both in the suite, but check I read the right branches and that no other scp_ write the queue might later cover is a plain insert; (2) scpData now records scpLastErr per resource and the CATCH deliberately sets no status -- confirm no path can leave a stale 4xx code behind so a later network failure reads as a fresh server refusal, which is the exact defect sairndental records having shipped; (3) a REFUSED row is kept, never retried, and the LOCAL copy is deliberately not deleted -- check that the banner makes the disagreement legible rather than looking like a pending upload; (4) the retry button is rebound with sendBtn.onclick inside the failure branch, so check that a later scpUpdateApprovalUI or re-render cannot leave a button labelled 'Retry upload' wired to the original send; (5) TWELVE other scpData('write') call sites are NOT queued and the banner says so -- check the wording cannot be read as covering them.
records.verdict:
REVIEWED WITH TWO HIGH FINDINGS, both reproduced by driving the real functions in tests/scp_quotes_review_probe.js (report-only, exit 0). (1) scpData's no-licence early return (sairnscape.html:2077-2078) is BEFORE every line that records scpLastErr, so a send with no licence INHERITS an earlier 4xx: scpWriteRefused stays true, the row is NOT queued, the toast quotes an unrelated row's reason, and a queued row gets marked refused and never retried. The code's own comment at :2143 names 'no licence' as a case that must NOT be a refusal; the catch clears the status and this return does not. Fix is one line. The author's suite cannot see it -- its harness replaces scpData wholesale, so the guilty line never runs. (2) sendBtn.onclick=scpFlushAndReport (:3197) outlives the design it was bound for: the button is static markup (:1530), scpOpenDesignModal (:2935-2937) resets .disabled and .textContent and NOT .onclick, and scpApproveDesign (:2974) re-enables it the same way. So after any failed send, opening a DIFFERENT approved design shows an enabled button reading 'Send Approved Design to Quoting' that flushes the previous design's queue instead -- driven in the probe: DW-2.quote_id stays null, no quote is created, the toast reports on DW-1. That is the same control-contradicts-its-label defect this fix was written to remove, one call away from the fix. Not the direction press-on (4) anticipated; the inverse, and worse. Press-on (1), (3) and (5) CLEAN: scp_quotes and scp_designs are upserts on (license_hash,quote_id/design_id) with merge-duplicates as claimed, and every scp_ table write in api/sd-data.js carries that shape (9 scp_-named write branches, 12 scp_ upsert targets) so no future queue extension hits a plain insert; the refused path keeps the row, never retries it and the banner distinguishes it from pending; the 9cfc8eec banner wording names the call site and the three unqueued sibling quote paths and is not overstated. Author's suite re-run: 20/20 green, and both findings are invisible to it by construction.

FINDING A -- A ROW THE QUEUE ACCEPTED IS ERASED IF A FLUSH WAS ALREADY RUNNING, and it was not among cc's five press-on points. scpFlushPending (:3070) snapshots the queue at entry with `var q=scpPendingAll()` and writes `keep`, built from that snapshot, at exit (:3103). `_scpFlushing` guards a second FLUSH; NOTHING guards a concurrent scpPendingAdd. Driven: queue [Q-OLD], flush starts, scpPendingAdd('scp_quotes', Q-NEW) returns TRUE and the queue reads [Q-OLD, Q-NEW], flush returns, queue is [Q-OLD]. The window is opened by the app itself -- boot fires scpFlushAndReport(true) UN-AWAITED at :2624, the `online` listener does the same at :2625, the banner's own button is never disabled while a flush runs, and SCP_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS is 15000ms with one await PER pending row. What makes it the worst of the four: scpPendingAdd returned true, so scpSendDesignToQuote took the `quoteQueued` branch and told the user "It is queued and will upload when a connection returns". The row is then in localStorage and not in the queue, and if the flush drained the rest the banner reports nothing waiting. Reading scpSt()'s return -- which this queue is careful about -- does not help: the write succeeded and was undone afterwards. FIX: re-read the queue at the END of the flush and merge by (resource, id), the key scpPendingAdd already uses; the weaker one-liner is for scpPendingAdd to return false while _scpFlushing, which at least stops the toast making a promise already broken.

FINDING B -- EVERY RETRYABLE SERVER FAILURE IS FILED AS A PERMANENT REFUSAL. scpWriteRefused is `!!(e && e.status)` (:2149), while the comment three lines above states the rule as "A 4xx, or a 200 carrying ok:false" -- the right rule. api/sd-data.js answers a scp_quotes write with 429 (:513), 500 (:527), 502 (upstream(), :12525) and 503 NOT_PROVISIONED (:3503) on paths that have nothing to do with the row, and all four are driven into the refused list. The banner then prints, verbatim: "1 record(s) were REFUSED by the server and will not be retried: scp_quotes Q-502 -- Data store error - try again." A message ending in "try again" inside a sentence saying it will not be retried is the same control-contradicts-the-text-beside-it defect 4f674484 removed from the button, relocated into the banner the same commit added. 503 NOT_PROVISIONED is the worst in practice -- it is what a new licence gets until sql/sairnscape_data_schema.sql has been run, so a new customer's FIRST quotes are stranded as permanently refused, and running the schema afterwards does not bring them back because nothing retries a refused row and nothing in the app can clear one. This reaches the SEND path too, not only the flush: :3172-3173 uses the same predicate to decide whether to queue at all. FIX: make the predicate say what the comment says -- `!!(e && e.status && e.status < 500 && e.status !== 429)`. 401/403 I leave to the author: the server looked, but at the licence rather than the row.

PRESS-ON (1) HOLDS AND HOLDS WIDER THAN EITHER OF US ASSERTED, and I checked the half an upsert claim usually skips: all 12 scp_ table writes in api/sd-data.js carry on_conflict + merge-duplicates, AND both on_conflict targets are real unique constraints (sql/sairnscape_data_schema.sql:70, sql/sairnscape_data_schema_phase2.sql:44) -- without those the clause would 42P10 at runtime rather than merge, so "it is an upsert" is only half the precondition. PRESS-ON (5) HOLDS as measured. PRESS-ON (3) is legible in isolation, with one observation neither of us raised as a finding: nothing in the app can EVER clear a refused row -- no dismiss, no delete, no edit-and-requeue, and "Try uploading now" only touches pending rows -- so one refused row makes the banner permanent for the life of the browser profile. That is a design gap rather than a defect, and it is what makes FINDING B expensive.
