The table is Tier A ('a claim sent to the wrong payer'), had read+write branches nothing ever called, and the resident selector in the HCBS modal was populated and never read -- so the write, whose contract requires resident_id, could not have been called. PRESS ON: (1) recording is on an EXPLICIT button, not on every route, to keep an append-only table free of exploration -- check that a biller cannot be left believing a determination was recorded when the write failed, and that alfRecordRoute's button states are exhaustive; (2) a REFUSAL is recorded with outcome:'refused' and a transport failure is NOT -- check alfRouteRecordable's code list (NETWORK, BAD_RESPONSE, HTTP_*) cannot miss a transport shape alfRoute can actually produce; (3) the whole result object is stored in data -- check nothing in it is PHI beyond what the table already holds, since alf_claim_routes rows carry resident_id and are management-read; (4) the id is 'ROUTE-'+Date.now()+random and the server 409s on reuse -- check two determinations recorded in the same millisecond cannot collide into a 409 the user reads as a failure; (5) prRenderRecorded runs on every panel render and is INDEPENDENT of the rules read beside it -- check a refused trail read cannot render as an empty trail.
records.verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21. The design calls the review asked for are all sound -- explicit-button recording rather than write-on-every-run, refusals recorded and LABELLED via outcome, the button following the outcome, and prRenderRecorded() called at the top of rPayerRouting() BEFORE the _prRules branch so an unreadable rule set cannot hide recorded determinations. Single write site (sairncare.html:3013), single read site (:3033), append-only enforced twice: the endpoint's 409 ALREADY_RECORDED plus 'grant select, insert' only and unique(license_hash, entry_id) at the DB, so no client path can edit or delete a row. THREE FINDINGS, none of which I fixed -- they are cc's to take or to reassign. (1) PRESS-ON 2 IS A REAL GAP AND I REPRODUCED IT AGAINST THE SHIPPED FUNCTIONS. alfRouteRecordable() is a DENY LIST of three transport codes, but alfRoute()'s own contract is 'return the full body, success or refusal', so the body can carry ANY code api/sd-data.js emits -- and upstream() emits NONE AT ALL. Extracting alfRouteRecordable/alfRouteOutcome verbatim by line range from sairncare.html and driving the nine bodies the route branch can actually return: NETWORK, BAD_RESPONSE and HTTP_* are refused as intended, and FOUR shapes where the engine never judged are still offered a Record button -- 401 NO_SESSION, 403 FORBIDDEN, 503 NOT_PROVISIONED, and 502 upstream() whose body is {error:{message}} with no code, so code resolves to '' and falls straight through. alfRouteOutcome() labels all four 'refused'. Three are contained BY ACCIDENT rather than by the guard (the alf_claim_routes write is gated on the same session and role, and NOT_PROVISIONED means the same SQL file did not run), but 502 is NOT contained: a PostgREST error on the alf_payer_rules read with alf_claim_routes healthy writes a PERMANENT append-only row asserting a billing determination of 'not routed' for that resident and service month, which is exactly what the function's own comment says must never happen. A deny list cannot enumerate codes that do not exist yet; the shape that closes it is an ALLOW list of the engine's determination codes, or stamping the HTTP status onto the body in alfRoute() and requiring 200 -- the engine only judges on 200. (2) THE FAILURE TOAST ASSERTS MISSED WHERE THE TRUTH IS UNKNOWN. alfData() collapses a 15s AbortSignal.timeout, a 409, a 503 and a real network error all to null, and alfRecordRoute()'s else branch says 'NOT recorded -- the determination did not reach the server. Nothing was saved; try again with a connection.' On a timeout the row may well have landed; the biller presses again, Date.now() mints a different id, and the append-only Tier A trail gets TWO rows for one determination with nothing marking the duplicate. This is the WROTE/MISSED/UNKNOWN vocabulary cc introduced for sd-data's soft-delete in the same batch of work, not applied here. Cheapest honest patch: call prRenderRecorded() in the else branch too, so the trail itself answers the question, and say UNKNOWN rather than 'Nothing was saved'. (3) PRESS-ON 5 HOLDS FOR A REFUSED READ AND FAILS FOR AN UNPROVISIONED ONE. The read branch answers 404/400 with {ok:true, data:[], provisioned:false} -- the server knows the table is not there and says so -- but alfData() returns d.data and DROPS the provisioned flag, so prRenderRecorded() sees [] and renders 'No routing determination has been recorded yet ... press Record this determination to enter it in the trail.' A table that does not exist reads as a billing trail that is merely empty, which is the same wrong conclusion press-on 5 asks about, arriving by a different route. PRESS-ON 1, 3 AND 4 CHECK OUT AS WRITTEN. Button states are exhaustive on the path that can reach them -- disabled+'Recording...', then 'Recorded' and left disabled on success, then re-enabled with the ORIGINAL label on failure, so no stale 'Recording...' and no button claiming what the toast denies. On PHI: the server deletes id/resident_id/service_month from the blob and stores the rest, so data carries outcome, program, the whole result and the whole inputs -- and for hospice, inputs carries hospice_principal_diagnosis and claim_principal_diagnosis, raw ICD codes, which IS PHI beyond what the table already held. I am accepting it rather than flagging it as a defect: the read is gated to ALF_MANAGEMENT_ROLES (owner, billing), a diagnosis is the basis of the determination and the thing a claim actually carries, so minimum-necessary is satisfied for a billing role. What I would change is that it is UNSTATED -- neither the schema nor the endpoint comment says the blob may carry diagnoses, and storing result and inputs WHOLESALE means any field the engine or a future modal adds lands in a management-read Tier A table without anybody deciding. On the id: ROUTE-Date.now()-random(1000) collides only if two browsers record within the same millisecond AND draw the same 1-in-1000 value, the server 409s rather than overwriting, and a retry mints a new timestamp, so the outcome is a misleading toast and not a lost or corrupted row -- which is finding 2 again rather than a separate defect. Nothing blocking was found; the trail records real determinations correctly today.

I REVIEWED THIS MODULE ON 2026-09-17 AND HAVE NOW CHANGED IT, so this review must go to a session that has done neither. PRESS ON: (1) the bank-rec identity is bank = as_of - outstanding -- check the SIGN on a deposit in transit versus an uncleared cheque against a real statement, because getting it backwards makes both errors cancel on a fixture with one of each; (2) untracked clearance keeps the OLD comparison rather than nulling the leg, which is a judgement I reversed mid-change -- check the disclosure sentence cannot be read as an adjustment having been made; (3) money_conservation's status branch is LABELLED unreachable and a sabotage confirms it -- check the label is still true after your own reading, not just mine; (4) dayOf moved to the shared isCalendarDate -- check no caller depended on the old shape-only behaviour, particularly around statement_date; (5) the client reverts an unsynced clearance -- check the revert cannot resurrect a clearance somebody else cleared on another device, which is the shape the VOID path beside it had to solve.
records.verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against 5e0b531f and af8fc7e0. Two of the five press-on questions come back CLEAN and I drove both rather than agreeing with them; three findings, all reproduced against the real module or the real function, none fixed -- they are cc's. PRESS-ON 1 IS CLEAN AND THE FIXTURES CANNOT CANCEL. The identity is bank = as_of - outstanding with outstanding signed by transaction type, and both directions are right: an uncleared cheque is signed -4000 so expected_bank comes out ABOVE the books at 14000, and a deposit in transit is +6000 so expected_bank comes out BELOW at 10000. Driven, both agrees:true. cc's own worry was that a fixture with one of each would cancel a sign flip; it cannot, because the two arms are SEPARATE fixtures each carrying exactly one kind, and the cheque arm pins expected_bank_cents by value. A flip breaks both. PRESS-ON 3 IS CLEAN AND I RE-DERIVED IT INSTEAD OF TAKING THE LABEL. The money_conservation PARTIAL branch genuinely cannot fire today, and the reason is not only the one written above it: ledgerCents and the as-of loop skip on IDENTICAL predicates (isVoided, cents()===null), so the identity can break only on an undated row; an undated row nulls bank_vs_ledger.agrees; and because allocation_vs_ledger is structural:true there are only TWO non-structural legs, so `compared` falls to at most 1 and the next line catches it. That last step is load-bearing and the comment does not state it -- the label is true BECAUSE there are exactly two comparable legs, and adding a third makes the branch reachable, which is what the comment says it is being kept for. Worth writing into the comment; not a defect. FINDING 1, AND IT IS PRESS-ON 2 ANSWERED IN A FIELD cc DID NOT NAME. The `why` sentence for the untracked case is exemplary and cannot be misread. The `independence` field beside it, in the same leg object, is a FIXED STRING that always reads "compared AS OF the statement date and ADJUSTED for outstanding items" -- including when clearanceStated === 0, which cc's own comment says is every practice today because nothing has ever written the field. Driven: untracked run returns clearance_tracked:false, outstanding_cents:0, expected_bank_cents:10000 identical to ledger_as_of_cents, agrees computed by the OLD comparison -- and independence asserting an adjustment that was not performed. `independence` is the per-leg provenance field this whole file uses to say what a leg MEANS, so it is the one a consumer quotes. Press-on 2 asked whether the disclosure could be read as an adjustment having been made: the disclosure cannot, and the sentence next to it does. Fix is to make the string conditional on clearanceStated, the same way `why` already is. FINDING 2, AND IT LIVES EXACTLY WHERE ADOPTION HAPPENS. clearance_tracked is a BOOLEAN over a PER-ROW fact, and `why` is set to the empty string the moment ONE row states clearance. Driven with 200 rows, one marked cleared, and a genuine uncleared cheque among the other 199: clearance_tracked:true, clearance_stated_rows:1, why:"", outstanding_cents:0 with the real cheque not in it, expected_bank_cents 96000 against a bank really holding 100000, agrees:false, status DISAGREES. Correct books, a normal uncleared cheque, a false alarm, and the disclosure switched OFF by a single marked row -- the precise over-sensitivity this change exists to remove, surviving in the state every practice passes through on the way to tracking clearance. clearance_stated_rows is reported with NO DENOMINATOR: the leg emits no as-of row count, so a consumer cannot compute coverage either. The error direction is safe (an alarm, not a silence) and the disclosure gap is not, because the sentence that would explain the alarm is exactly what disappears. Fix: report the as-of row count beside clearance_stated_rows, and make the disclosure fire on PARTIAL coverage rather than only on zero. FINDING 3, PRESS-ON 5, AND THE ANSWER RUNS THE OTHER WAY. cc asked whether the revert can RESURRECT a clearance another device made. It cannot. It can ERASE one, and it can discard an entire concurrent hydration, and both are the same class confirmVoid() thirty lines away was hardened against -- with the hardening not carried across. confirmVoid does THREE things: it refuses up front if the record is already in the target state ("another device can void the same transaction between the render and the click"), it stamps its own change with myVoidedAt so the rollback can tell ITS OWN void from somebody else's, and it RE-READS the ledger after the await (`var revertList = trustTransactions()`) before writing anything back. Its own comment says re-reading "is necessary and is not sufficient". lawSetClearance does none of the three. It captures `list` and `t` BEFORE the round trip and calls st('law_trusttx', list) in the revert, so a hydration landing during the await is written away wholesale -- not one row, the entire array. It restores prevOn/prevFlag unconditionally with no check that the record still carries THIS call's clearance, so a clearance another device recorded during the round trip is overwritten by this device's pre-action value. Its only up-front guard is status==='Voided'; there is no already-cleared-elsewhere refusal. AND cc's OWN NEGATIVE CONTROL CANNOT SEE ANY OF IT: tests/sairnlaw_trust_clearance_probe.py is 8 arms and 4 mutations, all four about the rollback's CONTENT (restores the date but not the flag, stops restoring at all, voided rows may clear, outstanding becomes an absent field), and every fixture has one device in play. The concurrency shape is invisible to it by construction, which is the same thing that made the original defect survive. Suite 5/5 and probe 8/8 green, re-run here. TWO SMALLER ONES. (a) An unreadable cleared_on falls back to the boolean: clearedByStatement is (clearedOn!==null && clearedOn<=statement) || (clearedOn===null && cleared===true), so {cleared_on:'2026-02-31', cleared:true} is treated as cleared BY the statement date -- driven, outstanding_cents 0. The row asserts a clearance date the module refused to read and the contradiction is discarded rather than reported. The arm at test line 425 covers an unreadable cleared_on WITHOUT the boolean; the combination is uncovered. (b) `if (signed >= 0) outstandingDeposits += 1` puts a zero-amount row in the deposits bucket whatever its type. PRESS-ON 4 IS CLEAN WITH ONE DISCLOSURE GAP. The dayOf move to isCalendarDate is right and the statement filter is per-statement (s.date !== null), so one impossible statement_date drops only that statement and the rest still sort -- an impossible date can no longer become the as-of boundary, which is the whole point. But if the ONLY statement carries an unreadable date, the leg says "no usable bank statement on file", which a practice that uploaded a statement with a typo'd date cannot tell from never having uploaded one. Same third-state discipline the rest of this file keeps. ONE THING I CHECKED AND DROPPED, recorded because the near-miss is worth more than the conclusion: lawSetClearance tests only `if(!syncResult)` while confirmVoid also handles `syncResult.rejected`, which looked like a server refusal being reported as success. It is not -- sdnData mints the {rejected:true} shape for exactly three codes (INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE, VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE, ALREADY_VOIDED), none of which a law_trusttx clearance write can produce, so every clearance failure returns null and the truthy test is correct here. Nothing blocking: the outstanding-item model itself is right, the signs are right, and the engine reports more honestly than it did before this change.

No product code: sairnlaw.html is untouched and the control asserts byte-identity. Closes one of the 38 uncontrolled Tier A suites -- measured at 169/59/110 before, 60/109 and TIER A 37 after.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, and it is not the diff.

(1) THE ARM I ADDED IS THE INTERESTING ONE AND IT WAS ADDED BY ME AFTER MY OWN MUTATION CAUGHT IT SILENT. Mutation 2 plants a HALF-ROLLBACK -- cleared_on restored, the `cleared` flag left true -- and the suite passed. I then added `assert.strictEqual(r.cleared, undefined)` and it bites. That is the author writing the assertion that makes his own mutation pass, which is one step away from tuning the test to the mutant. Check that the assertion is right for a REASON and not just for the arm: I claim the end state is `cleared:true` with no `cleared_on`, that sairnlaw.html:3533 branches on cleared_on first and `cleared===false` second so the badge reads "not tracked", and that the stale true is pushed on the next unrelated write of that row. Verify that reading against the real render path and the real write path, because if the consequence is different the assertion may be right by accident.

(2) MY FOUR MUTATIONS ALL TARGET lawSetClearance() AND THE SUITE ALSO EXERCISES lawMarkCleared() AND lawMarkOutstanding(), WHICH I DID NOT MUTATE AT ALL. lawMarkCleared holds the date validation -- the suite's "a bad date changes NOTHING and says so" arm -- and nothing in this control disables that regex. Try it: if the validation can be made to accept 'last Tuesday' and the suite stays green, that is an uncontrolled branch on the field the reconciliation's own dayOf() drops, which is the undated-row hole arrived at from the other side.

(3) IS FOUR THE RIGHT STOPPING POINT. A mutation that moves the st() to after a successful sync would change the failure semantics and I do not know whether the suite would notice.

(4) THE ANCHORS. Mutations 1 and 2 share the same two-line rollback block and differ only in which line survives, so each anchor carries both lines. records.verdict: REVIEWED. The control is sound -- probe 8/8, four mutations all refused, worktree byte-identical after, suite 5/5 -- and the added assertion is RIGHT. But ONE OF THE TWO REASONS GIVEN FOR IT IS WRONG, which is exactly what you asked to be checked. DECLARED FIRST: I wrote sairnlaw.html's clearing path. You authored this obligation so the gate lets me discharge it, and my independence is over YOUR PROBE, not over the product it controls -- a second reader on the product half would still be worth having. (1) THE RENDER-PATH CLAIM DOES NOT HOLD. I drove the real branch from sairnlaw.html:3533 over four end states rather than reading the branch order. Half-rollback (cleared:true, no cleared_on) renders NOT TRACKED -- and so does a CORRECT rollback, which leaves neither field. They are INDISTINGUISHABLE on screen, so 'the badge reads not tracked' is not a consequence of the half-rollback at all; it is the same thing the correct state shows. The reasoning in the comment reads as if the badge were a symptom and it is not. THE OTHER REASON IS THE LOAD-BEARING ONE AND IT IS CORRECT: every write of that row sends the WHOLE record -- sairnlaw.html:3284 (void) and :3454 both do sdnData('write','law_trusttx',t) -- so a stale cleared:true survives in the row and the NEXT unrelated write pushes a clearance nobody ever applied to the server, where the reconciliation then adjusts the bank leg for an item that never cleared. That is the real consequence, it is money, and it is enough to justify the assertion on its own. So: right assertion, and it needs its reason narrowed to the write path rather than the render path. Not right by accident -- right for one of the two stated reasons. (2) THE UNMUTATED FUNCTIONS ARE A REAL GAP AND THE SUITE HAPPENS TO COVER ONE OF THEM. Your four mutations are all inside lawSetClearance and the probe names lawMarkCleared / lawMarkOutstanding zero times. I planted the obvious one -- removing lawMarkCleared's YYYY-MM-DD validation entirely -- and the SUITE CAUGHT IT, so that arm has teeth today. What is missing is the CONTROL, not the coverage: nothing proves the date arm keeps its teeth, so it is in exactly the state your probe exists to end, one function over. A fifth mutation on that regex would close it and costs one entry. (3) THE ARM-WRITING CONCERN YOU RAISED ABOUT YOURSELF IS THE RIGHT ONE TO RAISE AND I DO NOT THINK IT LANDED HERE. Writing the assertion that makes your own mutation fail is only tuning-to-the-mutant if the assertion has no independent justification -- and this one has the write-path consequence, which is checkable without reference to the mutation at all. The failure mode would have been an assertion phrased in terms of the mutation ('cleared must not be true after a failed write'); yours is phrased in terms of the end state, which is the stronger form.

records.verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against 8e3a18a2. THREE OF THE FIVE PRESS-ON QUESTIONS COME BACK CLEAN AND I ESTABLISHED EACH FROM A SOURCE RATHER THAN FROM THE CLAIM. PRESS-ON 1, the status code: 502 is right, and the argument is in this file already -- `upstream()` answers 502 when the data store's answer cannot be used, so WRITE_UNCONFIRMED is the same fact through the same door. 409 is wrong because this endpoint already spends 409 on WRITE_CONFLICT, whose message asserts "Nothing was saved" -- the one claim an unconfirmed write cannot make, and reusing the code would put two opposite statements behind one status. 503 is wrong because it means try again later, and a blind retry is the harmful action here. NO CLIENT BRANCHES ON THE STATUS: sairncode.html's scPostEndpoint returns {ok:false, status, error} and both callers (saveStediKey, clearStediKey) read only error.code and error.message, so the UNCONFIRMED sentence reaches the admin verbatim. ONE ARGUMENT AGAINST, NAMED RATHER THAN SUPPRESSED: 502 is 5xx and generic retry layers treat 5xx as retryable. Nothing in this path auto-retries today -- scPostEndpoint does not, and Vercel does not auto-retry POSTs -- so it is safe now and it is the thing to re-check if a retrying client or gateway is ever put in front of it. PRESS-ON 2, the 409: HOLDS, and from the SCHEMA rather than from the claim. sql/sairncode_credentials_schema.sql gives sc_credentials exactly one unique constraint, unique (license_hash, credential_id), one CHECK (which PostgREST answers 400, not 409), and NO foreign keys. So the insert-race unique violation is the only 409 this endpoint can receive and MISSED is correct for all of them. STANDING DEPENDENCY, worth a line in the code: the branch discards the 409 body (`writeR.status === 409 ? null : await writeR.json()...`), so the day somebody adds an FK or an exclusion constraint, 23503 and 23P01 also arrive as 409 and this cannot tell them from the race -- a non-retryable failure would be retried once and then reported as "another administrator is changing service credentials right now". PRESS-ON 3, REPRODUCED AND EXTENDED TO THE PATH YOU DID NOT TEST. Four mutations driven in a throwaway worktree against api/sc-credentials.test.js: dropping the FIRST-PATH UNKNOWN guard is SILENT, dropping the FINAL GATE is SILENT -- exactly the two you reported -- and dropping the RETRY-PATH guard IS CAUGHT. So the answer to your question is yes: the retry path is independently pinned, which it has to be, because it RETURNS before the final gate and nothing downstream could cover for it. The redundancy claim on the main path also holds and I traced it rather than inferring it from the pair result: with the first-path guard removed, firstSays is UNKNOWN, noRowsMatched is false, writeRows is set to the null firstRows, and `if (writeRows === null) writeRows = await writeR.json().catch(...)` re-reads an already-consumed body and gets null again, so the final gate sees UNKNOWN and refuses. With the final gate removed the first-path guard refuses. Genuinely mutually redundant, not unpinned. FINDING 1, AND IT IS THE ONE THAT OUTLIVES THIS REVIEW: THE 2026-09-18 CHANGE SHIPS WITH NO NEGATIVE CONTROL. All six mutations in tests/sc_credentials_probe.py are from the earlier concurrency and auth work -- the precondition, the zero-rows detection, `clear` on each path, the role check, the session check -- and the ONLY 09-18 edit to that file was RE-AIMING a stale anchor, which the record correctly treats as a repair rather than as coverage. records.verdict: REVIEWED, ALL THREE QUESTIONS DRIVEN AGAINST THE REAL HANDLERS, AND ONE HIGH FINDING THE QUESTIONS DID NOT COVER. Evidence: tests/sd_data_unconfirmed_write_review_probe.js, report-only, exit 0. (3) wroteRow's UNKNOWN on a non-array is NOT over-broad: driven across all six body shapes these paths can receive -- [row] 200, [] 404 MISSED, {} 502, {data:{}} 502, null 502, unparseable 502 -- and the object shapes are unreachable because PostgREST returns an array unless the caller sends Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json, which this file never does (measured: zero Accept headers anywhere in api/sd-data.js). Worth knowing that the safety is a property of a header nobody writes rather than of an assertion; adding one to a future branch would 502 every successful write on it. (1) 404 is RIGHT, and the case you were worried about cannot arise: the path READS FIRST, so a read miss 404s with ZERO patches attempted and an already-_deleted_at row returns 200 already_deleted with ZERO patches attempted -- both driven. MISSED is therefore reachable only in the TOCTOU window, present at read and absent at write, which is genuinely anomalous and 404 is honest for it; 502 would blame the store for answering correctly. The caller change is in the SAFE direction: stonedesk.html:2144 branches on done===null, so a MISSED now warns 'deleted on this device but NOT on the server' -- which for a TOCTOU miss is TRUE. (2) the dnt-bi 502 CANNOT fire on a legitimately empty table, driven rather than read: [] -> 200 with 0 rows, [{data}] -> 200 with 1 row, {} -> 502 READ_UNREADABLE, null -> 502, unparseable -> 502, and 404/42P01 -> 200 with 0 rows and provisioned:false. THREE states kept apart on a path whose recorded defect was collapsing them. === THE FINDING, WHICH IS ABOUT THE WORD 'SWEEP' === The commit says this was found by the platform sweep for .json().catch(() => null). FOUR MORE SITES IN THE SAME FILE HAVE THE IDENTICAL DEFECT and one of them serves SEVEN TIER A RESOURCES. api/sd-data.js:12422 is the SAIRNcode soft-delete for sc_ar, sc_claims, sc_compliance, sc_credential_scope, sc_denial, sc_denial_events and sc_revenue -- structurally the same code as the generic path you fixed at :9908, same read-then-PATCH, same Prefer: return=representation, same .json().catch, same !ok-only check, same res.status(200).json({ok:true}). DRIVEN SIDE BY SIDE: on sc_claims a zero-row PATCH returns 200 ok:true and an unparseable body returns 200 ok:true, while the branch you fixed returns 404 NOT_FOUND and 502 WRITE_UNCONFIRMED for the same two inputs. The other three: :4135 bld_draws RETAINAGE RELEASE, which is MONEY rather than a delete and hands the caller release_log:trail describing a release that may never have been written; :2404 sd_customers soft-delete, whose READ half was hardened on 2026-09-04 with the sentence 'saying deleted would be reporting work that did not happen' while the WRITE half twelve lines below it was not; :11257 dnt_supplies. WHY THE SWEEP MISSED THEM, which matters more than the list: .json().catch(() => null) matches 27 sites in this file and most are reads handling null correctly. The defect is the catch AND a representation PATCH AND an ok:true -- three conditions, not one string. Grepping the symptom returned a haystack and the two obvious needles came out of it. The predicate that separates them is in the probe. FIX is mechanical and identical at three of the four, with wroteRow() and refuseUnconfirmedWrite() already module-scope: add the UNKNOWN and MISSED branches. :4135 needs its own 404 sentence because it is a release, not a delete. records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT, on a structurally different route from the author's: fourth's endpoint mock COUNTS upserts, mine CAPTURES THE UPSERTED BODY, because the question the author's arms cannot ask is not "did a row reach Supabase" but "is the row that reached it the string the validator approved". It is not. The gate is sound in its refusals and I found no way past it; the findings below are about what it lets through, what it over-refuses, and two defects in the Tier A resource it names that are larger than the one it closes. Re-ran everything first: 15/15 unit+endpoint arms pass, six sairnlaw suites green (billing_codes, billing_codes_mutation_control, citation_rule, csp, hydrate, trust_clearance), node --check clean on both files.

ANSWERS TO THE AUTHOR'S FOUR QUESTIONS.

(1) THE REFUSAL TO CHECK MEMBERSHIP IS RIGHT, and the other reading is not merely less good, it is wrong in a way worth naming. An unverified list used as a REFUSAL is not "a weak gate", it is a gate whose errors land on valid work: a firm types a genuine UTBMS code the list has wrong and the server rejects billable time, with no path around it. An invented code, by contrast, lands in a column a human reads on an invoice. Those are not the same cost. Fourth's call stands. I considered and REJECT the obvious middle path -- a SHAPE check, ^[A-Z]\d{3}$, which looks like it asserts nothing about which codes exist. It does: it asserts the standard's format, and LEDES in practice carries firm-specific and suffixed codes. Adding it would be the same category of assertion the module correctly declined, arrived at by a route that hides that it is one. Do not add it without verifying the standard first -- at which point the membership check is the better tool anyway.

(2) THE 32-CHARACTER BOUND CANNOT REFUSE ANYTHING REAL IN THE SHIPPED VOCABULARY and the bound is inclusive as documented -- driven, not read: 32 chars writes (200), 33 refuses (400). But see FINDING 1: the number is measured on a string the handler does not store.

(3) LEAVING matter_id AND hours TO THE CLIENT WAS THE RIGHT SCOPE CALL, and the diff matching its own reason is worth more than the two extra checks. But the field fourth did not list is the one that matters most, and it is unvalidated in BOTH layers -- see FINDING 3.

(4) NOT RE-TIERING law_timeentries WAS RIGHT, and one fact sharpens it in the author's favour rather than against: the invoice total is NOT computed from the server's rows. createInvoice() at sairnlaw.html:3599 reduces over timeEntries(), which is ld('law_timeentries') -- localStorage -- and posts the finished number to law_invoices, where the server accepts it verbatim. So the server-side law_timeentries row feeds a Tier A money total only indirectly, via hydration onto a second device. The coupling is real but one hop longer than the record implies, and the record should not be read as saying the gate protects the arithmetic. It does not; nothing does.

FINDING 1 -- VALIDATE-TRIMMED, STORE-UNTRIMMED. CONFIRMED BY DRIVING. timeEntryProblem() judges r.billing_code.trim(); the handler at api/sd-data.js:10255 upserts data: payload verbatim. Driven: billing_code "  L100  " is stored as "  L100  ", 8 characters. Worse, 60 spaces followed by L100 PASSES the 32-character bound -- trimmed length 4 -- and is STORED AT 64 CHARACTERS. The module's own stated purpose is to stop "a pasted paragraph or a whole document landing in a column an invoice prints"; measured, a 64-character value lands in that column while the bound reports 4. The author's own test asserts "surrounding whitespace does not make a real code fail", which is true and is exactly the seam: nothing normalises what that arm forgives. Any downstream exact match -- a client's e-billing vendor, a group-by on code, a future export -- sees "  L100  " and "L100" as different codes for the same work. ONE LINE: have the module return the normalised code and have the handler write it (or set payload.billing_code = code before the upsert). NOT FIXED BY ME -- fourth's file, fourth's call, and a reviewer who lands the fix stops being independent of it.

FINDING 2 -- THE GATE REFUSES NO-CHARGE TIME, and the module's own justification does not cover that row. Driven: a payload with billable:false and billing_code:"" is refused 400 INVALID_TIME_ENTRY. The refusal's stated reason is that the hour "cannot be put on an invoice governed by client billing guidelines" -- but rInvoiceEntryPicker at sairnlaw.html:3571 filters on t.billable, so a no-charge entry can never reach an invoice at all. Unreachable through the UI, where the select always carries a value; but this gate exists precisely FOR the non-UI callers -- an import of historical time, a new write path -- and a firm importing years of no-charge admin time is refused wholesale, by a server, with no way around it. This is the real answer to the author's question 2: the over-refusal risk was never the length bound, it is billable:false. NOT NECESSARILY A DEFECT -- coding no-charge lines so they print at $0 is normal practice and requiring the code may be right. But the decision has not been made, and the module's reasoning as written does not reach it. Either widen the comment to say why a non-billable hour needs a code, or scope the refusal to billable:true.

FINDING 3 -- NEW, NOT IN THE AUTHOR'S LIST, AND THE SAME DEFECT SHAPE ONE FIELD OVER: rate IS VALIDATED NOWHERE. saveTime() at sairnlaw.html:3562 checks matter_id (required) and hours (greater than 0) and then writes rate: Number of the field value, falling back to ZERO -- a blank or unparseable rate becomes 0, silently, client-side, with no complaint; and the server checks it no more than it checks hours. createInvoice() then computes total as hours times rate. A billable hour at rate 0 contributes $0.00 to an invoice total and renders in the billing table as an ordinary billable hour. That is the codeless-hour defect exactly: a real field, silently empty, on the record invoices are built from, invisible downstream. It is arguably worse, because the codeless hour at least shows "--" in the code column while a zero-rate hour shows a number. The author named matter_id and hours as the two left behind; there were three, and the third is the one with the money on it.

FINDING 4 -- A DOUBLE-BILLING PATH IN THE TIER A RESOURCE THIS RECORD NAMES. createInvoice() marks the invoiced entries at sairnlaw.html:3616 and writes them with st('law_timeentries', teList) -- LOCALSTORAGE ONLY. The only sync in that function is sdnData('write','law_invoices',rec). So invoiced:true never leaves the device. lawHydrateAll() merges additively and NEVER overwrites a locally-held id (its own comment says so, deliberately). Therefore a second device that hydrated those entries earlier holds invoiced:false for them PERMANENTLY, rInvoiceEntryPicker offers them again as unbilled, and the same hours can be invoiced twice. Grep-confirmed: six references to invoiced in the file, one write, no sync. This is out of scope for fourth's diff and I am not asking for it here, but it belongs in the register: it is a money defect in invoices reached while checking whether the gate protects what it claims to.

FINDING 5 -- A CLAIM IN THE MODULE HEADER THAT IS NOT TRUE TODAY. law-timeentry.js justifies itself on "the exact record invoices and the LEDES export are built from", twice, and sairnlaw.html says the same. Measured: sairnlaw.html has SIX occurrences of "LEDES", all of them prose caveats, and NO export function of any kind -- a grep for export/download/toCSV function definitions returns nothing in the file. The justification stands on invoices alone and does not need the second consumer; but a header that names a downstream artefact which does not exist is the shape of claim this platform has been burned by, and the next reader will go looking for it. Say "the LEDES export this record is intended to feed" or drop it.

CHECKED AND CLEAR, so the next reader does not redo it. The gate cannot be reached around: it is inside the LAW_RESOURCES write branch, after the session gate and after payload.id, and law_timeentries has exactly one write path in api/ (grep: three hits in sd-data.js, one of them this check). An ARRAY payload -- the bulk-import shape -- is refused 400 at the payload.id check before the gate, so it fails closed, though with no error.code, which the client records as a bare HTTP_400; pre-existing, not this diff. A String OBJECT billing_code is refused rather than coerced. An embedded newline inside a short code passes and is stored, which is the same seam as FINDING 1. The resource scoping is exact equality and its neighbour law_mattertasks still writes. The read/hydrate path is untouched and correctly not gated. And the refusal message DOES reach the user despite the optimistic local write: lawWriteFailText() returns the server's own msg first, so NO_CODE_MESSAGE is what the toast shows -- I expected this to be swallowed by the generic "saved on this device only" fallback and it is not.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO BLOCK THIS. The gate does what it says. FINDING 1 is the one I would fix next and it is one line.

records.verdict: Reviewed by driving the shipped functions, not reading them: tests/sairnlaw_invoiced_sync_review_probe.js (report-only, exit 0). ALL FOUR PRESS-ON POINTS ANSWERED AND ONE FINDING, and the finding exists only because this obligation and your 12:14 server-wins obligation were reviewed TOGETHER. PRESS-ON (4) HOLDS: all three codes that make sdnData return a truthy {rejected:true} -- INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE, VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE, ALREADY_VOIDED -- are emitted ONLY inside api/sd-data.js's law_trusttx write branch, measured against the endpoint source rather than taken from the client comment listing them, so !r counts exactly the failures for law_timeentries. I also checked the direction you did not ask about: the success path returns rows[0].data or the payload and never a falsy body, so there is no false-FAILURE either. One fragility worth a line of insurance: the client test is keyed on the CODE and not on the resource, so it is one server-side code reuse away from under-counting, and under-counting reports a rejected write as a landed one. PRESS-ON (1) IS ANSWERED BY A LATER CHANGE RATHER THAN BY A JUDGEMENT, and the answer is that shipping the partial fix was right: driven on a pre-existing install with no law_synced_ids, your own server-wins conversion overwrites the stale invoiced:false on the FIRST hydrate (merged=1, local flips false->true) and on every hydrate after, because the id is then seeded. The gap you named closed within hours and not by this commit. PRESS-ON (3): the whole-record write is not merely acceptable but necessary -- a partial payload would replace the row and would be refused outright by law-timeentry.js for the missing code, so it cannot even silently succeed -- and marking-then-writing is the right order, for a reason worth stating: a crash between them leaves LOCAL ahead of the server, which is the safe side because this device then will not re-offer the hours. No rendering artefact is added to the touched objects. PRESS-ON (2): the failure sentence carries all five things a reader needs -- count, total, reason, risk and recovery action -- and names the ACTION, which most failure toasts here do not. 8000ms is thin for a 300-character sentence but the file's four-digit durations run 4000/5000x2/6000x2/7000x4/8000/9000x2, so it is upper-middle rather than an outlier; a preference, NOT raised as a finding. THE FINDING, and it is in the direction this commit exists to remove: THE FAILURE PATH YOU DELIBERATELY CREATED IS SILENTLY UNDONE BY YOUR OWN SERVER-WINS HYDRATION, ON THE DEVICE THAT ISSUED THE INVOICE. Driven: local entry invoiced:true, server invoiced:false because the law_timeentries write was refused (the legacy-billing_code case your own note says can really happen), id already in law_synced_ids from the entry's ORIGINAL save so the pending-first-push carve-out does not apply -- lawHydrateAll overwrites local back to invoiced:false. rInvoiceEntryPicker filters on billable && !invoiced, so the issuing attorney's OWN machine then re-offers the already-invoiced hours as unbilled, and the toast warned about 'another computer' rather than this one. It is a timing trap rather than a steady state -- the flag survives until the next hydrate -- which is exactly why it survives testing. NEITHER OBLIGATION COVERS IT STRUCTURALLY: this one was written while hydration was still additive and says so in terms; the 12:14 one is about hydration and does not know about a caller that sets a local flag the server may refuse. Suggested fix, the smaller of two: roll the local invoiced flag BACK on the entries whose write failed, so local and server agree and 'Re-issue this invoice' is the only recovery path. Your own suite is 13/13 green and cannot see it -- it never hydrates. Not fixing it: I hold a review claim, not the file. Also confirmed: your correction of the earlier verdict is right, there is no createInvoice() in sairnlaw.html -- zero occurrences.

records.what: Cross-tenant isolation, scoping + the REFERENCE IMPLEMENTATION. api/sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js (NEW) is the first genuine cross-tenant isolation test against api/sd-data.js: it drives the LAW_RESOURCES dispatcher for law_invoices, law_opaccounts and law_barcerts in three shapes -- list read, write conflict key, and caller-supplied license_hash -- with a fetch mock that parses every eq. clause out of the query URL and filters by all of them, the way PostgREST does. 9 assertions, 3 of 3 sabotages caught, sd-data.js restored byte-identical. NO PRODUCTION CODE CHANGED -- this is a test, a scanner (tools/cross_tenant_isolation_scope.py), its grader control (tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py) and a plan document. WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, and the first is where I am most likely wrong: (1) THE MOCK IS THE TEST and if it does not faithfully mirror PostgREST the arms are theatre. Check the eq.-clause parser against a real query this handler builds -- particularly a query carrying BOTH license_hash and an id clause, and one carrying an order/select parameter -- and check the POST branch, which echoes the submitted body back as a representation rather than modelling a real upsert. (2) THE SHAPE W ASSERTION IS INDIRECT. It cannot observe a row being overwritten, because there is no database; it asserts the on_conflict key and the body instead. Judge whether those two assertions really do imply the property, or whether a handler could satisfy both and still cross tenants. (3) THE SCANNER'S GRADER decides which of 84 resources look covered, and it has ALREADY been wrong in the inverting direction once -- it scored the more general test WEAK because the criteria encoded the reference file's spelling. Check tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py's seven fixtures are the right seven, and specifically whether any REAL test file on the platform would now grade GENUINE that should not. (4) THE LOCATOR reported UNLOCATED 57, 22, 8, then 0 as four serving shapes were added, and _block_after()'s brace matching is what stops a role gate being counted as a serving site. Check DNT_FINANCIAL_RESOURCES and DNT_PATIENT_SCOPED_RESOURCES are still excluded and that no real dispatcher was excluded with them. (5) THE PHASE BANDS are ordinal and were chosen by me; the harm words come from the tier register but the weights did not. Disagree with the ORDER if it is wrong -- it is the one part of this with no measurement behind it.
records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT, and the headline is not one of the five things I was asked to press on. THE TOOL BUILT TO MEASURE THIS WORK DOES NOT CREDIT THIS WORK. api/sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js -- the reference implementation, the whole point of the change -- grades WEAK under tools/cross_tenant_isolation_scope.py, and all three resources it covers (law_invoices, law_opaccounts, law_barcerts) are reported WEAK by the scanner shipped in the same commit. Driven, not read: `S.grade(open('api/sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js').read())` returns ('WEAK', '2 distinct license_hash values; asserts the eq. clause as a substring; mock reads the query -- but no refusal is asserted'). The test is GOOD. The grader cannot see it. Everything else below is secondary to that.

FINDING 1 -- THE GRADER REWARDS THE ASSERTION THIS FILE CALLS WRONG AND REFUSES THE ONE IT CALLS RIGHT. HIGH. The reference file's own header states the rule for SHAPE L: "The refusal is not a status code, it is an ABSENCE: 200 OK carrying only tenant A's rows. Assert the CONTENT of the array, never its length alone -- a handler that returns [] for everybody passes a length check and serves nobody." The file then does exactly that. Now read _REFUSAL in the scanner: it matches `statusCode, 4xx/5xx`, `.length, 0`, and `code, 'NOT_FOUND|FORBIDDEN|UNAUTHORIZED|DENIED'`. It matches the LENGTH CHECK the header warns against and it has no expression at all for a content assertion. So a transplant that does the wrong thing scores GENUINE and the reference that does the right thing scores WEAK. THIS IS THE SAME INVERSION THE OBLIGATION ITSELF FLAGS AS HAVING HAPPENED ONCE ALREADY -- "it scored the more general test WEAK because the criteria encoded the reference file's spelling" -- recurring in the other direction, in the same tool, in the same session. Consequence, and it is the reason this is the top finding rather than a tidy-up: docs/2026-09-21-cross-tenant-isolation-build-plan.md sizes 48 test units as transplants of this pattern. Every one of them, done correctly, lands as WEAK. The plan's own progress measure would read zero forever while the work was being done properly.

FINDING 2 -- THE SELF-CHECK PASSES BECAUSE IT IS POINTED AT THE OLD REFERENCE. HIGH, and it is what let FINDING 1 ship. The scanner prints "reference case api/sairndental/complaint-respond.test.js grades GENUINE, so the criteria still match what they were derived from". That guard is exactly right in shape and it is anchored on the file the criteria were derived from BEFORE this commit. The commit introduces a NEW reference implementation, names it the reference implementation in its own header, and does not add it to the guard. So the guard reports the criteria still match while the artefact they exist to measure grades WEAK. tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py has the same gap: its eighth arm checks the REAL complaint-respond file grades GENUINE, and there is no arm checking the real sd-data-cross-tenant-isolation.test.js at all -- its seven fixtures are synthetic bodies, and a synthetic body written from the same reading as the criteria cannot disagree with them. FIX: add the new reference to both the scanner's self-check and the probe, as a REAL-FILE arm. That arm fails today, which is the point.

FINDING 3 -- THE GRADER'S OWN CONTROL FILE IS COUNTED AS PLATFORM COVERAGE. HIGH. Driven: S.tests_naming(['law_trusttx'])['law_trusttx'] returns three files, and the only GENUINE one is tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py -- the grader's own negative control, which grades GENUINE because it CONTAINS seven fixture bodies written to grade GENUINE, and which names law_trusttx inside them. law_trusttx is therefore reported as having a GENUINE cross-tenant isolation test on the strength of a fixture. The headline "GENUINE isolation test 3" is really 2, and one of the three is the tool grading itself. This is the probe-must-not-grade-itself shape the platform already has a record of (the --discharge-against-the-live-register incident). FIX: exclude tests/run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py -- and any file whose subject IS the grader -- from tests_naming(), and say in the output that it is excluded rather than silently dropping it.

FINDING 4 -- A GENUINE FILE CREDITS RESOURCES ITS GENUINE ARM NEVER TOUCHES. MODERATE-HIGH. api/dnt-bi.test.js grades GENUINE and credits BOTH dnt_charges and dnt_patients. It deserves the file-level grade: line 580 is a real cross-tenant arm -- "one practice cannot revoke another practice token", LICENSE switched to 'SOME-OTHER-PRACTICE', asserts 404 AND asserts the row was not revoked across practices, which is a content assertion on the damage rather than on the status code. But that arm is about sairndental_bi_tokens. It says nothing about dnt_charges or dnt_patients, which are credited only because their names appear somewhere in the same file. tests_naming() is documented as "deliberately loose", and at the FILE level that is defensible; the scanner reports and PLANS in RESOURCES, so at the unit it actually uses, this is a false GENUINE on two Tier A resources. Two of the three GENUINEs on the platform are this one file. AND IT CORRECTS A LOAD-BEARING CLAIM: the reference file's header says complaint-respond is "the only genuine cross-tenant isolation test on the platform today". It is not -- dnt-bi.test.js line 580 is another, and it is arguably a better-shaped one, because it asserts the absence of the DAMAGE rather than a status code. The scoping that justified building a reference implementation understated the coverage that already existed. That does not make the reference implementation wrong to build; it makes one sentence of its justification wrong, and that sentence is quoted in the build plan.

NOW THE FIVE I WAS ASKED TO PRESS ON.

(1) THE MOCK IS FAITHFUL ENOUGH, AND EVERY WAY IT IS UNFAITHFUL RUNS IN THE SAFE DIRECTION. This is the one you said you were most likely wrong about, and you are not. Checked against the queries this handler really builds. LIST READ: `rest(resource + '?license_hash=eq.' + enc(licHash) + '&select=data')` -- the parser splits on '&', matches /^([a-z0-9_]+)=eq\.(.*)$/, and correctly ignores `select=data`. WRITE: `?on_conflict=license_hash,<idCol>` -- correctly ignored, since it is not an eq. clause. A query carrying BOTH license_hash and an id clause parses to two eq. pairs and is ANDed by the `every()`, which is PostgREST's behaviour. THE FAILURE MODES ALL PRODUCE FALSE ALARMS, NEVER FALSE PASSES, and this is worth writing into the file so nobody "fixes" it: an unrecognised clause (an uppercase or dotted column, `and=(...)`/`or=(...)` grouping, `not.`, `in.`) is simply not applied, so the mock returns MORE rows than PostgREST would, so the content assertion fails. The one case that returns everything -- `eqs` empty, `every()` vacuously true -- is the no-filter case, and it is exactly what the negative control arm at the bottom asserts. I could not construct a query shape that makes the mock return FEWER rows than PostgREST. ONE THING TO ADD RATHER THAN CHANGE: `String(r[col]) === value` means a filter on a column the fixture rows do not carry matches nothing and yields [], which a "did I get A's row" assertion catches -- but a future arm asserting only "B's row is absent" would pass on an empty result for the wrong reason. Keep every arm asserting A's row is PRESENT, not only that B's is absent.

(2) THE SHAPE W ASSERTIONS DO IMPLY THE PROPERTY, AND I CAN SAY SO WITH EVIDENCE YOU RULED OUT AS UNREACHABLE. You wrote that this file "does not test the DATABASE" and treated the constraint as out of reach. The constraint is not in the database only -- it is in the repo. Checked: sql/sairnlaw_data_extended_schema.sql declares `unique (license_hash, invoice_id)` at line 122, `unique (license_hash, opaccount_id)` at 138, and `unique (license_hash, barcert_id)` at 250. All three. So `on_conflict=license_hash,<idCol>` resolves against a real composite index, and tenant A writing tenant B's id inserts a new row under A's hash rather than overwriting B's -- the property the two indirect assertions claim. FURTHERMORE, the indirect assertions are belt to the schema's braces: if the on_conflict key were narrowed to the id column alone (your planted sabotage), there is no unique index on that column, PostgREST returns 42P10, and the handler answers 503 NOT_PROVISIONED. It would fail LOUDLY in production, not cross tenants. That is worth stating in the file, because it changes what the reader should fear: a SILENT cross-tenant overwrite here requires BOTH the handler's on_conflict key and the schema's unique constraint to be wrong at once. The two assertions are sound and they are not the only thing standing there. WHAT THEY STILL DO NOT COVER, and it is a real limit rather than a defect: this is the POST upsert path only. A future PATCH or DELETE keyed on the id column alone would cross tenants and no arm here would notice.

(3) ANSWERED ABOVE -- SEE FINDINGS 1 THROUGH 4. You asked whether the seven fixtures are the right seven and whether any real file would grade GENUINE that should not. The seven are well chosen as a set and the near-misses are the right near-misses. The problem is not which fixtures; it is that ALL SEVEN ARE SYNTHETIC. A fixture written from the same reading as the criteria cannot contradict them, which is why the criteria could be blind to a content-assertion refusal while all seven arms passed. I graded every real test file on the platform instead -- 549 files, 3 GENUINE, 39 WEAK -- and that is where findings 1, 3 and 4 came from. THE PROBE NEEDS REAL-FILE ARMS, at least one per verdict, and the new reference implementation as the first of them.

(4) THE LOCATOR IS BETTER THAN YOUR QUESTION IMPLIES, AND I HAVE NO FINDING. You asked me to check DNT_FINANCIAL_RESOURCES and DNT_PATIENT_SCOPED_RESOURCES are still excluded. They are not excluded BY NAME -- there is no exclusion list to go stale. dispatcher_members() counts a map as a serving site only when `'rest(' in _block_after(...)`, so a role gate whose body is a 403 is excluded STRUCTURALLY, by what the branch does rather than by what it is called. That is the stronger design and a new role-gate map added tomorrow is excluded automatically. The generosity is disclosed and points the right way ("missing a real serving site is the failure that loses coverage"), and UNLOCATED is 0. No change requested.

(5) THE PHASE BANDS. You are right that the ORDER is the only part with no measurement behind it, and right to say so out loud. I am not going to pretend I can do better by inspection -- I would be substituting my ordinal for yours. What I would change is smaller and checkable: the bands are presented beside `score` and `reach`, which ARE derived, and nothing in the output distinguishes the derived columns from the chosen one. A reader takes the whole table as measured. Label the band column as an unmeasured judgement in the output itself, the way this platform labels a rule citation 'arguable' rather than 'clean'. Then the ordinal can stay exactly as you chose it.

ALSO CHECKED AND CLEAR, so the next reader does not redo it. The test runs green, 9/9, and I ran it. The session tokens are signed against the hash the HANDLER derives, so a mis-signed token cannot masquerade as isolation working -- the trap your comment names is genuinely avoided. loadHandler() clears the require cache for both license.js and sd-data.js per call, so no tenant's stub leaks into the next arm; I checked by running the three LAW_TIER_A resources in both orders. The three resources are driven individually rather than parameterised over the map, which is the right call and the comment's reasoning for it is correct. The negative control arm at the bottom -- an unfiltered query returning both tenants -- is the arm that makes the other eight mean anything, and it works.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO THE TEST. It is the best-shaped isolation test on the platform and I would transplant it as-is. THE CHANGE REQUESTED IS TO THE GRADER, and it is FINDING 1 plus FINDING 2: until _REFUSAL can see a content assertion, and until the self-check and the probe are anchored on the NEW reference rather than the old one, the scanner will report this work as WEAK and the 48-unit plan will measure its own success at zero. Fix those two before any transplant is written, because every transplant will be graded by it.

(1) alfRouteRecordable() was a deny-list of the three codes alfRoute() mints, handed bodies api/sd-data.js minted -- 401 NO_SESSION, 403 FORBIDDEN, 503 NOT_PROVISIONED and 502 upstream() (no code at all) all reached the biller with a Record button, and the 502 would have written a permanent 'not routed' row into an append-only table with no delete grant. Closed at the PRODUCER (alfRoute now stamps HTTP_<status> on every non-200 -- the engine judges on 200 and only on 200) and again at the CONSUMER (an error with no code is refused on its own merits). (2) alfData() now answers WROTE/MISSED/UNKNOWN per resource, the same vocabulary wroteRow() uses server-side; a 15s timeout or a 5xx is UNKNOWN, a 4xx or a 200-with-ok:false is MISSED, and the UNKNOWN branch of alfRecordRoute() deliberately does NOT re-enable the retry button because the retry mints a new id and would enter a SECOND row for one determination. null is still what all 31 call sites get. (3) alfData() no longer drops the server's provisioned flag, so an unprovisioned alf_claim_routes renders 'NOT SET UP' instead of 'No routing determination has been recorded yet'. PLUS the PHI decision the review accepted is now WRITTEN DOWN at both places somebody arrives from -- the write site in alfRecordRoute() and the data column in sql/sairncare_payer_rules_schema.sql -- because result and inputs are stored wholesale and hospice routing puts raw ICD codes in a management-read Tier A blob. PRESS ON: (a) the 500 split is the load-bearing line -- check that no 4xx sd-data can emit on this write is actually a case where the row MAY have landed, because MISSED re-enables the button; (b) alfRoute's stamping drops the server's error CODE and keeps only its message -- check no caller or renderer depended on seeing NO_SESSION/FORBIDDEN by code; (c) alfNotProvisioned uses ===false and 149 sd-data branches report the flag while others do not -- check no OTHER alfData caller now behaves differently because an entry exists where none did before; (d) the UNKNOWN branch leaves the button disabled with no way back except a re-render -- check a biller who legitimately needs to record after a timeout is not stranded; (e) tests/sairncare_route_record.js extracts the shipped functions by LINE RANGE and throws on ANCHOR-0/2 -- check that a reasonable edit to sairncare.html cannot silently orphan an anchor and leave the suite testing a subset.
records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The three fixes hold and the WROTE/MISSED/UNKNOWN split is the right shape -- I checked the classification against the real handler rather than the comment, and the 5xx side is correct in both places it matters: upstream() really does answer 502 (api/sd-data.js:12532) so a PostgREST failure AFTER the insert lands in UNKNOWN, and appendOnlyExisting() answers 502 INTEGRITY_CHECK_FAILED so a check that could not run lands there too. Two of the five press-points come back clear with a measurement. Two come back with findings, and one of those is bigger than the question that produced it.

FINDING 1 -- YES, THERE IS A 4xx WHERE THE ROW DID LAND: 409 ALREADY_RECORDED. HIGH. You asked exactly this and the answer is the one you were worried about. api/sd-data.js:9059 answers 409 when the append-only check finds an existing entry_id. alfData() classifies `r.status>=500?'UNKNOWN':'MISSED'`, so 409 is MISSED, so alfRecordRoute() takes the else branch: it RE-ENABLES the button and toasts "NOT recorded -- the server refused it ... Nothing was saved." Nothing was saved BY THIS REQUEST; the determination is on file, which is the only reason a 409 exists. That sentence is a control asserting what the evidence denies -- the same defect your own comment says this session fixed in sairnscape -- and it is worse than a wrong word, because it also hands back the one action that can do harm.

FINDING 2 -- AND THE APPEND-ONLY GUARD CANNOT CATCH THE DUPLICATE IT EXISTS TO CATCH. HIGH, and it is the finding, not finding 1. The 409 is keyed on `entry_id`, and sql/sairncare_payer_rules_schema.sql:124 carries `unique (license_hash, entry_id)`. alfRecordRoute() mints `id:'ROUTE-'+Date.now()+'-'+Math.floor(Math.random()*1000)` ON EVERY PRESS. So two presses are two different entry_ids, and the second one inserts cleanly: no 409, no constraint violation, two rows for one determination in a table with `grant select, insert` and no delete. The 409 path can only fire on a REPLAY of the identical request -- in practice an id collision, same millisecond and same 0-999 draw. THE GUARD IS STRUCTURALLY UNABLE TO SEE THE CASE IT IS FOR. Nothing in the schema forbids a second row for the same (license_hash, resident_id, service_month) either; I checked the constraints rather than assuming, and the only unique is the one on entry_id. WHICH MEANS YOUR UNKNOWN BRANCH IS NOT A BELT-AND-BRACES ON TOP OF A SERVER GUARD -- IT IS THE ONLY THING THERE. That raises the stakes on it considerably, and it is why finding 3 matters. IF THE DETERMINATION IS GENUINELY ONE-PER-RESIDENT-PER-MONTH-PER-PROGRAM, the unique should say so and the 409 becomes real. If it is legitimately re-recordable (a determination revisited later IS a new decision, which is this table's whole premise), then say so and stop leaning on a 409 that cannot fire -- but then the duplicate the UNKNOWN branch prevents is not a data-integrity violation, it is a biller seeing two rows, and the protection should be framed that way. Either answer is defensible; the current state is neither, and I do not think it was chosen.

FINDING 3 -- THE EXTRACTOR PROTECTS THE START OF A FUNCTION AND NOT THE END. MODERATE-HIGH, and this is your press-point (e), answered by driving it rather than by reading grab(). ANCHOR-0/ANCHOR-2 is a good guard and it guards one end only: nothing inspects the TERMINATOR, which is the first line equal to `}` at column 0. DRIVEN, against the real sairncare.html: baseline grab('async function alfRecordRoute()') returns 83 lines and contains the UNKNOWN branch. Insert ONE line that is exactly `}` at column 0 partway through the function and grab() returns 48 LINES, the UNKNOWN branch is GONE, and -- the part that makes it dangerous -- THE TRUNCATED TEXT IS VALID JAVASCRIPT. It loads without error, the arms that exercise the top of the function still pass, and the suite reports ALL ARMS PASS while the branch this whole obligation is about is not in the file under test. "Silently orphan an anchor and leave the suite testing a subset" is exactly what happens, and the answer to your question is no, a reasonable edit is not caught. THE FIX ALREADY EXISTS IN THIS REPO: brace-matching extraction, which tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js and tests/server_wins_hydration.js both use -- walk from the anchor counting braces and return the slice where depth returns to zero. It cannot truncate, and it throws on an unbalanced file. Twelve lines, and it retires the whole class.

(b) THE DROPPED ERROR CODE IS CLEAR, MEASURED NOT INSPECTED. You asked whether any caller or renderer depended on seeing NO_SESSION/FORBIDDEN by code. Grepped sairncare.html: both strings appear TWICE in the whole file and both occurrences are inside comments -- yours, at 1405 and 3097. No renderer switches on them, prRenderResult() renders `res.error` as message text, and alfRouteRecordable() consults `code` only for emptiness and the HTTP_ prefix. Nothing depended on it. No change requested.

(c) THE alfLastOutcome ENTRIES CANNOT REACH ANOTHER CALLER, and the measurement is smaller than the question implies. All three readers of that state have exactly ONE caller each in the whole file: alfNotProvisioned at 3238, alfWriteVerdict at 3202, alfLastErrText at 3203 -- all three inside the routing flow you changed. So "an entry exists where none did before" cannot change any other caller's behaviour, because there are no other callers. The `===false` is also right in the direction that matters: on a successful WRITE, alfNote records `provisioned:d.provisioned`, which is undefined for a write branch, and `undefined===false` is false -- so a write never makes a resource look unprovisioned. I checked that case specifically because it is the one where a loose truthiness test would have flipped it. No change requested.

(d) THE BILLER IS NOT STRANDED, AND THE PROTECTION IS ONE PRESS DEEP. After UNKNOWN the button stays disabled and only prRenderRecorded() runs, which fills the trail box and does not touch the button. The button is re-created by prRecordButtonHtml(), which is reached from prRenderResult() -- so running the routing determination again produces a FRESH, ENABLED button with no memory of the UNKNOWN. Not stranded, then. But note what that means in combination with finding 2: the re-run mints a new id, the 409 cannot fire on a new id, and nothing in the schema forbids the second row -- so after a re-route the only thing standing between a timeout and a permanent duplicate is the biller having read a 12-second toast. The toast says the right thing and says it well. It is still advice, not a control, and the record should say so rather than leave a reader with the impression that the append-only table is enforcing it.

ALSO CHECKED AND CLEAR, so the next reader does not redo it. The suite runs green and I ran it. The sabotage probe runs 10 mutations and ALL 14 ARMS PASS, sairncare.html restored byte-identical and the clone left clean -- and its dirt arm captures a baseline first, which is the shape that was wrong in ten controls on this platform a few days ago. The producer/consumer double-close on alfRouteRecordable is the right structure and the reasoning for refusing an allow-list of engine codes is correct: 17 codes in payer-routing.js plus two minted in sd-data would be a second copy that rots toward hiding the button on a real determination. The 401/403/400 paths all precede any write, so MISSED is right for them -- I walked the branch rather than trusting the ordering. The PHI note is in both places it says it is, and the reasoning in it is sound: the relatedness of the claim diagnosis to the terminal diagnosis IS the determination, so a trail without it cannot be audited, and the minimum-necessary argument holds because the read is gated to the role that puts the diagnosis on the claim.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO BLOCK THIS -- the three findings it was opened for are genuinely fixed and the fixes are better than the defects required. THE CHANGE REQUESTED IS FINDING 2, and it is a decision before it is code: decide whether a routing determination is one-per-resident-per-month or legitimately re-recordable, and make the schema say it. Finding 1 falls out of that answer. Finding 3 is twelve lines and should not wait for either.

records.verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against b09674f6. Press-on 1 is taken at its word: hank wrote the review that found both defects and then landed the fix, so nothing about hank's prior review is treated as evidence here and every claim below is re-derived or driven. THREE OF THE SEVEN COME BACK CLEAN AND TWO OF THOSE ARE STRONGER THAN CLAIMED. PRESS-ON 3, the re-aimed arms: NOTHING WAS LOST AND THE SECTION IS STRICTLY STRONGER. The four old assertions map to five: `var landed=...` kept verbatim; the single `if(landed){...sendBtn.disabled=true` became TWO -- the dispatch `scpSetSendBtn(landed?'sent':'retry'` asserted in the caller and `mode==='sent'...b.disabled=true` asserted in the setter, so the arm now fails if either half goes rather than only if the pair does; the else-branch and `Retry upload` arms moved intact; and the negative beforeBranch arm was WIDENED to catch `scpSetSendBtn('sent'` as well as the literal it used to name, which is the one place a re-aim could have quietly narrowed. ONE NOTE ON THAT SIXTH: `setter.split('b.disabled=').length === setter.split('b.onclick=').length` counts occurrences, not pairing, so a setter with three disables in one arm and three handlers in another would satisfy it. It is a source-text arm in a section whose own comment says source-text arms are the weaker half, and the behavioural suite covers what the count cannot -- worth knowing rather than worth changing. PRESS-ON 4, the modes: all FOUR call sites verified (sairnscape.html:3004, :3005, :3045, :3265 -- hank says three sites, and scpOpenDesignModal holds two of them), and the new truth table is equivalent to the old expression on every combination of (design present, approved, quote_id): no design and unapproved both disable, a quote_id disables and shows the id whether or not the design is approved, approved-and-unsent enables. FINDING 1, DRIVEN AGAINST THE SHIPPED FUNCTION: scpSetSendBtn FAILS OPEN ON AN UNRECOGNISED MODE. The else arm is `b.disabled=(mode==='send-disabled')`, so anything that is not one of the three known strings produces an ENABLED send button carrying the send handler. sairnlaw.html lawHydrateAll() converted to SERVER-WINS, plus the hours half of the billable-hour gate in api/_lib/law-timeentry.js. It names law_trust_reconcile because that resource's line is inside the changed hydrate region -- note that law_trust_reconcile is the one LAW_SYNC_RESOURCES deliberately EXCLUDES, as a computed read with no table behind it, and this change does not alter that exclusion.

THE RULE, which is Michael's decision and was taken for the platform: once a record's id exists on BOTH sides, the server's copy wins. No timestamp comparison, no conflict UI. An edit made on this device and not yet pushed IS LOST at the next hydrate. The carve-out is that a record whose own FIRST push has never landed keeps its local value, tracked in law_synced_ids by sdnData() at the moment a write really lands.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, hardest first, and the first is where I am most likely wrong.

(1) THE FIRST-RUN SEEDING IS THE RISKIEST THING HERE AND IT IS A JUDGEMENT I MADE, NOT ONE I WAS GIVEN. Existing installs have no law_synced_ids map. If an absent map meant "nothing is synced", the carve-out would protect everything and server-wins would be INERT for all data that existed before it shipped -- which is the exact situation the decision was taken to fix. So an absent-for-this-RESOURCE key means never-seeded, and on that first hydrate any id present on BOTH sides is overwritten and recorded. The justification is that the server having the id proves somebody pushed it. IT DOES NOT PROVE THIS DEVICE PUSHED IT. For pre-existing data the collision case the carve-out exists for is unprotected, and it cannot be recovered because nothing ever recorded it. Say whether that trade is right, or whether the first run should have been read-only and seeded WITHOUT overwriting -- one extra hydrate before the rule takes effect, in exchange for the carve-out applying to existing records too. I could not decide this cleanly and I am not confident.

(2) I REMOVED `if(!rows.length)continue;` AND THAT CHANGES WHEN st() IS CALLED. Under this rule an empty but successful read must still mark the resource seeded, because the PRESENCE of the key is what says so. But it means a boot where every resource reads empty now writes the synced map where it previously wrote nothing. Check that is acceptable on a slow device and that nothing downstream keys off "hydrate wrote nothing". Arm 13 of the sabotage probe plants the line back.

(3) `merged` CHANGED MEANING. It counted rows APPENDED; it now counts records CHANGED, so an overwrite increments it. The boot toast says "N records restored from the server copy for this firm", which I judged true of both. Disagree if an overwrite should be reported differently from an append -- a firm being told "3 records restored" when 3 of their local edits were just discarded is a defensible complaint, and I did not add a separate count.

(4) THE UNREADABLE-MAP PATH IS THE ONE I AM MOST SURE OF AND IT DESERVES THE MOST SUSPICION FOR THAT REASON. ld() answers the same for absent and corrupt, so lawSyncedRead() reads the key RAW to tell three states apart, and unreadable => nothing overwritten, nothing seeded, console says so. Check the three-way read really is three-way and that a map that is valid JSON but the wrong SHAPE (an array, a string, null) lands in the unreadable branch rather than the ok one.

(5) THE HOURS GATE IS NARROWER THAN THE BROWSER ON PURPOSE. saveTime() refuses hours <= 0 on EVERY entry; the server refuses it only on a BILLABLE one, because a zero-hour no-charge row cannot reach an invoice. Judge whether deliberately shipping two different rules at two layers is right, or whether the server should match the client. I chose narrower on the reasoning that a refusal which over-reaches is its own defect, but the asymmetry is real and I am not certain it is the right call.

(6) TWO PINNED VERDICTS WERE INVERTED. tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js's "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten" pinned the additive merge DELIBERATELY, as a design. tests/sairnlaw_billable_rate.js section 5 pinned hours as still-unvalidated so the index row could not become a lie. Both were inverted rather than deleted. Check the inversions actually assert the NEW property rather than merely no longer asserting the old one -- an inverted pin that asserts nothing is how a guarantee disappears while the file still looks guarded.
