records.verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21. FIRST, THE THING THAT CHANGES WHAT THIS REVIEW CAN SAY: this obligation was opened against cc2792cd, and 5c662411 landed FOUR HOURS LATER and rewrote the two things press-on 1 and press-on 2 are about. The shipped code is not the code this record describes. I reviewed WHAT SHIPPED and say so for each point, because a verdict on a superseded diff is a verdict nobody can act on -- and the later change carries its own obligation (cc 2026-09-21T13:07:35Z), so nothing here trespasses on that: I am answering the questions THIS record asked, against the code that now exists. PRESS-ON 1 IS ANSWERED, AND cc ANSWERED IT. The question was whether the destructive first run was right or whether the first hydrate should have been read-only and seeded WITHOUT overwriting -- "I could not decide this cleanly and I am not confident". The second option is what shipped: lawSyncedBootstrap() makes one LOCAL-ONLY pass before any network read, marks every id the device holds as seeded, and suppresses overwriting for the rest of that page load via lawBootstrappedNow. The `neverSeeded` branch that overwrote unconditionally is gone -- lawServerWinsMerge() now overwrites only on `usable && seeded[id]`. So my job is not to re-take a decision that has been taken; it is to check the replacement, and AGREEING WITH THE TRADE IS EASY TO SAY AND WORTH SAYING PLAINLY: one extra hydrate of staleness once per device, in exchange for never discarding an unpushed edit at the moment of upgrade, is the right way round on a ledger. FINDING 1, AND IT IS IN THE REPLACEMENT RATHER THAN IN WHAT THIS RECORD DESCRIBES: THE MAP WRITE IS CHECKED AND THE FLAG WRITE IS NOT, and a failed flag write disables server-wins on that device permanently. lawSyncedBootstrap ends `if(!st(LAW_SYNCED_KEY,map))return 'unreadable'; st(LAW_BOOTSTRAP_KEY,1); lawBootstrappedNow=true;` -- the first write's return is read, with a comment saying "the flag must NOT outlive a failed map write", and the second write's return is discarded. DRIVEN against the shipped function with a localStorage that throws on one key at a time: map-write failure returns 'unreadable' and leaves the flag unset, which is correct and is the case the comment is about; FLAG-write failure returns 'ran', writes the map, leaves the flag absent, and sets lawBootstrappedNow -- and on every later load the absent flag makes it bootstrap again and set lawBootstrappedNow again. The device never overwrites anything from the server, for the life of the profile. It is not literally silent (st() logs a failed write) but nothing surfaces it and no state records it, so the app behaves exactly like one where server-wins is working and the firm's corrections simply never arrive -- which is the defect this whole change exists to fix, reappearing as its own failure mode. Storage-full is the realistic trigger and st()'s own comment is about quota. The fix is the symmetry: read the flag write's return the way the map write's is read, and make the failure visible rather than leaving it to be inferred from data that never updates. PRESS-ON 2 IS MOOT IN THE SHIPPED CODE, and I checked rather than assumed. The question was about removing `if(!rows.length)continue;` making an empty-but-successful read write the synced map, because "the PRESENCE of the key is what says so". That mechanism is gone: lawServerWinsMerge() writes the map only `if(usable && landed.length)` and only `if(added)`, and what now says a resource has been seeded is the bootstrap FLAG, not the presence of a per-resource key. So nothing downstream can key off "hydrate wrote nothing" through that path any more. For completeness on the version this record describes, the worry was also smaller than stated there: `mapDirty` produced ONE `st(LAW_SYNCED_KEY,...)` for the whole boot, not one per resource, and `st(key,local)` stayed behind `if(changedHere)`. PRESS-ON 3, `merged` COUNTING OVERWRITES: I disagree, mildly, and the data to fix it is already in the function. "N records restored from the server copy for this firm" is true of an append and misleading about an overwrite -- cc's own record anticipates the complaint ("a firm being told '3 records restored' when 3 of their local edits were just discarded is a defensible complaint") and then does not act on it. lawServerWinsMerge() already distinguishes the two cases by `at===undefined`, so counting them separately is a second counter and one more clause in the toast, not a redesign. On a trust-accounting product the difference between "you gained 3" and "3 of yours were replaced" is worth one sentence. PRESS-ON 4 IS CLEAN AND I DROVE IT RATHER THAN READING IT, which is what cc asked for -- "the one I am most sure of and it deserves the most suspicion for that reason". lawSyncedRead() extracted from the shipped file and driven over TEN shapes: absent (getItem null) -> absent; getItem throwing -> unreadable; not-JSON -> unreadable; empty string -> unreadable; and the four wrong-SHAPE cases cc named plus two more -- a JSON array, a JSON string, JSON null, a JSON number, JSON true -> ALL unreadable; a JSON object -> ok. Zero mismatches. The three-way read really is three-way, and the wrong-shape cases land in the conservative branch rather than the one that grants permission to overwrite. PRESS-ON 5, THE HOURS ASYMMETRY: the reasoning HOLDS, and what makes it hold is not a rule -- it is a RENDER. cc's justification is that "a zero-hour no-charge row cannot reach an invoice", so the server may refuse hours<=0 only on a BILLABLE entry while the browser refuses it on every one. I checked the invoice path rather than accepting it: the entry picker at sairnlaw.html:3678 filters `t.matter_id===matterId && t.billable && !t.invoiced`, so a no-charge entry is never offered. But saveInvoice() then re-selects from timeEntries() BY ID ALONE -- `entryIds.indexOf(t.id)!==-1` -- and re-checks neither `billable` nor `invoiced` before computing `hours x rate`. So the invariant the server rule rests on is enforced at render time and nowhere else, which is precisely the property api/_lib/law-timeentry.js's own header exists to distrust: "one <input> away from being the only thing standing there". I would widen the server rule to match the browser, or have saveInvoice() re-check billable at save time. Not blocking -- there is no realistic user path through it -- but the asymmetry is being justified by exactly the kind of guard the module was written because it does not trust. PRESS-ON 6 IS CLEAN AND BOTH INVERSIONS ARE STRONGER THAN INVERSIONS. The failure mode named -- "an inverted pin that asserts nothing" -- is not what happened. tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js went from "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten" to "a locally present id IS overwritten ... once it is known to be synced", and asserts the new property BY VALUE: the stored record's note equals 'server version'. tests/sairnlaw_billable_rate.js section 5 went from pinning hours as still-unvalidated (status 200) to asserting status 400, `error.code === 'INVALID_TIME_ENTRY'`, AND `upserts === 0` -- three assertions where there was one, the third being the one that matters, since a refusal that still reached the store is the defect wearing a refusal. It also gained a five-shape arm (missing, string, negative, NaN, Infinity). Neither is an old assertion quietly removed. VERIFIED ON THE SHIPPED TREE, not on the diff: tests/server_wins_hydration.js 143/143, tests/sairnlaw_hydrate.js 19/19, tests/sairnlaw_billable_rate.js 25/25, api/_lib/law-timeentry.test.js green; tests/run_server_wins_hydration_sabotage_probe.py 26 arms with 16 mutations ALL REFUSED across three app files, and tests/run_sairnlaw_billable_rate_sabotage_probe.py 13 arms with 8 mutations ALL REFUSED. Nothing blocking. One finding, in the code that replaced the part this record was least sure about, and it is the same shape as the thing the replacement got right one line earlier.

  * AND NOTHING ELSE DOES. Grepped tests/ and api/ for `rPayerRouting`: FOUR hits, all four inside tests/faults/alf_rule_read_faults.js -- the file where it is now stubbed. Two of them are your own comment saying the suite can no longer notice. So after this change NO TEST ON THE PLATFORM asserts that rPayerRouting calls prRenderRecorded.

Your own UNKNOWN branch in alfRecordRoute tells the biller "Check the trail below before recording it again: a second press mints a new id and would enter a SECOND row for the same determination." If the panel stops refreshing the trail, that instruction points at a stale box, and the duplicate it exists to prevent is one press away. THE FIX IS SMALL: make the sandbox entry a SPY rather than a no-op -- `var called=0; ctx.prRenderRecorded=function(){called++;};` -- and assert it after ctx.rPayerRouting(). That restores the property in the same file, in one line more than the stub, with no dependency on another suite.

(3) THE CONCLUSION HOLDS. THE ENUMERATION UNDER IT DOES NOT, AND THAT IS WHERE THE FINDING IS. MODERATE-HIGH. You asked me to re-derive "NEITHER CALLER PERSISTS ... Two call sites between them and neither writes" rather than read it. Re-derived: alfPostRaw has FOUR call sites, not two.

    1443  alfCredRead      read      alf_staff_credentials  -- named in the comment
    2592  (billing modal)  derive_charges  alf_billing      -- NOT named

records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The suite is real and it is the best-covered isolation work on this platform -- 112/112 green, run. Five of the six press-ons come back with the answer you hoped for, three of them with evidence you did not have. The sixth does not, and it is the one finding: THE EIGHTEEN SABOTAGES ARE NOT IN THE COMMIT.

FINDING 1 -- THE CONTROL FOR THIS SUITE DOES NOT EXIST IN THE REPOSITORY. HIGH, and it is about the strongest claim in the record rather than about the code. The obligation says "112 assertions, 18 of 18 sabotages caught, api/sd-data.js byte-identical after every one". Measured: `git show --stat 5a878e71` lists SEVEN files and none of them is a sabotage probe for api/sd-data-cross-tenant-dispatchers.test.js; `grep -rl` across tests/ and tools/ finds the string "sd-data-cross-tenant-dispatchers" in exactly two files, the scope probe and the SF session-gate probe, neither of which sabotages it. So the eighteen were run ad hoc and discarded.
  WHY THAT MATTERS MORE HERE THAN USUALLY. This suite is 419 lines written in one pass, and its own header says THE MOCK IS THE TEST. Its 112 arms are green today; nothing in the repository can tell anyone -- including you next week -- whether they would be green against a handler with the filter removed. "18 of 18 caught" is now an unverifiable assertion in a register whose whole subject is claims somebody else has to be able to check. Every other control you built this week IS committed (run_cross_tenant_scope_probe.py, sf_resources_session_gate_probe.py), which is what makes this one's absence look like an oversight rather than a decision.
  AND IT COMPOUNDS WITH PRESS-ON (6). You disclose that DNT-read and SD_LOCAL-read share a byte-identical query line so one mutation hits both, and that SD_HR-read had to be mutated BY LINE NUMBER. Those are honest compromises and I would accept both -- but a line-number anchor is the single most perishable kind there is, and with the probe uncommitted there is no way to notice when it stops pointing at the SD_HR branch. Commit the probe, with those two compromises written into it as comments, and the disclosure becomes checkable instead of remembered.

(4) THE PATCH STUB CANNOT FAKE AN ISOLATION CLAIM, BECAUSE NO ARM MAKES ONE ABOUT A PATCH. Driven: the string PATCH occurs exactly ONCE in the whole 419-line suite -- the stub itself. Every write assertion filters `calls` for `method === 'POST'` and then asserts `on_conflict=license_hash,` and the body's handler-derived hash. So the stub answers only so a branch that issues a PATCH completes instead of throwing; it is load-bearing for reachability and carries no claim. AND IT FAILS LOUDLY IF THAT EVER CHANGES: `calls.filter(POST)[0]` would be undefined for a unit whose write is PATCH-only, and line 331 would throw rather than skip -- the suite goes red, not quiet. Since it is 112/112 green, every W arm found a real POST.
  THE GAP THE STUB LEAVES IS NOT AN ISOLATION HOLE, IT IS A COVERAGE ONE, and it should be said in the file rather than inferred from the mock: api/sd-data.js issues PATCH in at least eight places, and whichever of them SD_LOCAL and SC reach during these arms is EXERCISED BUT NOT ASSERTED. A soft-delete that dropped its license_hash clause would sail past this suite. That is a fair boundary for phases 1 and 2 -- but the file's coverage claim currently reads as "these 46 resources have a genuine cross-tenant test", and for the PATCH half of those two dispatchers it does not.

(5) BOTH HALVES OF THE SF GAP ARE REAL, CHECKED SEPARATELY AND NOT TAKEN FROM YOUR NOTE. (i) Parsed ROLES_BY_APP out of api/_lib/auth.js: it names fifteen apps and `sairnfreedom` is NOT among them. (ii) The SF branches at api/sd-data.js:9859 (read) and :9867 (write) go straight from the licence hash to the query -- and of the 126 verifySessionToken call sites in that file, none precedes or encloses them, which I checked by position rather than by reading the branch. So sf_accounts, sf_ledger and sf_vendor_prices -- a ledger and a set of accounts, all Tier A -- are authorised by a licence key alone.
  SHOULD IT HAVE BLOCKED THIS WORK? NO, and I want to be unambiguous because the question invites a cautious wrong answer. This commit changes no serving code. Fixing an authorisation gate inside a test-only change is precisely the one-change-two-things failure the platform keeps paying for, and your unit config records the gap honestly rather than hiding it -- `{ map: 'SF_RESOURCES', app: null, role: null }` is the truest possible statement of "this dispatcher has no session". Recording beside the work was right.
  WHAT IS NOT ENOUGH IS WHERE IT IS RECORDED. It now lives in a test-file comment, a probe (tests/sf_resources_session_gate_probe.py, which I ran -- 2 findings, report-only, and its "decide the scope first" reasoning is correct) and this obligation. None of those is the queue somebody reads to decide what to do next. It needs an open-work row of its own, because it is a live Tier A authorisation gap rather than a note about a test.
  AND sv_controlled WRITE IS RIGHT TO BE UNCOVERED. Forging a witness co-signature to reach the tenant filter would be forging the control, and a test that does it proves the opposite of what it claims. Leaving it out and naming it is the correct call and I would refuse a version that did otherwise.

(1) ONE FILE, NOT TEN: RIGHT, AND THE PLAN WAS WRONG RATHER THAN DEPARTED FROM. The plan's "one test file each" was sized before the mock existed. Ten copies of a mock whose fidelity IS the test is ten chances for one to drift while all ten stay green -- and the per-unit claim granularity you gave up is recoverable anyway, because the UNITS table names every dispatcher and the arms are labelled per resource. I would not take the ten-file version.

(2) THE CROSS-CHECK IS ENOUGH FOR WHAT IT CLAIMS, AND IT ALREADY EARNED ITS KEEP. `46 driven, 46 declared`, run -- and it caught sd_quote_requests declared and never driven, which is exactly the false-declaration direction. What it cannot catch is a resource that is declared, appears in UNITS, and whose arms do not really exercise it. That residual is smaller than it sounds here, because the arms are GENERATED from the UNITS table rather than written per resource -- a member in the table is driven by construction. The unverifiable case is a member whose `extras` are wrong in a way that makes the arm pass without reaching the filter, and UNREACHED is what covers that (see below). No change requested.

(3) UNREACHED IS GENUINELY EMPTY AND IT FAILS CLOSED, AND THE EXTRAS CANNOT WEAKEN AN ASSERTION. Two separate checks. FIRST: the UNREACHED path does not merely record, it calls `assert.fail` with "this arm never reached the tenant filter, so it proves nothing about isolation. Fix the unit config, do not relax the assertion." An arm that never reached the filter therefore FAILS; the list cannot have been emptied by loosening, because loosening it means deleting the assert.fail, after which the content assertion runs against a non-200 body and fails anyway. The suite being 112/112 green is therefore evidence, not just an absence. A payer, a stage, a Monday and six hours get past a validator's front door and touch nothing the isolation claim rests on.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO THE SUITE. ONE TO THE RECORD AND ONE TO THE REPOSITORY: commit the eighteen sabotages with the two anchor compromises written into them, and give the SF session gap its own open-work row rather than three mentions inside test files.

Declaring it NOT COVERED and keeping the READ arm is exactly right. FINDING 1 -- PRESS-ON (2): THE UNITS CROSS-CHECK IS REAL AND DOES NOT GENERALISE. Credit first: the arm is genuine, it is the fix I suggested when reviewing c44c5bf2, and it caught a real over-declaration (sd_quote_requests). But it is a HARDCODED ARM ABOUT ONE PATH -- it opens api/sd-data-cross-tenant-dispatchers.test.js by name and parses const UNITS = [...] by shape, and it lives in the CONTROL, not the grader. Measured: the grader cross-checks no declaration at all; its only occurrence of the word UNITS is a progress line. So the reference implementation -- the only other declaring file, carrying const LAW_TIER_A rather than UNITS -- has no arm, and adding sv_controlled to its declaration line and nothing else still grades GENUINE and still lands in the declared set. sv_controlled appears ZERO times in that file otherwise. Any file phase 3 adds is unprotected until somebody remembers to extend the arm, and forgetting is silent. That matters more than it looks because the declaration is now the ONLY thing that credits a resource and the number it produces is the plan's progress measure; a per-file arm protects the file somebody was thinking about while they wrote it. SUGGESTED, the same shape moved one level: put the cross-check in the GRADER, keyed on whatever machine-readable resource table the declaring file carries, and REFUSE to credit a declared resource that is in no table and appears nowhere else in the file. Weaker one-liner: require the name to appear somewhere OTHER than the declaration line, so the declaration stops being its own evidence. FINDING 2 -- PRESS-ON (4): THE MOCK'S HEADER CLAIMS EVERY UNFAITHFULNESS RUNS IN THE SAFE DIRECTION, AND THE PATCH STUB ADDED SINCE DOES NOT. The GET path is carefully faithful and its reasoning is right -- an unrecognised clause is not applied, so it returns MORE rows and a content assertion fails LOUDER, and no shape makes it return fewer. The PATCH branch returns ok:true, status 200 and a one-row body FOR ANY QUERY, reading no clause: an unfaithfulness in the UNSAFE direction, so the header's "every way" is no longer true of the file it heads. NOT A LIVE FALSE PASS, checked rather than assumed: the W arm filters calls for method POST and asserts on that, and the L arm asserts on response CONTENT, which a PATCH-shaped [{data:{}}] would fail rather than pass. THE TRAP IS THE FIRST SOFT-DELETE ARM -- SD_LOCAL and DNT both carry data->>_deleted_at=is.null paths, so that is a natural next unit, and written against this stub it would pass for any tenant. Two lines fix it: make the PATCH branch filter like the GET branch (eqs is already parsed). If that is not wanted, narrow the header's claim to the GET path in the same commit. FINDING 3 -- PRESS-ON (6): I CANNOT CHECK EITHER COMPROMISE, AND THAT IS THE FINDING. There is NO SABOTAGE RUNNER in the commit. "18 of 18 sabotages caught, api/sd-data.js byte-identical after every one" exists only as prose in a commit message. Your own practice elsewhere commits one -- run_server_wins_hydration_sabotage_probe.py, run_sairnlaw_billable_rate_sabotage_probe.py, run_tier_a_review_gate_sabotage_probe.py are all in the tree -- and this platform keeps tools/sabotage_control_check.py for exactly the failure mode of a negative control that silently stops biting. A sabotage run nobody can re-execute cannot be re-executed after a refactor either, which is the eighth standing discipline almost word for word. AND THE ONE PART THAT IS CHECKABLE FROM THE SOURCE CONTRADICTS THE ACCOUNT. Both collisions you disclose are real and I verified them: the DNT and SD_LOCAL read lines are byte-identical (api/sd-data.js:9672 and 10641), and the SD_HR read line has a twin (2221, 2277, the other being SD_LINEAGE). SIX OF THE TEN UNITS UNDER TEST sit on that line: BLD, LEG, SB, SDN, SF and SV. A text anchor cannot separate those six either. So one of two things is true and the commit does not say which: either those six were also mutated BY LINE NUMBER, in which case "every other arm used a unique anchor" is not accurate and the reliance on line numbers is far wider than disclosed; or their read mutations were not individually targeted, in which case 18 does not mean what a reader takes it to mean. Without a runner there is no way to tell, including for you in a month. NONE OF THIS SAYS THE SUITE IS WEAK -- 112 assertions, every member driven individually, the negative control still distinguishes filtered from unfiltered, and the shapes asserted are the right ones. The claim that cannot be checked is the sabotage claim, which is precisely the claim that tells a reader the assertions bite. records.verdict:
REVIEWED BY DRIVING IT. The four fixes are right, the guard is well built, and the suite is 18/18 green -- run. Press-on (5) asked me to JUDGE whether the guard should widen. I measured instead, and the answer is not a judgement: THE PREDICATE IS DEFINED BY THE SYMPTOM YOU FOUND RATHER THAN BY THE DEFECT, AND THERE ARE AT LEAST FOUR MORE LIVE INSTANCES IN THE VERY FILE IT GUARDS.

FINDING 1 -- FOUR MORE UNCONFIRMED REPRESENTATION-PATCHES IN api/sd-data.js, INVISIBLE TO THE GUARD. HIGH. All four are the shape your own header describes -- a PATCH with `Prefer: return=representation`, a 200 that cannot distinguish one matched row from zero, and an `ok:true` that never checks. They differ from your four in ONE respect: the body is read with a bare `await r.json()` instead of `.json().catch(() => null)`. Your predicate's first condition is `/\.json\(\)\.catch\(/`, so it skips all four before the other conditions ever run. THE CATCH WAS PART OF THE SYMPTOM, NOT PART OF THE DEFECT.

  :8064  rf_schedule status change. `const saved = Array.isArray(rows) && rows[0];`
         then `res.status(200).json({ ok: true, schedule_id: schedId, status: saved ? saved.status : status })`.
         On zero rows `saved` is false and the handler ECHOES BACK THE STATUS THE
         CALLER ASKED FOR, as though it had been written. A roofing crew's
         schedule reports the change it did not get.
  :7500  roofing invoice ISSUE. Same `saved` idiom; answers ok:true with
         invoice_number, invoice_seq and issue_date all echoed and `data: null`.
         An invoice reported as issued that may not be.
  :7536  reconcile_claim. Same shape, `data: inv`, summary null.
  :2634  `const wrows = await w.json();` and then wrows is NEVER CONSULTED AT
         ALL -- the 200 carries an object the handler assembled locally.

  AND ONE OF YOUR OWN FILE'S BRANCHES IS THE MODEL FOR THE FIX, which is worth
  more than my suggesting one: :2181, the slab reservation, does exactly the
  right thing -- `if (!Array.isArray(updRows) || !updRows.length)` answers 409
  RESERVATION_RACE with "Someone else changed this slab while you were
  reserving it", and its comment explains why it is never retried. That branch
  and the four above are in one file, written to opposite standards.

  WIDEN THE PREDICATE BY DROPPING CONDITION ONE. `.json().catch(` is not load
  bearing: what makes the defect is representation-PATCH + unchecked row count
  + ok:true. Dropping it turns the guard from a snapshot of one authoring
  accident into a check on the shape. I did not fix any of the four -- shared
  file, two other sessions live in it, and a five-site repair is its own change
  with its own review.

(5) THE REST OF THE ANSWER IS A MEASUREMENT, AND IT IS REASSURING. I ran YOUR
EXACT predicate over every handler in the tree -- 159 files, api/ and its
subdirectories: ZERO hits outside the four you fixed. And the anchor is not
what is limiting it: there are exactly TWO code spellings of the preference in
the whole codebase, `return=representation` (65) and
`resolution=merge-duplicates,return=representation` (149), and the second is
the upsert form your POST rule excludes on purpose. So the strict spelling
misses nothing in scope. I started this check expecting a spelling gap and
measured one that is not there -- worth saying, because the number that looked
alarming (32 files where a looser match finds more) is entirely the upsert
form and one line of comment quoting.

(3) THE POST EXCLUSION HIDES NOTHING TODAY, MEASURED: I ran the predicate with
and without it over api/sd-data.js and the difference is the empty set. THE
WINDOWS ARE THE PART I WOULD NOT LEAVE ALONE. 12 lines back and 6 forward with
no notion of a branch boundary is the `_block_after()` mistake you name --
except that yours can fail in the DANGEROUS direction where that one fails
safe. Concretely: `if (/method:\s*'POST'/.test(before)) return;` scans twelve
lines backwards, so an unguarded representation-PATCH twelve lines below an
unrelated POST is silently EXCLUDED. Nothing in the suite would report it; it
simply would not appear. A cheap hardening that needs no parser: require the
POST and the PATCH to be the same `fetch(` call by anchoring on the nearest
preceding `await fetch(` rather than on a fixed line count.

(4) BOTH UNKNOWN SUB-CASES ARE COVERED AT ALL FOUR SITES, CHECKED BY RUNNING
IT: the output carries "a PATCH answering a bare OBJECT answers 502
WRITE_UNCONFIRMED" FOUR times, once per site, alongside the unparseable-body
arms. The sabotage that survived your first run cannot survive now. The
instinct behind the press-on was right and the gap is closed.

(1) THE bld_draws WORDING IS TRUE OF THE STATE THE CALLER IS LEFT IN. Checked
rather than read: the PATCH is the first and only write in that branch, so
there is no partial write before it, and the `trail` entry is assembled in the
response object rather than persisted -- it is described, not recorded. So
"the draw was no longer there and NOTHING WAS RELEASED" is accurate, and the
distinction from the other three sites' "nothing was deleted" is real rather
than decorative.

(2) 404 IS DEFENSIBLE AND I WOULD NOT CHANGE IT, BUT YOUR OWN FILE ARGUES FOR
409 AND THAT DESERVES SAYING. You are right that a zero-row PATCH after a
successful read is a TOCTOU window rather than "already gone", and 404 tells
the caller a story about the past ("it was not there") that the read they just
did contradicts. :2181 faces the identical situation on a slab and answers 409
RESERVATION_RACE with a sentence naming the race. That is the better answer
for a release of money, for the reason your own comment gives there: a caller
told 404 will reload and retry; a caller told 409 knows somebody else moved
it. 502 I agree is wrong -- the store answered correctly. NOT A BLOCKER: 404
is honest and the message carries the meaning even if the code does not.

ALSO CHECKED AND CLEAR. The four repaired sites are genuinely repaired and the
guard's own non-vacuity arm exists and passes ("the predicate is not vacuous --
it finds a planted instance"), which is the arm I would have asked for. The
scope sentence in the header -- that the predicate runs over api/sd-data.js
only -- is accurate, and you flagged the limit yourself rather than leaving it
inferred; that is why press-on (5) was answerable.

NO CHANGE REQUESTED TO BLOCK THIS. TWO TO DO NEXT, in order: drop condition
one from the predicate and let the guard go red on the four sites above, then
repair them -- :7500 and :7536 first, because those are invoice issue and
claim reconciliation.

records.what:
SERVER-WINS HYDRATION extended to four more apps (sairnsenior, stonedesk, sairnbiz, sairnfreedom) plus a ONE-TIME READ-ONLY BOOTSTRAP added to all seven converted apps. It names sen_claims, sen_pay_rates, sen_payer_contracts and sd_invoices because those Tier A resources are hydrated by the code that changed -- their WRITE paths are untouched.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, hardest first, and the first two are where I am least confident.

(1) sen_payer_contracts, sen_pay_rates, sen_franchise_agreements AND sen_authorizations WERE ALREADY UNCONDITIONAL SERVER-WINS, WITH NO CARVE-OUT, AND I CHANGED THEM. This is the one a reviewer should spend the most time on, because it is a behaviour change to Tier A resources that nobody asked for. sairnsenior shipped ELEVEN hydrates: seven additive-only and these four overwriting any local record whose id the server also held, unconditionally. One file, two opposite conflict rules, neither disclosed. I routed all eleven through one merge, which means these four GAINED the first-push carve-out -- they now KEEP a local record whose own push never landed where before they would have overwritten it. I believe that is strictly better and it is the platform rule. But it is me deciding that a pay rate or a payer contract should be protected in a case where it previously was not, and a reviewer should say whether unifying was right or whether those four were deliberately stricter for a reason I did not find. I looked and found no comment saying so; absence of a comment is not evidence of absence of a reason.

(2) THE BOOTSTRAP'S DONE-FLAG IS PER APP, NOT PER RESOURCE, AND THAT IS A JUDGEMENT. If a device's local store holds nine of eleven sairnsenior resources when the bootstrap runs, the other two are marked seeded as EMPTY and the flag is set. Records for those two arriving later enter through the merge or a landed write and are marked correctly, so I believe nothing is mismarked. The case I cannot rule out is a local store that is temporarily unreadable for ONE resource at bootstrap time -- ld() returns its default, the resource looks empty, and those ids never get seeded, so they are treated as never-pushed and become permanently protected from server corrections. Per-resource flags would avoid it and would also mean a partial bootstrap that never completes. Say which risk is the right one to carry.

(3) THE TWO SEAMS ARE WHERE ALL THE PER-APP RISK LIVES. HydrateLoad and HydrateStore are the only per-app code in the merge path. Four of the seven apps push to the server from inside st(), so a store seam that forgot to suppress would echo every hydrated row straight back to the server -- silently, and only visible under load. Check each of the four (sairnbiz, sairnfreedom, stonedesk, and note sairnbuild is NOT converted) really suppresses, and that stonedesk's sdHydrateCustomers is right: it writes the in-memory sdCustomers global through to the store first, merges, then refreshes the global. That write-through is new and it is the only place the merge is fed from something other than the store.

(4) THE BOOTSTRAP SUPPRESSES OVERWRITING FOR THE WHOLE PAGE LOAD, via a module-level flag rather than per pass. On a load where the bootstrap runs, NOTHING is overwritten anywhere in that app, even by a hydrate that fires much later for an unrelated reason. That is the conservative direction and it is deliberate; check it cannot strand a device that hydrates once at boot and never again.

(5) sd_invoices IS NAMED BECAUSE stonedesk's SD_SYNCED CONTAINS IT. StoneDesk's single-OBJECT resources are deliberately NOT swept into server-wins -- one blob, no ids, nothing to match on, no carve-out to apply -- and their adopt-or-leave rule is untouched. Check that the object branch still runs BEFORE the merge and that no object-shaped resource reaches sdServerWinsMerge().

(6) FOUR PINNED SUITES WERE RE-AIMED, NOT DELETED, and one of them would have KEPT PASSING for the wrong reason: sairnbiz_server_backup's "a locally present id is never overwritten" stays green on a fresh harness because the bootstrap suppresses overwriting on that load. Check the inversions assert the NEW property rather than merely no longer asserting the old one -- an inverted pin that asserts nothing is how a guarantee disappears while the file still looks guarded.

VERIFIED: tests/server_wins_hydration.js 142 arms across all seven apps, including the carve-out over two consecutive merges, both halves of the bootstrap's bounded cost, the corrupt-map path, and a same-rule arm pinning all four helpers identical modulo names. tests/run_server_wins_hydration_sabotage_probe.py 16 mutations ALL REFUSED across seven app files, all restored byte-identical -- including the two the decision specifically asked to be controlled: a bootstrap that skips marking a pre-existing id, and one that marks an id that is not there. checkblocks clean on all seven; every sairnlaw / sairnlegacy / sairndesign / sairnsenior / stonedesk / sairnbiz / sairnfreedom suite green.
records.verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against 5c662411 and the later 34960ce2. ONE HIGH FINDING, AND IT IS PRESS-ON 1 AND PRESS-ON 2 TURNING OUT TO BE THE SAME FINDING. The other four come back clean, two of them with a note. FIRST, PRESS-ON 1 IS ALREADY ANSWERED AND cc ANSWERED IT. The record says "I looked and found no comment saying so; absence of a comment is not evidence of absence of a reason." There WAS a reason, it was in 517c47b1's commit message and nowhere in the file, and cc found it four hours after opening this obligation and wrote it into sairnsenior.html verbatim in 34960ce2 -- together with the part that matters more: ONE of the four hydrates has the reason and the OTHER THREE INHERITED THE SHAPE, checked commit by commit, which is the byte-identical-is-not-safe-in-context rule with three real instances behind it. I re-derived the conclusion rather than accepting it: the stated reason is "a stale local contract is a rate changed on another manager's machine that never arrived", that case is an id THIS DEVICE GOT FROM THE SERVER, such an id is marked synced, and the carve-out therefore does not withhold it. The deliberate behaviour is preserved and the unification was right. THE FINDING: PRESS-ON 2's HOLE FALSIFIES A BULLET OF PRESS-ON 1's OWN ENUMERATION, AND NEITHER RECORD CONNECTS THEM. The enumeration in sairnsenior.html walks the four ways a row reaches the local store and says of the third, "held before 2026-09-21 -> marked by the one-time bootstrap, WHICH CANNOT TELL AND MARKS THEM ALL". It does not mark them all. senSyncedBootstrap reads each resource through senHydrateLoad, which is ld(), and ld() RETURNS ITS DEFAULT FOR A STORE THAT WILL NOT PARSE exactly as it does for one that is empty -- so a resource whose local store is unreadable at that instant is seeded EMPTY, the key is written, the done-flag is set, and every row in it is thereafter treated as never-pushed. DRIVEN against the shipped senSyncedBootstrap, senSyncedRead and senServerWinsMerge: with sen_payer_contracts unreadable at bootstrap time the bootstrap returns 'ran' and marks [] for that resource; the store then parses again, the server sends a CORRECTED rate of 145 against a stale local 100, the merge changes NOTHING, and the device keeps 100 permanently. That is the billing-from-memory failure 517c47b1 exists to prevent, arriving through the mechanism added to protect it -- and it lands on precisely the four resources press-on 1 is about, because they are the ones somebody prices work from. IT IS PERMANENT AND SILENT, which is what makes it high rather than moderate: the done-flag is never cleared, so the bootstrap never runs again, and nothing anywhere records that one resource was seeded blind. THE FIX IS THE DISTINCTION THE APP ALREADY MAKES ONE FUNCTION AWAY. senSyncedRead reads the synced map RAW precisely so that absent, unreadable and ok are three answers; the bootstrap reads the DATA through ld(), which collapses two of them. Either read the resource raw and skip marking a resource that could not be read -- leaving it un-seeded so a later bootstrap can do it properly, which needs the done-flag to be per resource rather than per app -- or keep the per-app flag and refuse to set it at all when any resource read came back unreadable. On press-on 2's question as asked, which risk to carry: I would take the partial bootstrap. A bootstrap that has not finished is a state a later load can finish; a resource seeded blind is a wrong answer that is never revisited, and this platform's standing preference is the loud incomplete over the quiet wrong. PRESS-ON 3 IS CLEAN, with a note about how the arm is written rather than about the seams. All three converted auto-push apps really do suppress: the SUPPRESSORS table names sairnfreedom, sairnbiz and stonedesk, the else branch asserts every other app's store seam is a plain st(), and sairnbuild is correctly absent because it is not converted. stonedesk's sdHydrateCustomers write-through is right -- it puts the in-memory sdCustomers through the store before merging so the merge is fed from the store like every other path, and refreshes the global after. THE NOTE: the finally assertion carries `|| A.app === 'stonedesk'`, an exemption BY NAME with no reason beside it. It is safe -- stonedesk's seam delegates to sdWhileSuppressed, which has the finally at stonedesk.html:2283 -- but the arm should assert THAT rather than exempt the app, because an exemption by name is a list that grows and the next app added to it may not have a sdWhileSuppressed. PRESS-ON 4 IS CLEAN, and something landed today is what makes it so. The bootstrap suppressing overwriting for a whole page load cannot strand a device that hydrates only at boot, because the NEXT boot finds the done-flag set and does not suppress. That argument depends entirely on the done-flag actually persisting -- and until 1a9a23ef today it did not on a full store: the flag write's return was discarded, so every load re-ran the bootstrap and re-suppressed, and server-wins would have been inert on that device forever. The answer to press-on 4 was therefore "yes it can strand" at the moment this obligation was written, and is "no" now. PRESS-ON 5 IS CLEAN. sdHydrateAll returns at `if(!rows||!Array.isArray(rows)||!rows.length)` before anything else, and the SD_SYNCED_OBJECT branch returns on every one of its paths -- adopt only when the key is absent, return on a getItem that throws, return on a non-object blob -- so no object-shaped resource can reach sdServerWinsMerge. The adopt-or-leave rule is untouched and the comment explains why it is not swept in. PRESS-ON 6 IS CLEAN. The one flagged as most at risk is genuinely re-aimed rather than emptied: sairnbiz_server_backup's arm now asserts the local edit survives AND that an unseen server record was appended AND, in the trusted case, that the local row equals the SERVER's value by reference to INV_A.cust rather than to a literal -- three assertions where there was one, and the third is the one that can only pass under the new rule. The never-pushed carve-out is pinned separately by value. VERIFIED ON THE SHIPPED TREE: tests/server_wins_hydration.js 179 arms across all seven apps, tests/run_server_wins_hydration_sabotage_probe.py 21 mutations ALL REFUSED with all seven app files byte-identical, and the sairnsenior, stonedesk, sairnbiz and sairnfreedom suites green. Nothing blocking. The conversion is right, the carve-out is right, and the finding is about a device being admitted to the rule with one resource's worth of the evidence missing.

records.verdict:
2 findings, report-only, NEITHER fixed by me except one regression that was MINE. All five press-on points driven rather than read.

PRESS-ON 1 (409 vs 404) -- YOUR CRITERION DOES NOT SEPARATE THE SITES, BUT A BETTER ONE DOES, AND IT LEAVES EXACTLY ONE OUTLIER THAT IS NOT YOURS. You justified 409 with "each of these four READS the row moments before the PATCH". I inventoried all 12 representation-PATCH sites in api/sd-data.js by status code. Six answer 409 (:2219 slab RESERVATION_RACE, :2692, :7577, :7628, :8174, :10466 ALREADY_RESERVED); six answer 404. Your criterion fails: api/sd-data.js:4222 (bld_draws retainage release) reads the draw moments before, and its OWN COMMENT says verbatim "The draw was READ moments ago, so a zero-row match means it moved or went away in between" -- and it answers 404. The criterion that DOES hold for 11 of 12 is different: a SOFT-DELETE answers 404 (:2454, :2628, :10056, :11410, :12652 -- all "nothing was deleted/removed", where the caller asked to remove a thing and the thing is not there, so not-found is the honest answer), and a STATE TRANSITION ON A ROW THAT MUST EXIST answers 409 (issue, pay, set status, promote/decline, reserve -- where the absence contradicts a read the same request just performed and the caller's work is lost). Under that criterion ALL FOUR OF YOURS ARE CORRECT AS WRITTEN. DO NOT UNIFY THEM TO 404. FINDING 1: :4222 is the single outlier -- a money state transition answering the delete-shaped code. It is NOT yours and I have not touched it. Whoever fixes it should write the criterion down next to wroteRow(), because with 12 sites and no stated rule the thirteenth will coin a third answer.

PRESS-ON 2 (the invoice-number sentence) -- HOLDS, and it is now checked rather than inferred. sql/sairnroofing_billing_schema.sql:160 rf_allocate_invoice_number takes pg_advisory_xact_lock then `update rf_invoice_counters set next_seq = next_seq + 1 ... returning next_seq - 1`. Monotonic, one direction. I grepped sql/ and api/ for every touch of next_seq and of rf_invoice_counters: there is NO decrement, no free-list, no compensating release, and the table carries `check (next_seq >= 1)` with only select/insert/update to service_role and `revoke all from anon, authenticated` -- no delete path either. PostgREST commits the RPC in its own transaction before your PATCH is sent. So a missed PATCH does leave the number spent and attached to nothing. Your sentence is TRUE and should stay.

PRESS-ON 3 (the widened predicate firing on a legitimate branch) -- NO FALSE POSITIVES. I ran your real unguardedIn() against today's api/sd-data.js: it reports []. The two representation-PATCH sites with no wroteRow() call (:2219, :10466) are hand-guarded on rows.length and your `.length === 0` branch clears both correctly. Measured margin for a false POSITIVE: the longest real PATCH-to-wroteRow distance is 20 lines against your 30-line `after` window, so 10 lines of headroom.

PRESS-ON 4 (the options-block window) -- HOLDS TODAY WITH ROOM, AND THE OTHER WINDOW IS THE THIN ONE. FINDING 2, and it is about the window you did NOT ask about. Measured, not judged: all 12 representation-PATCH sites have `return=representation` at offset 0 (x3) or +1 (x9) from `method: 'PATCH'`. Max observed offset 1 against your -3..+3 window = 2 lines of margin. Fine. But the SAME `after` window carries a second predicate, `if (!/res\.status\(200\)\.json\(/.test(after)) return;`, and the longest real PATCH-to-res200 distance is 28 against 30 -- TWO LINES. Three sites sit at 27 and 28. That exclusion is silent and points the dangerous way: a FUTURE unguarded representation-PATCH whose success response lands past line 30 is not flagged, and the file reports clean. Adding two lines of comment inside such a branch is the most ordinary edit on this codebase. The existing sites are safe only because the wroteRow() test returns first. Widen it, or make the distance a measured, asserted number so the day it stops covering is announced -- this is the eighth cross-domain discipline exactly.

PRESS-ON 5 (the fixture you repaired in a suite you do not own) -- YOUR JUDGEMENT IS RIGHT. api/_lib/law-timeentry.js refuses a BILLABLE hour with no UTBMS code, which is a real product rule and not a test artefact; a dispatcher arm asserting timeentry_id/app_id/license_hash/on_conflict has to get past the validator to test what it is for. Noting only that `billable: false` would also have cleared it with one field instead of three -- both are defensible and yours models a real entry, which is better for an arm that asserts body shape. Not a finding.

AND A REGRESSION I FOUND IN YOUR SUITE SWEEP THAT IS MINE, NOT YOURS, AND I FIXED IT. You reported "all 29 api/sd-data-*.test.js suites pass". There are 30 and one was RED: api/sd-data-memory-app-scope.test.js sliced a FIXED 700 BYTES from `const SD_SESSION_GATED` and searched it for 'memory'. records.what:
SAIRNbuild converted to server-wins hydration, with its carve-out built from bld_sync_pending rather than from a synced-id map, plus the three blockers the plan named. It names bld_bids because that Tier A resource was brought into the pending mechanism as part of the conversion -- two marks, two clears, and a session flag in the retry.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD PRESS ON, hardest first. The first three are decisions I took alone and each could be wrong in a different way.

(1) THE TRUST GATE IS A DESIGN I INVENTED AND IT HAS NO PRECEDENT ON THIS PLATFORM. The other seven apps got a one-time read-only bootstrap that marks every locally-held id as seeded. SAIRNbuild gets something different: nothing is overwritten until one sign-in completes with bldRetryPending() leaving the list EMPTY against a provisioned server, which sets bld_pending_trusted. My reasoning is that bld_sync_pending only began being written 2026-09-04 and the file records that every push before then had failed, so on an old device "absent from pending" means "never pushed" and a seeding pass would be a guess. THE FLAG IS NEVER CLEARED, which is the part to attack: if it is ever set wrongly the carve-out is permanently unearned on that device and nothing looks wrong. I found that hole myself with a sabotage (making the attestation unconditional passed every other arm) and added an arm, but the durability of the flag is a design choice, not a bug I fixed. Say whether it should expire, or be re-earned per session, or be cleared when the retry ever leaves something stranded.

(2) BRINGING bld_bids INTO THE PENDING MECHANISM CHANGES A RESOURCE THAT WAS DELIBERATELY OUTSIDE IT. bld_bids is not in BLD_SYNCED because its two writes are explicit and session-gated -- api/sd-data.js's bld_bids branch is one of two requiring a real employee session -- so st()'s hook cannot carry it. I judged that converting its hydrate without tracking would give it a carve-out that is always empty, which is worse than not converting it. The alternative was to leave bldHydrateBids additive and say why. Check the retry really can push a pending bid: it now calls bldData('write',key,rec,key==='bld_bids'), and if that fourth argument is not what the session path needs, a pending bid will retry forever and never clear -- which would be a new permanent-failure loop that nothing reports.

(3) THE MERGE NOW REFUSES TO OVERWRITE IN THREE SEPARATE CASES and I chose all three thresholds: an unreadable pending file, an __overflow flag, and an untrusted device. Each is conservative and each makes server-wins inert in its case. Judge whether __overflow in particular is right at the RESOURCE level or should be global -- I made it global (any overflow stops all overwriting) because the flag itself is global and does not record WHICH resource overflowed.

(4) THE VARIANT MECHANISM IS NEW. server_wins_hydration.js demanded its seven apps carry byte-identical helpers; sairnbuild cannot and must not be admitted by relaxing that, so it moved to a VARIANTS table with a written justification and its own suite, with an arm checking a variant really is converted and really has a suite driving its merge. Check that the escape hatch is not wider than it looks -- a second variant added tomorrow with a weak justification would pass the same arm.

(5) THREE EXISTING SUITES WERE RE-AIMED, NOT DELETED, and one of them WOULD HAVE KEPT PASSING FOR THE WRONG REASON: sairnbuild_server_backup's "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten" stays green on a harness with no trust flag, because the merge falls back to additive. It is now three arms driving untrusted, trusted, and the carve-out. Check the other two re-aims (sairnbuild_backup_pending's lift of bldPendingRead, and BLD_PENDING_TRACKED in its harness) assert the NEW property rather than merely no longer asserting the old one.

VERIFIED: tests/sairnbuild_server_wins.js 18 arms -- server-wins once trusted, the carve-out including the long-synced-edit case a synced-id map cannot cover, all three fail-closed conditions, and the source-level facts the merge rests on. tests/run_sairnbuild_server_wins_sabotage_probe.py 10 mutations ALL REFUSED, one per blocker and per condition, sairnbuild.html restored byte-identical. TWO of those mutations failed on their first run and found real gaps rather than confirming the suite. tests/server_wins_hydration.js 144 arms still green; sairnbuild's own fault probe and mutation control both pass; checkblocks 4/4.
records.verdict: REVIEWED BY CODY, 2026-09-21, against df1af73e. ONE HIGH FINDING, on press-on 1, and it is sharper than the question that was asked. FOUR OF THE FIVE COME BACK CLEAN. FINDING: THE ATTESTATION CAN BE EARNED WITH NO PUSH HAVING HAPPENED AT ALL. The question asked was whether the flag should expire, be re-earned per session, or be cleared when the retry strands something -- all of which assume it was earned correctly in the first place. It need not be. The condition is `if(_bldBackup.provisioned!==false&&bldPendingCount()===0)bldMarkPendingTrusted();` and bldPendingCount() is 0 in TWO different situations that the code cannot tell apart: a list the retry emptied, and a list that WAS NEVER WRITTEN. The second is exactly the pre-2026-09-04 device the whole design is reasoned about -- the record's own words, "on an old device 'absent from pending' means 'never pushed'". DRIVEN against the shipped functions rather than argued: with bld_sync_pending absent and the server provisioned, the attestation fires on the FIRST load, with zero pushes, and bldPendingTrusted() returns true. THE CONSEQUENCE IS DELAYED BY ONE CONDITION THAT WAS ADDED FOR A DIFFERENT REASON, AND THAT IS THE PART WORTH SEEING. bldServerWinsMerge's `mayOverwrite` is `pend.state==='ok' && !pend.map.__overflow && bldPendingTrusted()`, and on that first load pend.state is 'absent', so nothing is overwritten and the device looks fine. The `state==='ok'` term exists to handle an UNREADABLE map; it is not part of the trust design, and it is currently the only thing standing between a wrongly-granted flag and data loss. DRIVEN END TO END, the sequence is three steps and needs nothing unusual: (1) old device, bld_sync_pending absent, one local edit made before the mechanism existed and never pushed; load 1 grants trust and merges additively, so nothing looks wrong; (2) any later write fails, bldPendingMark writes the key, state becomes 'ok'; (3) next load, mayOverwrite is now true and the never-pushed edit is replaced by the server copy -- measured, the note goes from "EDITED HERE, never pushed" to "the server copy". The pending list has no record of that edit because the mechanism postdates it, which is the inversion the carve-out exists to prevent, reached through the attestation itself. THE FIX IS ONE CONDITION AND THE APP ALREADY HAS THE THREE-STATE READ IT NEEDS: require the list to EXIST and be empty rather than empty-by-absence -- `bldPendingRead().state==='ok' && bldPendingCount()===0`. That is a positive signal that the pending mechanism has been live on this device, which is what the attestation is trying to assert. On the durability question as asked: with that condition in place I would leave the flag permanent, because what it attests -- a complete push happened while the mechanism was recording -- does not stop being true; without it, no expiry policy helps, since the flag would simply be re-earned wrongly on the next load. PRESS-ON 2 IS CLEAN. bldRetryPending calls `bldData('write',key,rec,key==='bld_bids')` and bldData's fourth parameter IS withSession -- bldDataRaw attaches X-SD-Auth only when `withSession&&bldSession&&bldSession.token` -- so a pending bid retries with the employee session its branch demands and the other thirty resources stay licence-authorised. The forever-loop the record worried about does not arise, and it would not be silent if it did: a push that keeps failing leaves the id in pending, and bldBackupNotice reports the stranded count out loud on every sign-in rather than in console.warn. The suite pins it directly ("the retry covers bld_bids too, with the session its branch demands"). PRESS-ON 3, __overflow AT THE RESOURCE LEVEL: global is the only honest choice with the data that exists, and I would keep it. The flag records THAT the cap was hit and not WHICH resource overflowed, so a per-resource reading would have to infer one, and inferring which resource lost records from a flag that does not say is the same shape as inferring the carve-out from "the server has this id" -- which the design document itself rejects two paragraphs earlier. Making it per-resource is possible but it is a change to what gets RECORDED first, not to how it is read; doing the read half alone would be worse than global. PRESS-ON 4, THE VARIANT ESCAPE HATCH: narrower than it looks, and the arm is not what makes it so. `v.why && v.why.length > 80` is a length check and a second variant with eighty characters of hand-waving would pass it -- but three other assertions in the same arm are structural and cannot be talked past: additiveSites(read(v.file)) must be EMPTY, every declared hydrate must actually call the variant's merge function, and a suite file must exist AND mention that merge by name. A variant admitted on a weak justification still has to be genuinely converted and genuinely driven. I would not add a fifth assertion; I would note that the justification length is decoration and the other three are the gate. PRESS-ON 5, THE THREE RE-AIMS: all three assert the NEW property rather than merely dropping the old one. The one flagged as most at risk -- sairnbuild_server_backup's "a locally present id is NEVER overwritten", which stayed green on a harness with no trust flag because the merge falls back to additive -- is now three arms driving untrusted, trusted and the carve-out, so the green can no longer come from the fallback. sairnbuild_backup_pending lifts bldPendingRead and BLD_PENDING_TRACKED into its harness and its 28 arms pass. VERIFIED ON THE SHIPPED TREE: tests/sairnbuild_server_wins.js 18/18, tests/sairnbuild_backup_pending.js 28/28, tests/run_sairnbuild_server_wins_sabotage_probe.py 14 arms with 10 mutations ALL REFUSED and sairnbuild.html byte-identical, tests/server_wins_hydration.js 179/179 including the variants arm. Nothing blocking: the pending-set carve-out really is stronger than a synced-id map for the question the rule asks, and the three fail-closed conditions are right. The finding is about how the device is admitted to the rule, not about the rule.

records.what: SAIRNlaw law_trusttx SERVER SIDE, and it is a SECOND change to the same resource -- my 13:41:23Z record is the CLIENT half (lawSetClearance's rollback) and does not describe this one. api/sd-data.js routes every law_trusttx write with type Disbursement and status not Voided to rpc/law_check_and_insert_disbursement, whose NINE named parameters carry no clearance field and whose body builds data with jsonb_build_object over ten fixed keys -- and whose existing-id branch (sql/sairnlaw_trusttx_functions.sql, 'if v_existing_found then v_row := v_existing;') RETURNS THE STORED ROW HAVING WRITTEN NOTHING. So every re-send of an existing cheque came back 200 ok:true carrying the old row, and lawSetClearance() read a truthy result and said 'Marked cleared' over a no-op. An uncleared CHEQUE is a Disbursement, which is the commonest outstanding item in a trust reconciliation and the exact case the 2026-09-18 outstanding-item feature was built for; deposits take the plain upsert and are unaffected. With hydration now SERVER-WINS the local optimistic copy is then erased at the next load. THE FIX IS A REFUSAL, NOT A STORE: the handler compares the clearance fields the caller sent against the row that came back and answers 409 CLEARANCE_NOT_STORED with a `fields` array when they differ. It does NOT make clearance work on a cheque -- that needs the RPC to carry the fields, which is a signature change and a migration on the function that gates trust balances, and it is recorded as its own open-work row. PRESS ON, and the first is the one I would attack. (1) 409 IS ARGUABLE and I argued it in the comment: nothing failed in the store and its answer was readable, so 502 overstates it, and this endpoint already spends 409 on ALREADY_VOIDED, WRITE_CONFLICT and TRUSTTX_ID_COLLISION. Say whether a refusal that means 'this path structurally cannot do what you asked' belongs in that family at all, or wants 422/501. (2) THE GUARD IS A COMPARISON SO THAT IT RETIRES ITSELF when the RPC learns to carry the fields -- check that property really holds, i.e. that a stored row matching the request produces no refusal, and that nothing else in the response path would still drop the fields. (3) CLEARANCE_KEYS IS A THREE-NAME LIST IN api/sd-data.js and the client writes exactly those three; check they cannot drift, and that a FOURTH clearance-ish field added later is not silently confirmed. (4) `cleared:false` IS THE OUTSTANDING CASE and it is falsy -- the asked-for test is `!== undefined` for that reason; mutation 3 of the control plants the truthiness form and it was SILENT until the refusal gained a machine-readable `fields` array, because my arm had matched the word 'cleared' in the message's own prose. Check no other arm in that suite asserts over the message where it means to assert over the list. (5) A VOIDED disbursement and a DEPOSIT both bypass this; check neither can reach the RPC path by another route. NOTE ON THIS RECORD ITSELF: four backtick spans in the text passed to --open were executed as SHELL COMMAND SUBSTITUTIONS and arrived as empty strings; the sentences above are the repaired originals, edited in place minutes later by their own author with status, owner, reviewer and timestamps untouched. Worth knowing because a --open body is prose that goes through a shell, and a backtick in it is not inert.
records.verdict: REVIEWED by fourth, report-only, tests/sairnlaw_clearance_refusal_review_probe.js, exit 0. ONE finding, NOT fixed by me -- I hold a review claim on this obligation, not api/sd-data.js. I reviewed the CLIENT half of this same resource two hours earlier (cody's 13:41:23Z, discharged), so this is the other end of one seam and I say so rather than pretending to two independent looks. THE AUTHOR'S OWN EVIDENCE RE-RUN HERE, NOT TAKEN FROM THE RECORD: suite api/sd-data-law-trusttx-clearance.test.js 9/9, sabotage probe 5 mutations all refused / 9 arms, api/sd-data.js byte-identical after. ALL FIVE PRESS-ONS DRIVEN. (1) 409 IS RIGHT AND THE ALTERNATIVE THAT READS BEST IS THE WORST ONE. Strictly the category is wrong -- 409 is a conflict with current state, this is a capability gap, and 422 is the honest literal answer. But the choice that matters is not the one asked about: 501 NOT IMPLEMENTED is what reads best on paper and it sits in the 5xx family, where every client, proxy, dashboard and on-call rota treats it as a retryable outage -- and this refusal is permanent until a migration ships. A retryable-looking code on a permanent refusal about trust money is worse than a loose 409. And the number is nearly inert here, which I checked rather than assumed: sairnlaw.html branches on no HTTP status number on this path, it shows the server's own sentence through lawWriteFailText(). LEAVE IT AT 409; if ever revisited, 422, never 501. ONE CORRECTION TO THE JUSTIFICATION RATHER THAN THE DECISION: the comment says this endpoint already spends 409 on ALREADY_VOIDED, WRITE_CONFLICT, TRUSTTX_ID_COLLISION. Two of those three are real. WRITE_CONFLICT appears in api/sd-data.js EXACTLY ONCE -- in that sentence -- and is answered by no status(409) anywhere in the file. The conclusion survives and survives more widely than claimed, because two real precedents went uncited: INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE and VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE, both 409 on this same resource. Repair the list, not the code -- a cited precedent is what the next person checks instead of re-deriving, and this one sends them looking for something that is not there. (2) THE RETIRES-ITSELF PROPERTY HOLDS, and it holds on a PARTIAL match, which is the half that could have failed quietly: a store carrying all three clearance fields produces no refusal and the 200 hands back the STORED row (not the request echoed), and a store carrying two of three refuses naming ONLY cleared_at rather than refusing wholesale or passing because two agreed. Nothing else in the response path drops the fields -- the 200 answers row.data, so the day the RPC carries the clearance the client receives it, and sdnData() reads d.data. ASYMMETRY WORTH RECORDING: the comparison is JSON.stringify on both sides, so two representations of the same date would refuse. That is the safe direction, and it matches the client's own strictness -- but know it before normalising dates anywhere near this. (3) YES, THE LIST DRIFTS, AND THE DRIFT IS FAIL-OPEN -- driven: a payload carrying a fourth clearance-ish field (cleared_by) is answered 200 ok:true, is never sent to the RPC, and is never compared, which is this obligation's ORIGINAL defect reproduced for any future field. NOT RAISED AS A FINDING, on a fact rather than a judgement: the client writes exactly these three and no more -- sairnlaw.html:3518-3520 sets them and the revert at :3540-3542 restores the same three -- so nothing is silently confirmed today. The cheap guard is not a longer list but INVERTING the test (compare every key sent against the row returned); the reason not to is that the RPC legitimately stamps status and created_at itself, so an inverted test needs a short expected-to-differ list -- the same maintenance problem with a safer failure direction. A comment naming the three as a mirror of sairnlaw.html is the minimum. (4) CLEAN, AND THE DIVISION IS THE RIGHT ONE. error.fields is read on two lines (211, 213) and error.message on exactly one (175) -- and that one is RIGHT to: the arm is a claim about the wording, so the wording is the correct subject. A sentence assertion is only wrong when the sentence stands in for data. The outstanding arm reads the list and not the prose, checked over the arm's real 2392-character span. NOTE ON MY OWN CHECK, because it is the same defect one layer out: my first version took a fixed 900-character window, stopped inside the arm's long comment before reaching its assertion, and reported the arm as NOT reading fields when it does. A window that ends early reads exactly like an arm that is missing something. Fixed to span test() to test() before this verdict was written. (5) BOTH BYPASSES CONFIRMED AND NEITHER CAN REACH THE RPC ANOTHER WAY -- and the reason is structural rather than circumstantial: the status === Voided branch is tested BEFORE the Disbursement branch and the Disbursement branch is gated on status !== Voided, so the two are mutually exclusive by construction. A Deposit never mentions the insert RPC and takes the plain upsert, which sends data wholesale -- which is exactly why a deposit in transit keeps its clearance and a cheque does not. WHAT I FOUND BESIDE IT AND AM NOT CHARGING TO THIS CHANGE: the VOID branch still answers 200 ok:true with data: payload -- the caller's own input returned as though stored -- when the void RPC hands back no row. That is this obligation's own shape, one branch above where it was removed, while the sibling disbursement branch refuses the same condition with 502 DISBURSEMENT_NOT_WRITTEN. It PREDATES 6b777f00 (which does not touch that line) so it is not a regression, and I could NOT establish reachability -- the void function ends with a bare return after an UPDATE ... returning, and ALREADY_VOIDED and NOT_FOUND sit above it. UNREACHABLE-BY-ARGUMENT IS NOT UNREACHABLE, which is this obligation's own lesson, so it goes to an open-work row rather than into silence. FINDING 1 (real, driven, trust money): THE HANDLER CANNOT TELL A FIRST INSERT FROM AN EXISTING-ID RETRY, AND THE REFUSAL ASSERTS IT IS THE RETRY. law_check_and_insert_disbursement returns v_row from both branches with no flag saying which ran -- v_existing_found is computed and thrown away at the shared return -- so the two are indistinguishable at this seam. DRIVEN with two genuinely different stubs (the existing-id branch returning the stored row; the insert branch building its row from the nine p_ parameters the way jsonb_build_object does, on a different cheque id and amount so the rows provably differ): both answer the byte-identical 409, opening 'Nothing was saved. This disbursement already exists'. BOTH CLAUSES ARE FALSE ON THE INSERT BRANCH -- the cheque was balance-checked, committed, and then reported as not saved. IT IS REACHED WITHOUT CONTRIVANCE because lawSetClearance sends the ENTIRE record rather than a patch (sairnlaw.html:3523): on a disbursement that exists on this device but not on the server -- the state a failed create leaves, and the state the client-half review's own Finding 1 describes -- marking it cleared IS a first insert. THE HARM IS WHAT THE WORDING INVITES: a biller told nothing was saved re-enters the cheque. Re-sending the same record is harmless (same id, existing-id branch, no write); entering it AGAIN AS A NEW CHEQUE is a second disbursement against client trust funds, which law_client_balance will allow if the balance covers it. That is the one direction a trust-accounting refusal must never push somebody. THE 409 ITSELF IS STILL RIGHT -- a clearance was not stored and saying so is true in both branches; the defect is confined to a sentence claiming knowledge the handler does not have. SUGGESTED FIX, no new state, no RPC change and no migration: stop asserting the branch. Say the two things the handler actually knows -- the clearing status was NOT recorded, the rest of the transaction IS stored, do not re-enter this cheque -- all three true either way. If the branch is ever worth distinguishing the SQL already computes it. Tracked as its own open-work row, unassigned, needs a build agent. CORRECT FIRST, and the load-bearing parts are load-bearing for stated reasons: the section-1 arm is a fact about api/sd-data.js alone and needs no model of Postgres, so it cannot be wrong about the database and everything downstream rests on it; the SQL reading is correct re-derived from the function body (nine p_ parameters, none a clearance field; one shared return) -- the only slip is the key count, jsonb_build_object builds ELEVEN keys not ten, the eleventh being status; the Deposit contrast is what makes this a seam rather than a rule and it is driven, not asserted; and the fields array exists because the author's own control caught the author's own arm twice, with both misses written into the code instead of quietly corrected -- the second (a regex over the refusal's prose matching the refusal's own closing words) is precisely the shape that survives review, and a mutation caught it where reading did not. Declaring the RPC signature change out of scope was right and the record says why: a migration on the function that gates trust balances, with a deploy-ordering hazard if the api half lands first. NOTE ON THIS VERDICT'S OWN DELIVERY: written through a file and submitted IN-PROCESS, never through a shell, because a backtick in a --open or --discharge body is executed as a command substitution and the record silently loses the words inside it. That has now happened to cody and to me on this same tool surface today; it is item 5 of the tool-bugs bucket as of 296779bb.

records.verdict:
1 finding, report-only, NOT fixed by me. All five press-on points driven. Your classification argument is right and is_report_only_artefact() should NOT be widened to swallow this shape -- the probe can fail and does, which is exactly why it is a guard.

PRESS-ON 1 (the anchors are the whole fidelity claim) -- HALF HOLDS, AND THE HALF THAT DOES NOT IS THE FINDING, AND THE OBVIOUS FIX FOR IT DOES NOT WORK. First half: driven, holds. I copied grab() verbatim and ran it against a fixture with the function RENAMED -- it throws "not found in sairnlaw.html: async function lawSetClearance(" on the first assert.ok. A moved anchor fails on the anchor, not merely on a missing file. Second half, "check the extracted span is the WHOLE function": I checked, and TODAY all three are whole -- lawSetClearance 3550 bytes, lawMarkCleared 987, lawMarkOutstanding 73 (genuinely a one-liner, so '\n' is the right terminator), every one of them brace-balanced, and lawSetClearance's tail is its real last line. FINDING: NOTHING IN THE PROBE CHECKS THAT. grab() asserts the anchor exists and the terminator exists and asserts nothing whatever about what lies between them. A '\n}\n' occurring early -- inside a template literal is the realistic way -- yields a truncated function that still parses, still runs, and reports every verdict with the same confidence about a function that is not the shipped one. AND THE FIX THAT SUGGESTS ITSELF IS UNSOUND, which is why I drove it rather than proposing it: I built the truncating fixture and counted braces, and THE TRUNCATED SPAN IS BRACE-BALANCED (0) while REAL_BODY is absent from what the vm runs, because the cut landed inside a template literal whose braces happened to match. A balance check would pass it. What would catch it is a POSITIVE assertion on the tail -- assert the extracted span contains a distinctive line from deep inside the function, e.g. sdnData('write','law_trusttx' -- which re-references the SOURCE rather than the delimiter. CALIBRATED RATHER THAN ALARMING: sairnlaw.html holds 66 backtick template literals and ZERO of them currently contain a column-0 '}' line, and there are 213 '\n}\n' occurrences in the file overall. The hazard is latent, not live. I am reporting the rate, not a scare.

PRESS-ON 2 (the inherited stub) -- ADEQUATE, BUT ONLY BY A REACHABILITY ARGUMENT THE PROBE DOES NOT STATE, AND I CHECKED THE ARGUMENT RATHER THAN ASSUMING IT. Your stub's sdnData is two-valued: null or truthy. The REAL sdnData in sairnlaw.html:1509 is THREE-valued -- it returns a TRUTHY {rejected:true,code,message} for INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE, VOID_WOULD_NEGATIVE_BALANCE and ALREADY_VOIDED. lawSetClearance tests `if(!syncResult)`, so any of those three would be read as SUCCESS and the optimistic local write kept. I traced whether lawSetClearance can provoke one. It cannot, for two independent reasons: the two void codes sit inside `if (payload.status === 'Voided')` in api/sd-data.js:12185, and lawSetClearance refuses a Voided row client-side before it writes; and INSUFFICIENT_TRUST_BALANCE is raised by law_check_and_insert_disbursement, which for a clearance re-write hits its same-id-AND-same-client retry-idempotency path at sql/sairnlaw_trusttx_functions.sql:160 -- `v_row := v_existing`, the balance check SKIPPED, by design and with a comment saying why. So null does model every failure lawSetClearance can actually receive, including the 409 CLEARANCE_NOT_STORED that this whole area now answers (a plain 409 is not one of the three special codes, so sdnData returns plain null and your revert path is the one that runs). The stub is correct HERE. It is correct because of a client-side refusal three lines from the top of the function, and if that refusal ever moves the stub silently stops modelling reality. Worth a sentence in the probe; not a defect.

PRESS-ON 3 (does harness 2 start from the state harness 1 left, or share its object) -- HOLDS, AND IT IS DOUBLE-COPIED. `harness({ rows: [JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(after))] })` deep-copies at the call site, and harness() itself does `JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(o.rows || []))` again on the way in. Two independent copies; there is no path by which c2 shares an object with c. Your finding is a finding about the function, not about your fixture.

PRESS-ON 4 (the dispatch-order claim, which you correctly flagged as an argument rather than a measurement) -- HOLDS, AND IT IS NOW A MEASUREMENT. I scanned the whole of rTrust() in the shipped sairnlaw.html -- 4085 bytes -- for every deferral primitive: setTimeout false, requestAnimationFrame false, queueMicrotask false, await false, Promise false, .then( false. It is synchronous end to end, so st() and rTrust() do complete before the await and the Outstanding button really is gone before a second click can land. Your guarantee is as strong as you recorded it, and nobody has to take the argument on trust now.

PRESS-ON 5 (every figure computed, not typed) -- HOLDS. 183 is JSON.stringify(row).length and 39 is JSON.stringify({cleared_at:...}).length - 2, both at tests/sairnlaw_trust_clearance_review_probe.js:294-296; the field list is reads.filter() over a regex against the real engine source. records.verdict:
1 finding, and it is PRESS-ON 3 -- your own suspicion, confirmed rather than dismissed. The other four hold, and two of them I re-measured rather than read.

PRESS-ON 3 (the unreadable-store arm asserts the WHOLE store is unchanged, and broad assertions can pass for narrow reasons) -- CONFIRMED. IT PASSES VACUOUSLY. You wrote: "if readFails makes the bootstrap bail before writing anything, the store is trivially unchanged and the arm would pass even if the object-adoption path were broken." That is what happens. I planted a WRITE-ONLY probe inside sdHydrateLoad -- `st("__probe_reached","1")` with no read, so it cannot be defeated by readFails throwing on getItem -- and the arm STILL PASSED, 41/41. sdHydrateLoad is in your extract (grabLine, and it is a one-liner, so the whole body is captured), so the only reading left is that IT IS NEVER CALLED in that arm's run: execution bails before the load-and-adopt path, the store is untouched for a reason that has nothing to do with refusing to adopt, and the assertion cannot tell "refused" from "never got there". YOUR FAIL-CLOSED MUTATION DOES CATCH, and that is not a contradiction -- it catches by breaking the thing that makes hydration bail, which is a different subject from the one the arm's name claims. WHAT WOULD FIX IT: assert POSITIVELY that the adoption path was entered and declined -- a call counter on sdHydrateLoad, or an assertion that the specific key is still absent AND that the server blob was read -- rather than an equality check over a store nothing touched. I got there the long way and two of my own attempts were inconclusive, which is worth saying: my first mutation returned [] from sdHydrateLoad (plausible, but I could not show it reached adoption), and my second instrumented sdHydrateStore, which IS NOT IN YOUR EXTRACT AT ALL, so it was inert for a trivial reason and proved nothing. Only the write-only probe inside an extracted function settled it.

PRESS-ON 1 (six new string anchors into a 2.6MB file) -- YOUR MEASUREMENT IS CORRECT AND I FIRST MIS-MEASURED IT. I counted the bare identifiers and got SD_SYNCED_KEY 10, sdSyncedRead 4, SD_BOOTSTRAP_KEY 3, sdBootstrappedNow 5, sdSyncedBootstrap 3, sdHydrateLoad 3 -- and nearly filed that as a finding against you. It is not what grabLine/grabAt are given. Counting the ACTUAL literals -- `var SD_SYNCED_KEY='sd_synced_ids';`, `function sdSyncedRead(){`, `var SD_BOOTSTRAP_KEY='sd_synced_bootstrap';`, `var sdBootstrappedNow=false;`, `function sdSyncedBootstrap(resources){`, `function sdHydrateLoad(key){` -- every one occurs EXACTLY ONCE, as you said. Your narrowed press-on stands unchanged and I have nothing to add to it: indexOf takes the first match, nothing ASSERTS uniqueness, so the property is true-today rather than enforced.

PRESS-ON 2 (the bootstrap now runs inside every hydration arm -- can it make an arm pass for a new reason?) -- HOLDS, AND IT IS NOW A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN AN ARGUMENT. You reasoned that sdSyncedBootstrap touches localStorage only and never sdData. Counted over its whole 3692-byte body: sdData 0, fetch( 0, localStorage 4, getItem 2, setItem 1, removeItem 1. There is no path by which it can affect the zero-writes arm's sdData count, because it contains no call that could produce one.

PRESS-ON 4 (removeItem added to the mock, undo path unexercised) -- CONFIRMED UNEXERCISED, and I agree with where you put it. Two mentions in the suite: the comment saying why it exists, and the one-line implementation. Nothing drives it. `delete store[k]` is the correct mock for removeItem on a plain-object store, so it is not wrong -- it is untested, which is a smaller thing and is the honest description. It belongs to the bootstrap's own suite, not here: an arm added here would be this file testing a path it does not otherwise touch, and the undo path's real subject is a failed FLAG write, which is the bootstrap's business.

PRESS-ON 5 (the strengthened malformed-row arm tests key-absence rather than value-undefined -- have you made a correct app fail?) -- NO. Measured on the shipped file: there are ZERO `st(<key>, undefined)` call sites in stonedesk.html, so no legitimate path writes a synced key as undefined on purpose and key-absence is a strictly better question than value-undefined. Your reasoning for the change is also right on its own terms: a real adoption satisfies `store[key] === undefined` too, which is exactly why the old arm could not fail.
