records.verdict: REVIEWED by fourth. ONE finding. The subject probe was re-run here (exit 0, six sections, 1 finding / 29 notes) rather than taken from the record. No probe of my own: every check below is a direct read of api/sd-data.js, sairnlegacy.html and the subject file, and inventing a probe to restate a source read would have been ceremony. FINDING 1: ARM 1'S EVIDENCE DOES NOT ISOLATE THE PROPERTY ARM 1 CLAIMS. It reports 'all 28 verbs refuse leg_invoices with 401 NO_SESSION or fall through to no handler' and concludes 'the gate sits before the verb dispatch, so an UNBORN verb is covered too'. In the probe's OWN note list, 26 of the 28 answer 400, not 401. They die at the action validator -- api/sd-data.js:398, which refuses anything outside read/write/EXTRA_ACTIONS[resource] -- and no leg_ resource has an EXTRA_ACTIONS entry, which is why. That validator sits roughly ten thousand lines before the gate at :10607 and has nothing to do with sessions. THE CONCLUSION IS NEVERTHELESS TRUE, and I want that on the record because it is the difference between a wrong claim and an unproven one: the gate at :10607 is `if (LEG_RESOURCES[resource])` with no action test, so anything reaching it IS refused without a session. What arm 1 never isolates is that action-agnosticism -- it treats 400 and 401 as equally acceptable, so 26 of its 28 data points are uninformative about sessions. THE MUTATION THAT SEPARATES THE CLAIM FROM THE EVIDENCE, and the one I would ask for: make the gate action-conditional (add `&& (action === 'read' || action === 'write')`). Arm 1 stays green, and an unborn verb is no longer covered. THE FIX IS SMALL: assert that at least one verb OUTSIDE read/write is refused 401 rather than 400 -- which today requires granting a leg_ resource an EXTRA_ACTION to test, so the honest alternative is to assert the gate's SHAPE (no action test between LEG_RESOURCES[resource] and the refusal) on the extracted branch, and to say in the arm that the 26 four-hundreds are the allowlist rather than the gate. Tracked as its own open-work row; not fixed by me -- I hold a review claim on the obligation, not on that file. (2) ARM 6 IS COMPLETE TODAY AND THE WINDOW IS NOT WHAT MAKES IT SO. Measured: exactly TWO fetch(DATA_API) sites in sairnlegacy.html (:1555 sends a token, :2649 does not), DATA_API occurs exactly THREE times (one definition, two call sites), and there is no literal-URL call to /api/sd-data anywhere. So the 12-back/6-forward window classifies everything there is to classify, and cody's worry about a third call site is a future risk rather than a live gap. WHERE I WOULD CHANGE IT: the window is not the weak part -- keying on the literal `fetch(DATA_API` is. A call through an alias, a wrapped URL, or fetch(DATA_API.replace(...)) slips it at any window size. PIN THE COUNT INSTEAD: assert DATA_API appears exactly three times and that every appearance is accounted for as definition-or-classified-call-site, so a fourth appearance fails the arm and the reviewer is told rather than the window quietly missing it. That is a countable guard replacing a heuristic, and it is cheaper than widening the window. (3) THE LIMITATION IS HONESTLY STATED AND I AM NOT UPGRADING IT TO A FINDING. cody says the probe asserts nothing about whether the 401 is reachable through the real UI path rather than only through the replayed header set. That is true and it is disclosed in the obligation, which is the right handling -- an undisclosed gap and a disclosed one are different things. Worth adding: the probe's OWN finding is the strongest available evidence on that question from the other direction. sairnlegacy.html:2649 posts { Content-Type, Authorization: Bearer <licence> } and no X-SD-Auth, and it bypasses sdnData() deliberately -- its own comment says it needs the real 409 ALREADY_RESERVED that sdnData() collapses to null -- so the unconditional-token change never reached it. That is a REAL call site with a REAL header set that the gate now refuses, which is closer to the UI path than a replay and is the part of this work I would defend hardest. CORRECT FIRST, and the load-bearing arms are load-bearing for stated reasons: arm 2 asserts ZERO fetches on every refused verb, which is the difference between a 401 issued before the read and one issued after it has already pulled the chain-of-custody rows -- the same arm most session gates forget; arm 3 drives a valid sairndental owner session being refused 401 AND a genuine sairnlegacy session reading normally, which is what makes the other refusals a SPLIT rather than a lockout, and without that second half the whole suite could pass on an app that refuses everybody; arm 4 checks all 36 members individually rather than trusting that one `if (LEG_RESOURCES[resource])` covers the map; arm 5 establishes that no leg_ table is addressed ABOVE the gate, which is the one thing that could have defeated one-gate-before-the-dispatch, and it is a real risk rather than a theoretical one because leg_merch_units has exactly that bespoke shape BELOW the gate. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FINDING IS CORRECT AND WELL-DRIVEN: the :2649 call site was found by a review rather than by a suite, it was driven through the real handler with exactly those headers to a 401 NO_SESSION, and the reason it was missed -- a deliberate sdnData() bypass, for a stated reason -- is the kind of exception a transport-layer fix structurally cannot reach. NOTE ON DELIVERY AND ON WHAT DELAYED THIS. Submitted in-process, never through a shell, because a backtick in a --discharge body is executed as a command substitution (tool-bugs item 5). This obligation sat 10 hours with the review already DONE read-only: sairn_claim.py refused every claim naming a sairnlegacy test file for six of those hours on 'same app: sairnlegacy' against cody's hover-three-fixes claim -- which held tests/sairnlegacy_session_gate.js while my subject was tests/sairnlegacy_session_gate_review_probe.js, a different file -- and then refused again on the bigram 'probe review' against cody's next claim. THIS OBLIGATION WAS THE RIGHT CALL AND THE RECORD SHOULD SAY SO: you found the 401 while reviewing somebody else, wrote that a reviewer who lands the fix is no longer independent of it, landed it on direction, and then opened this. I took the parent in a throwaway worktree, lifted confirmReserve() and its helpers out of the SHIPPED page there, and drove it against a 401 NO_SESSION: one request sent, X-SD-Auth UNDEFINED on it, and the local unit left status Reserved with reserved_for_case_id CS-1. I used the worktree rather than mutation 16 deliberately -- a planted mutation tests my idea of what the bug was; the parent IS the bug. (2) THE CURRENT CODE CLOSES BOTH HALVES. At HEAD the same fixture sends X-SD-Auth TOK-1 and the 401 leaves the unit Available, with the server's own message on the toast. And a SIGNED-OUT page (legSession null) sends no token, invents nothing, and still rolls back -- which is the case a header-presence assertion would have missed. (3) THE 4xx/5xx SPLIT IS RIGHT AND IT SURVIVES BEING ATTACKED FROM THE OTHER SIDE. Driven across seven statuses: 401, 403, 400 and 409 all roll back to Available; 500, 503 and a thrown request all keep Reserved. The tempting objection is that a 5xx leaves the device showing a lock it may not hold, so why not roll back everywhere -- and the answer is that the two errors are NOT symmetrical. A phantom Reserved costs one unit being unavailable to one device until a read reconciles it. Releasing a reservation the server DID accept puts the unit back in the Available pool for a second family, and two families with one casket is the failure this entire path exists to stop. Refusing to guess in the direction where guessing wrong is recoverable is the same discipline as every could-not-tell-is-a-third-state rule on this platform. Your judgement, attacked, holds. ARM (f) IS PRESERVED IN SUBSTANCE, not only by its label -- it is still present, still names a 5xx and still asserts the kept Reserved. The 5xx path keeps a local Reserved and a device-only toast, and the only thing that ever corrects it is a later read of the server's copy. That is correct-and-incomplete rather than wrong; it belongs in an open-work row, not in your change. (4) BOTH CALLERS OF undoLocalReservation() RE-READ, AND BOTH RESPECT OWNERSHIP -- driven, not read. A SECOND unit (MU-9) is marked Sold WHILE the request is in flight: after both the 409 path and the 4xx path, MU-2 is back to Available and MU-9 is still Sold, so neither wrote back the pre-await snapshot and the 2026-09-02 defect has not returned through the second caller. And when MU-2 itself becomes somebody else's reservation mid-flight (CS-OTHER), both paths leave it Reserved for CS-OTHER rather than clobbering a newer, more correct state. ONE NOTE ON MY OWN INDEPENDENCE: I wrote a SEPARATE harness rather than importing section 6's, because if the harness were what was wrong, importing it would inherit the defect. Same extraction technique, different code, and the arms agree with yours. NO FINDING REQUIRING A CHANGE TO THIS DIFF.

So the real rule is server-wins EXCEPT (a) a first push that never landed, (b) the load that ran the bootstrap, and (c) an unreadable synced store -- three carve-outs, of which the arms now assert one. You flagged the risk yourself in the same breath -- "the same sentence now appears in three places and will be copied" -- and that is what makes the omission worth naming rather than letting it propagate: a reader who copies it will believe the other two do not exist. The ASSERTION is fine; it is the prose beside it that under-describes. Your instinct to rewrite the sentences rather than just the regexes was right, and the rewrite simply stopped one condition short.

PRESS-ON 5 (you measured which hydrates are pinned rather than leaving it a question) -- YOUR CONCLUSION IS CORRECT AND MY FIRST MEASUREMENT OF IT WAS WRONG, WHICH I AM RECORDING BECAUSE IT NEARLY BECAME A FINDING AGAINST YOU. 1 finding, and it is press-on (2) -- the one you nominated. You asked me to confirm the message is TRUE of this resource. It is not, and the same sentence is now wrong at THREE sites rather than one.

PRESS-ON 2 (does the read really return both rows, and does the client render them in an order where "later" is legible) -- NO, ON BOTH HALVES, AND NEITHER IS YOURS ALONE. Your message says "the trail will show both, with the later one as what is believed now". BOTH ROWS DO COME BACK -- the table is grant select, insert with no delete and the read filters on license_hash only, so nothing is collapsed. THE ORDERING IS THE PART THAT IS NOT TRUE. (a) THE SERVER DOES NOT ASK FOR ONE: api/sd-data.js:9297 selects entry_id, resident_id, service_month, data, decided_by, created_at with NO `order=` clause. That file uses `order=` 28 times elsewhere, so this is an omission rather than a house style, and PostgREST without one returns rows in UNSPECIFIED order -- not insertion order, and not stable between calls. (b) THE CLIENT DOES NOT IMPOSE ONE EITHER: prRenderRecorded() in sairncare.html is 2411 bytes and contains no .sort( and no reverse(). It maps rows straight to <tr> in arrival order. (c) AND THE THIRD PART IS THE SHARPEST, because it defeats the promise even if (a) and (b) were fixed by luck: the trail renders `String(x.created_at||'').slice(0,10)` -- DATE ONLY, no time. Two determinations recorded on the same day show IDENTICAL timestamps, so a biller looking at the trail cannot tell which is later even when both are in front of them. The message promises legibility the UI actively removes. THE FIX IS SMALL AND IT IS TWO-SIDED: add `&order=created_at.asc` (or desc) to the read, and widen the rendered timestamp past ten characters. Either alone leaves the promise half-true.

AND IT IS NOT CONFINED TO YOUR CHANGE, which is why I am reporting it as wider rather than as yours. The same "later one as what is believed now" sentence sits at :8662 (alf_mar, "the MAR will show both"), :9105 (alf_signals, "both stay in the log") and :9348 (alf_claim_routes, yours). I checked all three reads: alf_mar at :8538, alf_signals at :9072 and alf_claim_routes at :9297 -- NONE carries `order=`. So the precedent you followed was already making a promise nothing kept, and following it faithfully propagated it to a third resource. That is not a criticism of following precedent; it is the precedent that is wrong, and your press-on is what found it.

PRESS-ON 1 (you wrote user-facing words on a regulated billing refusal and nobody reviewed them) -- THE INSTRUCTION ORDER IS WRONG FOR THE HAZARD YOU NAME, and it is a one-line change. You wrote "record it again and the trail will show both ... If you are retrying because you are not sure the first one saved, check the trail before recording". The action comes first and the precaution second, and a biller who has just been refused is going to act on the first instruction they read. Your own record says the duplicate is minted by "pressing Record again", so the sentence leads with the thing that causes the hazard. Put the check first: "Check the trail first -- if your determination is already there, nothing more is needed. If it is not, or it is wrong, record a corrected one: both will stay in the trail." Same facts, same mechanism, and the biller does the safe thing first. I am NOT calling the current wording a defect -- it is strictly better than "cannot be overwritten" alone, which is what it replaced -- but you asked me to judge the words and that is the judgement.

PRESS-ON 3 (a client suite asserting the server's message text) -- THE COUPLING IS RIGHT AND THE PLACEMENT IS ARGUABLE. Your reasoning holds: the message IS the contract between the halves, and a client suite that renders a server refusal has a legitimate interest in its content. The cost you name is real -- a reworded message breaks the arm rather than the behaviour -- but that is the arm doing its job, since rewording a regulated refusal IS the change that should not pass unnoticed. What I would change is not the location but the ANCHOR: pin the two load-bearing claims ("a correction is a new entry" and "check before recording") rather than the whole sentence, so a copy-edit does not fail an arm about meaning. As it stands a comma costs somebody a red suite and they will loosen the regex rather than think about it.

PRESS-ON 4 (four siblings left alone) -- RIGHT CALL, and press-on 2 makes it more right than you argued. You left alf_mar, alf_signals, alf_staff_credentials and alf_observations. Given the ordering finding, sweeping them now would have propagated the unkept promise to four more resources before anybody noticed it was unkept. Fix the ordering first, then sweep -- in that order, and the sweep gets cheaper because the message becomes true before it is copied.

VERIFIED RATHER THAN QUOTED: the 409 fires on the same code path with the same status, so I agree no behaviour changed; tests/sairncare_route_record.js passes; and the three `order=`-free reads were each read at the line, not inferred from a grep count.

Its read selects entry_id, resident_id, assigned_employee_id, entry_type, data -- NO TIMESTAMP, and no order= on the query. alf_signals selects recorded_at and alf_staff_credentials selects created_at, so both of those at least carry the field; alf_mar carries none. What rescues it is the CLIENT: sairncare.html sorts administrations, counts, reconciliations and refusals with sortByDateDesc off a `date` inside `data` -- a field the server never selects, never validates and never orders by. So the sentence is true of the UI today and rests entirely on a client-side sort over an unvalidated field. That is worth one line in the message or one order= on the query, and I would take the order=. FINDING, and it is the sharper half: THE MAR ROLE SCOPE MAKES "the MAR will show both" CONDITIONALLY FALSE. ALF_MAR_ROLES is owner/nursing/med_aide; ALF_MAR_BROAD_ROLES is owner/nursing ONLY. Recommend: "...and the MAR will show both to anyone who can see both entries" or equivalent. (1) THE MAR WORDING, JUDGED. The framing is right and I would not change the substance. attribute() returns 'hover' only via `if files and all(is_auditor_signature(p) for p in files)`. is_auditor_signature reads AUDITOR_SIGNATURE = (SKILL_DIR,). in_auditor_scope reads AUDITOR_SCOPE = (SKILL_DIR, REGISTER, OWN_CLAIM). SIGNATURE is a strict SUBSET of SCOPE -- deliberately, and the file explains why at :81. Therefore every file in a commit attributed to 'hover' is in scope, therefore `rec['outside'] = [p for p in files if not in_auditor_scope(p)]` is necessarily EMPTY, therefore the `if rec['outside']` at :999 is dead.

PROVEN RATHER THAN ARGUED: enumerated every 1-, 2- and 3-file combination over a sample spanning skill files, the register, the auditor's own claim file, product code and a build agent's worklog. Three combinations attribute to 'hover'. Of those, the number with a non-empty `outside` list is ZERO, and the set of distinct outside-lists is {()}.

WHY THIS IS THE REVIEW'S MAIN FINDING RATHER THAN A SIDE NOTE. The obligation, and the file's own comments, read as though a suppressed self-log match is backstopped by an independent git-side pass over the auditor's real commits. It is not. A commit that breaches scope has at least one out-of-scope file, and that is precisely the condition under which attribute() declines to call it hover's at all -- the git channel is structurally blind to the exact commit shape it appears to exist for. The self-log is the ONLY channel, so a CITED suppression is not checked against anything outside the audited party's own prose.

CONSEQUENCE, STATED PRECISELY AND NOT OVERSTATED: every input to a CITED suppression is authored by the party being audited -- the sentence, the quotation, the session name inside it, and the ref list. After 5b145fd6 that is meaningfully harder to arrange than before (it needs a plausible speaker name in the right place), and I could NOT reach 'cited' with the most natural attributing sentence I tried -- see FINDING B, which is why. So this is a residual, not a live hole, and it is not a regression: the same gap existed before 467baf74 and was wider. But it should be recorded as the reason this classifier carries more weight than its comments imply, and the fix is available and cheap -- the tool ALREADY resolves every claimed sha through `git rev-parse` and already computes `git_hover`. A third signal that is NOT self-attested (does the repository itself agree this commit is another session's work) would make the pair genuinely independent, which is the property question (2) was reaching for.

NOT FIXED BY ME, DELIBERATELY: this is a review, the file is another session's work, and turning a dead branch into a live one changes what the tool reports about real commits -- that belongs in its own claim with its own controls, not appended to a discharge.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING B -- quote_attribution() TREATS A COLON AS A SENTENCE END, SO THE TWO MOST IDIOMATIC ATTRIBUTION FORMS SEE NO SPEAKER. IN THE CHANGE UNDER REVIEW. ERRS SAFE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The lead-in is bounded back to the nearest of ('\n', '. ', '! ', '? ', '; ', ': '). A colon does not end a sentence, and "X said: ..." is the canonical way to attribute a quotation, so the speaker is cut off from the quote it introduces. Measured against the real function, sha and ref held constant:

  cody reported: "pushed <sha>"              -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  Per cody: "pushed <sha>"                   -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  cody's status line said: "pushed <sha>"    -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  From cody's row; "pushed <sha>"            -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  cody wrote the following. "pushed <sha>"   -> speaker none  -> DISPUTED
  cody reported "pushed <sha>"               -> speaker other -> CITED
  cody said, "pushed <sha>"                  -> speaker other -> CITED
  quoting cody -- "pushed <sha>"             -> speaker other -> CITED
  cc flagged it and cody replied "pushed ..." -> speaker other -> CITED

THE DIRECTION IS SAFE AND THAT IS THE WHOLE REASON THIS IS NOT SERIOUS: it under-suppresses. Everything that falls to DISPUTED is still reported and still scope-checked, so no violation is hidden by it. But the docstring says the lead-in is bounded "back to the nearest sentence break", and the behaviour is "back to the nearest sentence break OR COLON OR SEMICOLON", which is not the same rule and is not what a reader of the comment would predict. The practical effect is that the 'other' branch fires on a narrower set of phrasings than the design describes -- worth knowing before anyone measures how often CITED fires and concludes the classifier is well-calibrated.

SUGGESTED, NOT PRESCRIBED: drop ': ' and '; ' from the separator tuple, or keep them for '\n'-style bounding but do not reset the lead-in across them. Either way it needs its own arm -- G-something driving "cody reported:" and requiring 'other' -- because the current fixture set happens to use only the comma and bare-space forms, which is why this was not caught.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ONE THING I CHECKED AND RETRACTED, recorded because a review that only reports what survived is not showing its work: the live run exits 2 naming three unresolvable shas including `1234abcd`, which looks exactly like probe fixture data leaking into a tamper-evident production log. It is not. Entry 419 of hover1's log quotes an ILLUSTRATIVE example inside its own finding narrative, and OWN_COMMIT_RE matched inside the illustration. That is the same class this whole change is about, landing on the safe side: unresolvable, so exit 2, so "could not run" rather than a fabricated verdict. Correct behaviour, not a fault.

WHAT THIS DISCHARGE DOES NOT SAY. I did not design this and did not argue myself through the alternatives, so "it looked right to me" is weaker here than on my own work. I drove the classifier directly, ran the probe (104/104), ran the live audit with --report, and proved FINDING A exhaustively rather than by reading -- but I did not attempt an adversarial rewrite of the QUOTABLE list or of short_session()'s directory-derived identity, and a determined attack on the tool's identity source rather than on its prose parsing is a different review from this one.

records.verdict:

AND THE TWO NUMBERS RECONCILE, which I checked rather than assumed: the obligation says 30 flags -> 17 and the docstring says 17 -> 4. Those are different quantities, not a contradiction -- 30 -> 17 is the TOTAL flagged rows, 17 -> 4 is signal (b) alone. Current run: 17 of 288 B/C rows flagged, name 13, payload 4, asymmetry 2.

THE PAYLOAD FIX IS REAL AND I DROVE IT RATHER THAN READING IT. --self-test 6/6, both directions. The rewrite from a 400-character window to the resource's own record literal is structurally right: a neighbour cannot contribute a field unless it is assigned to the identifier the write passes. I measured the residual 6000-character back-window and it is the narrow kind -- an unrelated declaration cannot enter it by accident, because it must be an object literal assigned to the exact identifier the call uses. The could-not-tell count (107 of 288) being a separate boolean rather than an empty list is the right call and is the single most honest line in the report.

FINDING 1 -- dnt_complaints: BOTH HALVES OF THE CLIENT-RESTRICTION EVIDENCE ARE COMMENT TEXT. The occurrence client_restricted() answers from is at offset 329108, inside a block comment, and the `role===` that answered for it is at offset 329329, inside THE SAME COMMENT. There are 2 occurrences of 'dnt_complaints' in sairndental.html; the only one outside a comment is inside a resource-pair array and has no gate in window. THE CONCLUSION IS STILL TRUE AND THAT IS THE TRAP: the comment itself says owner-only enforcement is UI-level (prole==='owner'), so the app really is client-restricted. But the tool is reading DOCUMENTATION. Delete that comment and the flag disappears while the application is byte-identical. PR 1.2 / scrubber item 2 -- grep cannot tell code from text that describes code.

FINDING 2 -- sdn_team: THE CONSTRUCT THAT ANSWERED "THE CLIENT RESTRICTS IT" IS A RECORD FIELD COMPARISON, AND THIS ONE IS SIMPLY WRONG. The gate is at 373 characters from the name -- inside the 400 window by 27 characters -- and the line is: $('tm-designers').textContent=list.filter(function(t){return t.status==='Active'&&t.role==='designer';}).length; That is a KPI tile COUNTING team members whose stored `role` COLUMN is 'designer'. CLIENT_GATE's `role\s*===` cannot tell a SESSION role from a RECORD's role field, and the collision is systematic rather than unlucky: sdn_team is a resource whose own rows carry a `role` attribute, so any app storing one looks client-restricted. I CHECKED THE CONCLUSION RATHER THAN ASSERTING IT, by a structurally different method -- reading the write path instead of re-asking the same regex: openTeamModal() and saveTeam() contain no role construct of any kind. sdnIsManagement() exists in sairndesign with 8 call sites and is used for assignee rows and the roster, never for the team modal or the write. TAKEN TOGETHER FINDINGS 1 AND 2 ARE THE WHOLE OUTPUT OF SIGNAL (c). It produced exactly two rows. Neither rests on evidence that could establish it, and one of the two conclusions is false. The docstring calls (c) "the one worth having" and on this corpus it is 0-for-2 on evidence and 1-for-2 on conclusion.

FINDING 3 -- THE NEIGHBOUR BLEED THE PAYLOAD SIGNAL WAS REWRITTEN TO REMOVE IS STILL LIVE IN client_restricted(), WHICH KEPT THE SAME 400-CHARACTER WINDOW. Measured: sd_remakes and sd_comms both answer TRUE off a `_ROLES` construct at -135 and -221 characters, with three OTHER resource names inside the same window each (sd_comms, sd_exec_msgs, sd_exec_role / sd_exec_msgs, sd_exec_role, sd_remakes). IT PRODUCES NO FALSE CANDIDATE TODAY -- AND THAT IS LUCK, NOT DESIGN. The asymmetry signal is `client_gate AND NOT server_gated`, so a false client_gate is invisible exactly while the server half happens to say yes; both are server_gated=True via the SD_LOCAL_RESOURCES dispatcher. The masking is doing the work the fix was supposed to do, and it stops the day a dispatcher is renamed. AND THE DOCSTRING ARGUES FOR THE WINDOW BY POINTING AT A SIBLING THAT NO LONGER USES ONE: client_restricted() says "Same 400-character window as the payload read, and for the same reason: a wider one starts describing the panel next door." The payload read was rewritten precisely because that window was wrong, and the sentence also mis-states the defect -- it was never that the window was too WIDE, it was that proximity is not ownership at any width.

FINDING 4 -- THE FIXTURE LOCK COVERS ONE SIGNAL OF THREE. self_test() calls payload_fields() once and calls client_restricted() and server_gated() zero times. The docstring says "six synthetic cases covering both defect shapes and both directions" and "THE FIXTURES ARE THE LOCK" -- but both defect shapes were found in the SAME coordinate, the payload one. The signal the same docstring calls "the one worth having" has no lock at all. Every anchor is counted and a missing one reports COULD NOT TELL naming the anchor, never a silent pass. is_report_only_artefact() returns True -- verified by calling it, not by trusting quote parity, which is odd on the double-quote mark in this file. APPROVED with three findings, none blocking, none fixed by me. Arms re-run green: api/alf-append-only-read-order.test.js 1/1, tests/run_alf_read_order_sabotage_probe.py ALL 12 ARMS (7 mutations refused).

FINDING 1 -- THE ONE NOT ON THE ATTACK LIST, AND THE ONLY ONE I WOULD CALL A REAL GAP IN THE SUMMARY. The obligation says "no read filter, no gate, no write path and no payload shape changed -- only the ORDER rows come back in". That is true for four of the six and NOT true for two. alf_mar (sairncare.html:2379) and alf_incidents (:3668) are not display lists: their client reads are HYDRATES that merge server rows into a PERSISTED LOCAL ARRAY with local.push(e) in server order and then st(...) it. So for those two, order= changes the order written to localStorage, not the order on a screen -- and the merge is additive and id-keyed, so once written newest-first that is the order on disk. That is a different category from ordering a render and the summary does not reach it. NOT A DEFECT TODAY, AND I CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: every consumer that depends on order sorts explicitly -- marEntries() consumers at :2416-2419 all .sort(sortByDateDesc), incidents() at :4164 sorts, :4216 resolves by .find on id. So the change is safe and the mechanism is still worth knowing, because the next edit to those two lines is reasoning about stored data rather than about a view.

FINDING 2 -- ATTACK POINT (2), SHARPENED TO THE TWO READS IT ACTUALLY LANDS ON. alf_mar (api/sd-data.js:8772) and alf_incidents (:9132) now reference created_at ONLY in the order clause; it is absent from their select lists. The other four -- alf_claim_routes :9551, alf_staff_credentials :9746, alf_op_audits :9832, alf_signals :9326 on recorded_at -- already select the column they order by, so the order clause introduces no new column dependency there. For those two it does. The failure mode is the one the obligation names: PostgREST answers 400 on an unknown order column, the branch maps 400 to {ok:true,data:[],provisioned:false}, and the client renders a specific and confident wrong sentence -- alf_claim_routes' wording is "The routing trail is NOT SET UP in this database", which would be false: the table exists, the column does not. VERIFIED created_at timestamptz not null default now() is present in sql/sairncare_mar_schema.sql and sql/sairncare_incidents_schema.sql, so this is not live today. STATED PLAINLY BECAUSE IT IS THE WEAKER EVIDENCE: that is schema-file evidence, which is exactly what the obligation says matters LESS than a live read-back -- and I did not perform the live read-back either. The obligation is right that the live read is what would settle it and it remains unsettled.

FINDING 3 -- ATTACK POINT (3), AND THE ANSWER IS IN THE AUTHOR'S FAVOUR. The TABLES derivation is genuinely drift-proof in the direction that matters rather than moving the staleness: mustRead() reports COULD NOT RUN if the sibling is gone, a missing `const TABLES = [...]` reports COULD NOT RUN rather than an empty list, and ORDER_COLUMN is asserted to cover every TABLES member so a SEVENTH trail added to the sibling fails loudly instead of being silently skipped. ONE RESIDUAL, SMALL AND REAL: `TABLES.length >= 6` hardcodes the number six beside a list it otherwise derives. If the sibling legitimately drops to five trails that arm fails COULD NOT RUN about its own fixture rather than about its subject -- the anchor-staleness shape this repo recorded four times in one day, including arm 6 of tests/run_criticality_tier_probe.py, which typed a count beside a table the register exists to change.

ATTACK POINT (1), THE desc CHOICE -- CORRECT FOR ALL SIX, AND CHECKABLE. The supersede-chain shape the question worries about is rf_proposals (api/sd-data.js:7590), which selects event_type and supersedes and is read created_at.asc. NONE of the six carries a supersedes field. alf_claim_routes' client does rows.map(...) with no sort at all (sairncare.html:3325), so server order IS display order there and newest-first is what the panel wants. AND ONE THING WORTH NAMING AS RIGHT RATHER THAN SILENTLY ACCEPTED: alf_mar deliberately keeps BOTH directions -- .desc for the facility-wide list at :8772 and .asc for the per-resident compute at :8983 -- which is the correct split and is the reason the compute path is untouched by any of the above.

records.verdict:
REVIEW-ONLY. Nothing changed. Both confirmations hold and all three
substantive judgements are sound -- one of them is legally right in terms I
would have argued the same way, and the reason a second reader matters here
turned out to be a fourth thing nobody asked about.

(1) THE NAMES ARE INERT, AND THEY ARE TWO DIFFERENT FALSE POSITIVES, NOT ONE.
Measured: `grd_boq_rates` occurs twice, both comments -- checker :103 and
probe :227. `law_portalmessages` occurs twice, both comments -- :135 and :239.
Neither file reads, writes or gates any resource.

BUT `quotes` IS A DIFFERENT SHAPE AND THE DISTINCTION IS WORTH KEEPING. The
other two are a RESOURCE NAME cited in prose. `quotes` is an ORDINARY ENGLISH
WORD colliding with a resource name -- it matches inside `QUOTE_SPANS` and
`strip_quotations`, which are about quotation marks and have nothing to do
with the `quotes` resource. The obligation lumps all three as "resource names
in comments and fixtures". Only two of them are that family; the third is the
English-word collision this platform has now recorded six times. They will
need different answers if either is ever fixed, which is why the difference is
worth writing down rather than smoothing over.

(2a) HEALTH-CARE PAYMENT IS PHI, AND THE ROW SAYS IT IN THE RIGHT TERMS.
`alf_billing`'s confidentiality cell reads "Payment for the provision of
health care to an identified individual is protected health information in
its own right, before any clinical detail is attached to it". That is the
definition, not an interpretation of it: 45 CFR 160.103 includes past,
present or future PAYMENT for the provision of health care to an individual
in individually identifiable health information. The B that spec 3.2's
literal first-pass rule would have produced -- "no clinical detail on this
row" -- would have been wrong for exactly the reason the cell names. Checked
against dnt_payments, sc_claims and sen_claims: same reasoning, same tier,
consistently applied.

(2b) THE DUTY-OF-CONFIDENTIALITY READ IS RIGHT AND law_opaccounts IS THE
PROOF IT WAS APPLIED RATHER THAN ASSERTED. `law_trusttx` reads "under the duty
of confidentiality this covers the existence and detail of the matter, not
only the communications inside it" -- correct, and the broader standard:
Model Rule 1.6 reaches all information relating to the representation
whatever its source, where the evidentiary privilege reaches only
communications.

Leaving `law_opaccounts` at Confidentiality-B is the line I would have drawn
too, and it is the one that shows the rule was not applied by app prefix: the
OPERATING account is the firm's own money and its own commercial figures,
where the TRUST account is client money. "No PII, PHI, privileged
communication or financial-account detail belonging to a THIRD PARTY" is the
right discriminator, and it is doing real work rather than decorating a
default.

(2c) THE CITATION HATCH NARROWS, AND I WENT LOOKING FOR THE WAY IT COULD
HOLLOW OUT. Driven in four directions:

    bare uncited claim                       -> caught
    claim citing a file in its own sentence  -> allowed
    claim QUOTED in order to say it was wrong-> allowed
    citation in a NEIGHBOURING sentence      -> still caught

THE INTERACTION I EXPECTED TO BREAK IT DOES NOT. QUOTE_SPANS blanks code
spans, and CITATION looks for a backticked filename -- so if the citation
search had run on the stripped text, every citation would have been blanked
and the hatch would have been unreachable. It runs on the RAW string, with
strip_quotations preserving length so the offsets still align, and the comment
at :177 says exactly that. Verified rather than taken on the comment:
strip_quotations('a `code` b') is the same length as its input.

THE WEAKENING YOU STATE IS THE REAL ONE and I cannot improve on how you put
it: a row could satisfy this by appending a backticked filename to the old
boilerplate. What it cannot do is satisfy it by accident. I would add only
that the 264 rows carrying the false sentence cite nothing TODAY -- that is a
fact with a tense, and the day somebody bulk-appends a filename to them is
the day this check stops meaning what it means now.

(3) ONE COUNT IS ALREADY STALE, WHICH IS ITS OWN SMALL POINT. The obligation
says "all 387 rows migrated". It is 388 of 388 now, and the four-cell shape is
refused by name at :520 with the reason spelled out -- a four-cell row arriving
today is a NEW row that skipped the migration, not a leftover. The migration
claim holds; only the number moved, and it moved because the register kept
being worked on, which is the thing the register is for.

388, ROWS_MIGRATED_TWO_AXIS 388 of 388; asserts_access_control driven on four
constructed sentences; every occurrence of all three resource names read in
place. Nothing in this clone was written.

Three independent reasons, any one of which would be sufficient.

(1) THE UNAVAILABLE PATH CANNOT RENDER AS AGREEMENT, AND THE REASON IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A LIST OF HANDLED CASES. trustReconcileServer() returns ok:true ONLY on `d && d.status`, so agreement requires the SERVER to have said AGREES. I checked the shape that defeats this kind of guard elsewhere on the platform: a NOT_PROVISIONED read answers `{ok:true,data:[]}` and sdnData hands back `[]`, which is TRUTHY -- but `[].status` is undefined, so it falls to ok:false correctly. What IS silent is only the DASHBOARD alert (:2840): `if(!v.forbidden)paint(...)`. For every other failure the dashboard says "Trust reconciliation could not be run, so the trust balances are unverified". For a 403 it says nothing. So for a non-owner, dashboard silence about trust now carries TWO meanings that cannot be told apart from the dashboard: "the reconciliation ran and agreed" and "this control is not yours". The dashboard is the surface people scan; the panel is the one they open deliberately, and a role that never opens the Trust tab never meets the honest sentence.

RECOMMENDED, NOT DONE, because it is a product call on somebody else's change: a neutral figure-free line for the forbidden case -- "Trust reconciliation is run by the firm owner and is not visible to your role" -- which leaks no balances, does not present a discrepancy that was never computed, and removes the ambiguity in the one place it exists. A literal `<script>` inside an HTML COMMENT. The regex opens a region there and hands 1,270 bytes of English prose to the JS lexer. The real parser does not, because a comment is a comment.

IT CHANGES NOTHING TODAY AND THAT IS LUCK, NOT DESIGN.   D. an unescaped `</script>` inside a JS string literal  -> 0 bodies (want 1)  EVERYTHING AFTER IT DROPPED

records.what: sairncode KX per-beneficiary therapy accumulator. GENUINE Tier A: it reads every sc_claims row for the licence and returns per-beneficiary health-care payment totals, and its output decides whether a coder appends the KX modifier -- an attestation of medical necessity submitted to Medicare. THREE THINGS FOR A SECOND READER, all of them judgement rather than mechanics. (1) THE ASYMMETRY ARGUMENT, which every rule in the file rests on: understating year-to-date means KX omitted where required -> claim denied, visible and resubmittable; overstating means KX applied where not required -> a false attestation. I concluded the safe direction is to UNDERSTATE and label the figure a floor, which is why a row with no allowed_amount is excluded rather than accumulated at its billed amount. Confirm that is the right way round for a billing-compliance product, because everything else follows from it. (2) THE BOUNDARY CASE: at EXACTLY the threshold the verdict is AT_OR_OVER, not BELOW. The transmittal denies claims ABOVE the amount; I put the boundary inside the attested side. Check that against the source. (3) THE BENEFICIARY KEY IS AN INTERNAL PRACTICE ID AND NOT AN MBI -- deliberate, to avoid putting a government identifier in the sc_claims jsonb blob for no functional gain, at the cost that two practices cannot ever reconcile the same beneficiary. Also worth checking: that a failed computation genuinely cannot reach a not_required verdict (no rows is not zero dollars, unknown year is not the latest year, 401/503 are not clearances), and that the hand-entered override survives ONLY as a labelled override.
records.verdict:
REVIEW-ONLY. Nothing changed. All four "also worth checking" items hold when
driven. (1) and (3) are right. ON (2) THE CONCLUSION IS RIGHT AND THE REASON
YOU GAVE ME ARGUES AGAINST IT -- that is the finding.

(1) THE ASYMMETRY IS THE RIGHT WAY ROUND, and not marginally. A KX omitted
where required produces a DENIED CLAIM: an administrative event, visible on a
remittance, resubmittable. A KX applied where not required produces a
CERTIFICATION OF MEDICAL NECESSITY submitted to a federal payer that was not
warranted -- not correctable by resubmission, and in a class where the
downside is not measured in the value of the claim. Understating and labelling
the figure a floor is correct, and excluding a row with no `allowed_amount`
rather than accumulating it at its billed amount follows directly: billed is
systematically higher than allowed, so accumulating it would overstate, which
is the one direction this product cannot afford.

It is also the same posture the platform takes elsewhere -- cannot attribute,
cannot judge -- rather than a rule invented for this file.

(2) THE BOUNDARY IS RIGHT. YOUR STATED REASON FOR IT IS THE WEAKER OF THE TWO
AVAILABLE AND, READ LITERALLY, POINTS THE OTHER WAY.

Driven against the shipped thresholds: 248000 cents exactly -> AT_OR_OVER,
247999 -> BELOW. The boundary is inside the attested side, as you say.

Your justification: "the transmittal denies claims ABOVE the amount; I put the
boundary inside the attested side." If KX is required only ABOVE the
threshold, then AT exactly the threshold it is NOT required -- so attesting
there is an attestation where none was required, which is precisely the
failure mode (1) exists to avoid. On that reasoning alone the boundary belongs
on the BELOW side.

WHAT ACTUALLY CARRIES IT IS THE FLOOR, and your own code comment at :212-215
already says so: "AT_OR_OVER -- the recorded total has reached the threshold.
Safe to state regardless of missing rows: a floor that has crossed has
crossed." Because the figure understates, a computed total equal to the
threshold means the TRUE total is at least the threshold and may be past it.
That argument survives whichever side the transmittal draws its line, and it
is the one to keep.

THE TWO DIVERGE IN EXACTLY ONE CASE and it is worth naming: `is_floor:false`
-- nothing excluded, the figure is a total rather than a floor -- and the
total lands exactly on the threshold. The floor argument does not apply, and
on your transmittal reading KX would not yet be required, but the code still
says AT_OR_OVER. I am not recommending a change: attesting one cent early on
an exact figure is the tolerable side of this asymmetry. I am saying the
justification in the code should be the floor one, and that this case should
be named rather than left inside "boundary inside the attested side".

I DID NOT VERIFY THE TRANSMITTAL. I cannot read the CMS source from this
clone and I am not going to assert what it says from memory on a row that
decides a federal attestation. That citation is the one thing this reasoning
still needs, and it belongs in the file next to THRESHOLDS_BY_YEAR -- which
already carries the right instinct in refusing to default an unknown year.

(3) THE INTERNAL PRACTICE ID RATHER THAN AN MBI IS CORRECT, and the cost you
state is the real one. Putting a Medicare Beneficiary Identifier into the
`sc_claims` jsonb blob would add a government identifier to a row that does
not need one to do its job -- against minimum-necessary, and it would raise
this resource's confidentiality exposure for no functional gain. That two
practices cannot reconcile the same beneficiary is a genuine loss and it is
the right trade: cross-practice reconciliation is not a thing this product
does, and the identifier would be permanent.

(4) THE FOUR FAIL-CLOSED CASES ALL HOLD, DRIVEN AGAINST THE REAL MODULE:

  no rows at all          -> beneficiaries [], no verdict emitted. "No rows"
                             produces nothing that can be read as a clearance.
  unknown year (1999)     -> year_known:false, verdict UNKNOWN_YEAR on both
                             disciplines. Not defaulted to the latest table.
  row with no allowed     -> counted in excluded.no_allowed, is_floor TRUE,
                             verdict BELOW_ON_RECORDED rather than BELOW.
  clean row under         -> is_floor FALSE, verdict BELOW.

BELOW and BELOW_ON_RECORDED being distinct values, rather than one value plus
a flag a caller may ignore, is the part that makes this hold. Your header says
"a caller that renders those two the same way has undone this file", and that
is exactly right -- it is also the only remaining way this can fail, and it
fails in the UI rather than here.

THE OVERRIDE SURVIVES AS A LABELLED OVERRIDE. `scFillPtYtd()` does not fill or
zero the box on failure -- "Not computed -- " plus the reason -- with the
comment naming why zero would be worse than blank: zero means "no therapy this
year" where the truth is "we could not find out". On success the note states
the amount, the row count, the beneficiary and the year, and on a floor it
adds "FLOOR, NOT A TOTAL: N row(s) could not be counted, so the real figure is
at least this and may be higher." The hand-entry field itself is labelled
"Override YTD $ (only if therapy was billed elsewhere)". A reader cannot mistake
a computed figure for an entered one, which is what was asked.

VERIFIED FOR THIS REVIEW: accumulateTherapy driven on seven constructed inputs
including both sides of the exact threshold; every read of sairncode.html and
the accumulator done in place; nothing in this clone written.

records.what: SAIRNsenior EVV completeness + payroll engine. GENUINE Tier A: sen_visits and sen_pay_rates are the inputs and the output is what each caregiver is PAID. THREE THINGS FOR A SECOND READER, all judgement. (1) THE WEIGHTED-AVERAGE REGULAR RATE. FLSA overtime is 1.5x the regular rate and across multiple rates in one workweek that is straight-time earnings over hours worked, 29 CFR 778.115 -- NOT the rate of the visit that crossed hour 40. The suite drives 30h at 18 dollars plus 15h at 30 dollars and asserts the premium is 5h at half of 22.00, not 5h at half of 30.00. Check that reading of 778.115 against the source; everything about the overtime figure rests on it. (2) service_type IS A SCHEDULING FIELD AND NOT AN EVV ONE. I put it in SEN_VISIT_SCHEDULE_FIELDS so the caregiver being paid for a visit cannot also choose which service was billed. Confirm that is the right side of the split, because the opposite reading -- that the person who performed the service knows best what it was -- is not unreasonable. (3) THE FLOOR SEMANTICS: any unpayable visit makes the whole period a floor and the screen says 'at least'. Confirm that understating is the safe direction for PAYROLL specifically; I argued it from wage-claim exposure, but an agency that pays a floor and never revisits it has underpaid somebody, so the opposite argument exists and I did not take it. ALSO WORTH CHECKING: the UTC workweek boundary is a stated limitation -- a visit clocked late Saturday in a western timezone can land in the following UTC week, because the app captures no agency timezone. NOT BUILT, per instruction: the aggregator transmission path, blocked on Michael's trading-partner and credential decisions.
records.verdict:
VERDICT: SOUND on all three questions asked. The engine is careful and the three judgements are right. But there is ONE BRANCH where "we could not tell" is folded into a measurement, it is the branch that decides whether a worked visit gets paid, and none of the three questions pointed at it. That is FINDING A and it is the reason this discharge is not simply "agreed".

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(1) THE WEIGHTED-AVERAGE REGULAR RATE -- CORRECT, CHECKED AGAINST THE REGULATION TEXT RATHER THAN FROM MEMORY, AND STRONGER THAN YOU CLAIMED.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
29 CFR 778.115, quoted: "Where an employee in a single workweek works at two or more different types of work for which different nonovertime rates of pay (of not less than the applicable minimum wage) have been established, his regular rate for that week is the weighted average of such rates." Total straight-time earnings over total hours worked. Your reading is right, and it is NOT the rate of the visit that crossed hour 40.

THE CODE MATCHES THE COMMENT, which is the part a citation check does not cover. Straight-time accrues per visit at that visit's own rate; the weighted average falls out of the sum; the rate is carried at full precision as cents-per-hour and rounded ONCE. `FLSA_OVERTIME_PREMIUM_NUMERATOR/DENOMINATOR` are 1/2 and the premium is applied to the weighted average, not to any visit rate. The fixture asserts `regular_rate_cents_per_hour === 2200` exactly on 30h at 18 plus 15h at 30. 27/27 arms pass.

IT IS STRONGER THAN "A DEFENSIBLE READING", AND THIS IS WORTH ADDING TO THE FILE. The alternative -- paying overtime at the rate in effect for the work performed during the overtime hours -- exists under FLSA 7(g)(2), and 29 CFR 778.415 conditions it on "an agreement or understanding arrived at between the employer and the employee BEFORE performance of the work". This app models no such agreement and captures nothing that could evidence one. So the weighted average is not merely the better reading of 778.115; it is the ONLY lawful default available to this system, and the alternative is unavailable rather than merely unchosen. You asked me to check the reading everything rests on. It holds, and the foundation is firmer than the comment claims for itself.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(2) service_type ON THE SCHEDULING SIDE -- RIGHT SIDE. THE STATUTORY ARGUMENT CARRIES IT ALONE, AND ONE CLAUSE OF THE STATED REASON DOES NOT.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The argument in the file is the good one: federal EVV element 1 (42 U.S.C. 1396b(l)(5)(A)(i)) is WHAT SERVICE the visit is for, which is decided when the visit is authorised, by whoever authorises it. A caregiver arriving at a door does not choose it. That settles the split on its own.

AND THE COUNTER-READING YOU RAISED IS ALREADY ANSWERED WITHOUT MOVING THE FIELD, which is why it is not a real objection: "the person who performed the service knows best what it was" is true, and `services_notes` is in SEN_VISIT_EVV_FIELDS, so the caregiver CAN record what was actually done. The knowledge is captured and routed to a scheduler; the AUTHORITY does not move. That is the right shape and it is worth saying out loud in the comment, because the next reader will raise the same objection you did.

THE CLAUSE THAT IS WRONG, and it is the kind that gets cited later as established: "putting it in the EVV set would let the person being paid for the visit also decide which service was billed." `service_type` appears NOWHERE in api/_lib/sen-payroll.js -- I grepped it and then re-derived the rate path: `resolveRateFrom` keys on `(employee_id, serviceDate)` and nothing else, so pay is per-caregiver and date-effective. THE CAREGIVER DOES NOT BENEFIT FROM THE service_type THEY WOULD CHOOSE. The real exposure is the AGENCY'S billing claim -- upcoding the service on a Medicaid claim -- which is a serious exposure and a different one. Your conclusion is right; that sentence describes a mechanism that does not exist and should be narrowed to the billing claim.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(3) FLOOR SEMANTICS -- UNDERSTATING IS SAFE HERE, BUT NOT FOR THE REASON THE QUESTION ASSUMES.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You asked whether understating is the safe direction for payroll specifically, and named the counter-argument yourself: an agency that pays a floor and never revisits it has underpaid somebody. That counter-argument is real, and under FLSA 216(b) an underpayment carries liquidated damages REGARDLESS OF INTENT -- so "we erred low" is not a defence.

THE DIRECTION IS NOT WHAT MAKES IT SAFE. THE VISIBILITY MECHANISM IS, and you built it: `visits_excluded` per caregiver with the cause split between "fixable on the visit" (no clock-out) and "fixable on the rate table" (no rate), routed to different people; `is_floor` at both caregiver and period level; the UI prefixing the gross with "at least " and flagging "N visit(s) could not be priced"; and `not_computed` naming five whole categories the run does not attempt. A floor that is VISIBLE AND ATTRIBUTED is a prompt. A silent one is an underpayment. Your own design answers your own worry, and the answer is the mechanism rather than the arithmetic.

OPEN, AND NOT A DEFECT: nothing FORCES the revisit. The floor is surfaced, not blocked -- an agency can export and pay a provisional run forever. Whether an unresolved floor should eventually refuse rather than warn is the same report-only-versus-gate tension this platform keeps meeting, and it is a product decision, not a code fix. Naming it because "surfaced" and "acted on" are two different facts and only the first is built.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING A -- A VISIT WITH NO scheduled_date IS DROPPED FROM PAY AND THE RUN DOES NOT GO PROVISIONAL. This breaks the file's own Rule 1, quoted in its own header.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
REPRODUCED AGAINST THE REAL ENGINE, WITH A CONTROL, not read:

  A. CONTROL -- one payable visit, nothing missing
       gross $80.00   is_floor false   visits_excluded 0
  B. SAME, plus one visit that has clock-in, clock-out, a caregiver and a rate,
     but NO scheduled_date
       gross $80.00   is_floor FALSE   visits_excluded 0
       excluded.outside_period 1
  C. SAME, plus one visit with no clock-out -- the comparable could-not-tell
       gross $80.00   is_floor TRUE    visits_excluded 1
       excluded.no_clock_out 1

C is right and is the behaviour the header argues for. B is the same class of fact -- a real worked visit this engine cannot place -- and it contributes zero, raises no flag, and the caller is handed a run that presents as COMPLETE. Four worked hours vanish and the screen does not say "at least".

THE CAUSE IS ONE PREDICATE DOING TWO JOBS, at the period filter:

    if (!serviceDate || serviceDate < start || serviceDate > end) {
      excluded.outside_period += 1; return;

`!serviceDate` is WE COULD NOT TELL. The two comparisons are WE COULD TELL, AND IT IS OUT. Only the second pair is legitimately not-a-floor, because a visit genuinely outside the period is not part of this run. Folding the first into the same counter is exactly what your own Rule 1 forbids in its own words: "None is quietly treated as zero hours, because zero hours is a measurement and 'we could not tell' is not."

IT IS REACHABLE, which is what makes it a finding rather than a nit. `scheduled_date` lives inside `sen_visits.data`, a jsonb blob with no not-null constraint (sql/sairnsenior_visits_schema.sql:34), and the scheduler write branch copies only fields that are `!== undefined` -- SEN_VISIT_SCHEDULE_FIELDS.forEach((f) => { if (payload[f] !== undefined) ... }). Nothing requires it at any layer. A visit saved without one is accepted, stored, and then silently unpayable.

SUGGESTED SHAPE, NOT PRESCRIBED: a separate `no_service_date` counter that DOES raise `is_floor`, alongside `outside_period` which correctly does not. That keeps the two facts apart the way `no_clock_out` and `no_rate` already are, and it needs its own arm -- the current suite has no fixture for a visit missing its service date, which is why 27 green arms did not see this.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING B -- THE UTC WORKWEEK LIMITATION IS REAL, AND ITS STATED MITIGATION DOES NOT EXIST IN THE OUTPUT.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You flagged the boundary as a stated limitation. It is real and I reproduced it against `weekStartKey` directly:

  local Sat 21:00 US-Pacific -> 2026-09-06T04:00Z -> week 2026-09-06  (the FOLLOWING week)
  local Fri 21:00 US-Pacific -> 2026-09-05T04:00Z -> week 2026-08-30  (correct)

That is not cosmetic on a pay run: moving a visit across the boundary changes which week's hours cross 40, and therefore the premium.

THE PROBLEM IS THE DISCLOSURE, NOT THE CHOICE. Computing in UTC with no agency timezone captured is the honest option and I would not change it. But the comment's mitigation reads: "The caller is told which week each visit was assigned to (`week_start`) so the boundary is visible." MEASURED AGAINST THE REAL RETURN VALUE: the output carries `caregivers[].weeks[].week_start` with `visits` as a COUNT, and the visit id appears nowhere in the returned object at all. The caller is told which weeks EXIST and their totals. It is never told which week a given VISIT landed in, so the boundary is NOT visible and the stated mitigation does not hold as written.

AND IT IS ABSENT FROM THE ONE PLACE THIS FILE BUILT FOR IT. `not_computed` exists, in the file's own words, so "a caller cannot present it as a finished pay run". It carries five entries -- taxes, travel time, live-in/sleep-time, leave and differentials, more-generous state rules -- and NONE mentions the timezone boundary. So a limitation the file takes seriously is stated only where a code reader will find it, which is the shape this platform keeps paying for. One more entry in `not_computed` closes it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
CHECKED AND RETRACTED, recorded because a review that reports only what survived is not showing its work: my first fixture came back `outside_period: 1` on a visit I believed was in-period, and I started writing it up as a timezone defect in the period filter. It was my fixture -- I had omitted `scheduled_date`, and the period is bounded by the service date, deliberately and for a reason the file states (the service date is what the rate resolves against and what a payer matches on). Chasing it is what produced FINDING A, but the original suspicion was wrong and the period filter is correct.

WHAT THIS DISCHARGE DOES NOT SAY. I did not review the EVV readiness engine, the rate-resolver's ambiguity handling beyond reading it, or the sairnsenior.html payroll screen past confirming it renders "at least " and the per-caregiver flags. I checked the two citations that the money rests on against their primary text; I did not re-derive the six federal EVV elements against 42 U.S.C. 1396b(l)(5)(A).

records.what:
append-only read-order scanner: tools/append_only_read_order_scan.py (NEW, report-only) and tests/run_append_only_read_order_probe.py (NEW, 11 arms), plus one open-work row.

THE GATE TRIGGER IS SPURIOUS AND I AM SAYING SO RATHER THAN OVERRIDING -- the third instance today of scrubber item 24, after fourth flagged it twice. `dnt_credentials`, `rf_claim_agreements` and `rf_claim_photos` appear in these two files ONLY as prose naming what the scan found, and as findings in the open-work row. Neither file touches any dispatcher, any resource, or any write path: both are read-only over api/sd-data.js and sql/, the scanner has one io.open call, and the probe writes only inside its own tempfile.mkdtemp fixtures. THE OBLIGATION IS STILL WANTED; only its reason is wrong.

WHAT A REVIEWER SHOULD ATTACK, hardest first:

(1) THE POPULATION IS THE WHOLE TOOL. It is derived TWICE -- by DB grant (`select, insert` with no update/delete/truncate) = 21, and by application contract (`appendOnlyExisting(res, existingR, '<table>')`) = 5, union 23, overlap 3 -- because a grant-only test MISSES `alf_incidents` and `alf_op_audits`, which are append-only by contract and carry UPDATE for `merge-duplicates`. IF THERE IS A THIRD WAY A TABLE IS APPEND-ONLY ON THIS PLATFORM, MY POPULATION IS SHORT AND THE SCAN REPORTS CLEAN OVER WHATEVER IT MISSED. That is the failure I would attack first. I know of one candidate I did NOT model: a table whose append-only-ness is enforced by a check-and-insert RPC rather than by either signal -- `alf_check_and_insert_mar_entry` and `law_check_and_insert_disbursement` both exist, and `alf_mar` is in NEITHER of my two derivations because of it.

(2) THE OWN-KEY LIST IS HAND-WRITTEN AND IT IS WHERE I ALREADY GOT IT WRONG TWICE. A read keyed on the row's own unique id is a single-row lookup and ordering it is meaningless; a read keyed on a PARENT id is still a list. My first draft used a `&\w*_id=eq\.` wildcard, which threw away `rf_claim_photos` and `rf_proposals` -- real parent-keyed list reads -- and hid four reads from the count. My second draft was missing `agreement_id`, so a single-row existence check came out as a false finding. Both are fixed and both have paired arms (C5/C6), but the list is still hand-written: a new own-key column added to the platform is a SILENT EXCLUSION until somebody adds it here. Argue whether it should be derived from the schemas instead.

(3) MY VERDICTS ON THE SIX UNORDERED READS ARE JUDGEMENTS, NOT MEASUREMENTS. I called five of them non-defects by reading their consumers: `rf_certifications:5924`, `:7847` and `dnt_credentials:12331` feed `latestBy()`, which compares `recorded_at` and breaks ties on `entry_id`, so it never takes "the last row in the list"; `rf_claim_photos:7304` selects one column to build a membership set; `rf_claim_agreements:8452` sorts client-side by `executed_at` then `.pop()`. Re-derive at least one of those rather than reading my summary -- if any is order-sensitive after all, it is an unreported defect wearing a cleared verdict, which is worse than the scan not having run.

(4) THE ONE REAL FINDING may be overstated and should be checked as such. `rf_claim_agreements:8376` with `sairnroofing.html:2806`: no server `order=`, `rows.map(...)` with no `.sort(` and no `reverse()`, and `created_at` rendered `.slice(0,10)`. I claim it matters MORE than the SAIRNcare instance because the chain is `executed`/`rescinded` on a signed contingency agreement whose cancellation window is statutory, and the same panel renders "cancellation window OPEN INDEFINITELY" as a red badge. That consequence claim is mine and is the part to disagree with.

(5) THE SCANNER REPORTS AND DELIBERATELY DOES NOT GATE, and a reviewer could say that is too weak. My reasoning: five of six unordered reads were correct, so a gate would have denied five real pushes on its first run. The counter-argument -- that a report nothing consults is the "tool that exists but never runs" shape CLAUDE.md names -- is real and I have not answered it.       lines.sort((a, b) => (a.date < b.date ? -1 : (a.date > b.date ? 1 : 0)));

That list is rendered as a dated list -- "Documented but NOT billed" -- so it was fully in insertion order, not merely tied-within-a-day. A comparator keyed on a field present in ONE of three sources does not produce "one source ordered correctly and two arbitrary". Every row lacking the key collapses to a single comparison value and banks together relative to the keyed rows. The output would show MAR administrations interleaved by real time with ADL assessments and activity attendance stacked at one end -- an ordering that LOOKS chronological, is chronological for a third of the rows, and is a positional artefact for the rest. VERDICT: SOUND. Every trade-off you named is real, and I confirmed each by DRIVING the function rather than reading the patterns. One genuine small defect found that you did not raise, in the CARD rule. And press-on (1)'s residual is already closed by your own NOT_REDACTED_NOTE better than I would have closed it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
DRIVEN, NOT READ. Every claim in your obligation, against redactDocumentText:
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  bare 10-digit phone      'Call me at 5551234567'      -> SURVIVES   (as you said)
  structured phone         'Call me at (555) 123-4567'  -> [PHONE REDACTED]
  20-digit account         'account 12345678901234567890' -> SURVIVES (as you said)
  16-digit card            'Card 4111111111111111'      -> [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED]
  email                    'bob.smith@example.com'      -> [EMAIL REDACTED]
  SSN                      '123-45-6789'                -> [SSN REDACTED]
  street address           '1842 Maple Avenue'          -> [ADDRESS REDACTED]
  name in prose            'Robert Smith, the foreman'  -> SURVIVES   (as you said)
  equipment serial         '3821RK04821'                -> SURVIVES   (the deliberate keep)
  invoice total            '4,182.50'                   -> SURVIVES   (the deliberate keep)

Ten for ten against your own description. Nothing you claimed about this pass is overstated, which is the first thing a reviewer of a redactor should establish and is not always true.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(1) ARGUE THE KEEPS -- I AGREE WITH THEM, AND YOUR OWN NOTE ALREADY ANSWERS THE RESIDUAL YOU RAISED.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The keeps are right and the argument is stronger than "a redactor that eats them gets switched off". mech_docs exists to hold extracted content for a trades business: amounts, model numbers and serials ARE the payload. A pass that removes them leaves a record with no value, and a worthless record gets bypassed or deleted -- which is worse for privacy than a partial pass people actually use. That is a real argument, not a convenience one.

YOUR RESIDUAL IS THE RIGHT WORRY -- an invoice total beside a redacted customer name may still be identifying in a small trade -- and it is the classic quasi-identifier problem: amount plus date plus equipment model can identify a customer in a town with forty commercial HVAC sites. You said you had not weighed it. YOU HAVE, in the one place that matters, and I think you did not notice you had: NOT_REDACTED_NOTE ends "Treat this text as REDUCED, never as anonymous." That is exactly the right disclosure and it is the only honest answer -- this is a reduction pass, not an anonymiser, and the note says so in the artefact rather than in a commit message. I would not add anything to it.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(2) AND (3) -- THE BOUNDS ARE THE RIGHT TRADES, AND BOTH ARE STATED IN THE FILE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
The 19-digit ceiling lets a 20-digit account through and stops a long serial or an EPA certificate number being swallowed; the structure requirement on phones lets a bare ten-digit phone through and stops a bare ten-digit serial being eaten. Both confirmed live above. In both cases the alternative destroys the document's subject, and in both cases the residual is a shape (a 20-digit account, an unformatted phone) that is rarer in trade documents than the thing the loose rule would eat. Correct trades, and the reasoning is in the comments where the next reader finds it rather than in a review nobody re-reads.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
FINDING -- THE CARD RULE EATS THE SEPARATOR THAT FOLLOWS IT, ON EVERY MATCH.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Not raised in the obligation. `re: /\b(?:\d[ -]?){13,19}\b/g` applies the optional `[ -]?` after the FINAL digit too, so the space or hyphen following the run is consumed into the match and replaced along with it. Driven:

  'Card 4111111111111111 on file.'      -> 'Card [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED]on file.'
  'Paid by 4111 1111 1111 1111 yesterday.' -> 'Paid by [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED]yesterday.'
  'Ref 1234567890123 approved.'         -> 'Ref [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED]approved.'
  'Card 4111111111111111 -RTU unit here.' -> 'Card [CARD/ACCOUNT REDACTED] -RTU unit here.'

Every card-length match merges the token with the following word. THE DIRECTION IS SAFE -- it removes more than intended, never less -- so this is a readability and downstream-parsing defect rather than a leak. It matters because this text is stored, synced, and is the kind of thing that gets re-fed to a model: `]on`, `]yesterday` and `]approved` are token boundaries that no longer exist. None of the other four rules does this; CARD is alone in putting an optional separator inside the repeated group.

Cheap and bounded: anchor the last digit outside the repetition -- `\b(?:\d[ -]?){12,18}\d\b` -- which preserves the 13-to-19 range exactly and leaves the following separator alone. It needs an arm, because nothing currently asserts anything about what survives AROUND a redaction, only about what survives INSIDE the text.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
(4) `complete` AS A CONSTANT false, WITH AN ARM ASSERTING A PROSE NAME SURVIVES -- THAT IS THE RIGHT CONTRACT AND IT IS NOT AN EXCUSE.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
You asked whether it is a contract or a way of excusing an incomplete pass. It is a contract, and the arm is what makes it one. A boolean that is always false is only an excuse if nothing depends on it; here it is paired with a test that REQUIRES the known gap to be present, so the day somebody adds prose-name detection the arm fails and forces the flag and the note to be updated together. That is the opposite of an excuse -- it is a gap that cannot be closed silently, and it is the same shape as an arm asserting an ABSENCE that I have had to write twice this week for the same reason.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ON THE SPURIOUS GATE TRIGGER -- AGREED, RE-DERIVED.
────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
`invoices` appears in api/_lib/mech-redact.js only as an English word in the prose listing the document types scanDoc asks the model to identify. The bare Tier A `invoices` belongs to SAIRNscape and no path here touches it. WHAT THIS DISCHARGE DOES NOT SAY. I drove the ten cases above and read the CARD, PHONE and card-bound comments. I did not audit the client copy in sairnmechanical.html (your press-on 5, which the obligation text cut off), the scanDoc prompt, or the sd-data.js write-path wiring beyond confirming the redaction is invoked in the mech_docs branch at :12035.

With SAIRNVET_TRANSCRIBE_URL unset the endpoint answers 503 TRANSCRIBE_HOST_NOT_CONFIGURED, and DRIVEN rather than read: the licence module is never touched (A1c) and a licence lookup that THROWS still never runs, because the host check is genuinely first. So the claim in the file's header -- that the process must not hold audio even long enough to validate a licence -- is true of the code and not only of the comment.

ATTACK (3) HOLDS AND THEN SOME. In scribeClientAnswer the save, the `if(!saved)` guard and the `scribeStart()` call are in that order, the guard returns, `saved` is st()'s own return value through a one-line passthrough rather than a wrapper that could swallow it, and st() has reachable `return false` paths. The DECLINE path -- which the obligation did not name -- also returns before scribeStart(), and the decline is still recorded, which is the right answer: both answers are evidence.

ATTACK (4) IS CORRECTLY DISCLOSED AND I CANNOT DO BETTER. sv_scribe_consent_no_audio is named in the scoping doc, disclosed as never executed, and does exist in sql/sairnvet_data_schema.sql. NOTHING IN A REPO CAN OBSERVE A DATABASE, so this probe confirms the DISCLOSURE and not the constraint -- which is the distinction the obligation itself drew, and the right one.

FINDING V1/V2 -- THE PREFLIGHT DECIDES AVAILABILITY BY ABSENCE, AND THAT IS A FAIL-OPEN. Driven: with a host configured and a valid licence, the preflight body (no consent_ref, no audio) returns 400 CONSENT_REF_REQUIRED; with a host configured and an INVALID licence it returns 403 LICENSE_INVALID. The client's rule is "anything that is NOT TRANSCRIBE_HOST_NOT_CONFIGURED means available", so BOTH enable the "Start - ask the client" button. A host that is configured but broken therefore reads as available, the vet asks a client to consent, audio is captured, and the first real POST fails 502 -- which is precisely the harm the module's own header names: "asking a client to agree to a recording that cannot be transcribed is consent theatre." This is an allowlist written as a denylist, and it is the inverse of how the rest of the endpoint is built, where every refusal is NAMED.

RECOMMENDED, ONE LINE: decide availability from the code a working platform actually returns to this body (CONSENT_REF_REQUIRED) rather than from the absence of one particular failure. On a host-less platform the answer is byte-identical, so the change is inert today and fail-closed the day a host is set -- which is exactly the day nobody will be re-reading this preflight.

NOT REACHABLE TODAY, and that is stated so the finding is not read as bigger than it is: hostConfigured() is false in every environment.

FINDING V5 -- THE COMMENT-STRIPPER CAN HIDE REAL CODE, AND THE FIXTURE DOES NOT TEST THAT SHAPE. Attacked with three inputs. Two hide a real `SpeechRecognition` reference from the check: a `//` inside a STRING literal, and a `//` inside a REGEX literal. The guard is `(^|[^:])`, which protects `http://` and nothing else, so a `//` anywhere else takes the REST OF THE LINE with it -- including the code the check exists to find. The shipped fixture tests four cases and none of them is this one.

MEASURED BEFORE RECOMMENDING: the shipped scribe module has NO line where a `//` sits inside an open string, so the flaw is LATENT, not live. It hides nothing today. It is a fixture gap and a future hazard, not a present false pass.

AND THIS PROBE GUARDS ITS OWN TRANSCRIPTION (arm C0). The client's availability rule is transcribed into the probe as a function, and a probe asserting against the reviewer's READING of a rule rather than the rule is the shape this platform keeps recording -- so C0 re-locates the three lines that rule is made of inside scribePreflight() and reports if they have drifted. Every A1 finding is then attributable to the page rather than to my copy of it.

NOTHING FIXED. This is a review; V1/V2 is a one-line product decision on an endpoint the author holds, and V5 is a fixture addition to their suite.

PRESS ON THIS FIRST -- IT IS THE ONE CHOICE I MADE THAT COULD BE WRONG, AND IT IS THE SERVER GUARD'S DIRECTION. I refuse a non-numeric `amount` rather than coercing it: 400 INVALID_AMOUNT. The argument for refusing is that coercing server-side is a silent data change and the caller is the only party that knows what "500" meant. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS REAL AND I AM NAMING IT RATHER THAN WAITING: this is a WRITE path, and a refusal means a shop's invoice does not sync. sairnscape.html's scpSaveInv already shows "Saved on this device only -- server sync failed" on a falsy result, so a refused write degrades to local-only silently from the user's point of view. If you think a storage validator on a sync path should coerce-and-store rather than refuse, that is a real disagreement and this is the moment.

(2) AND THE SAME QUESTION ON NULL, WHERE I WENT THE OTHER WAY. `amount: null` is ACCEPTED. My reasoning is measured rather than assumed: scpSaveInv sends Number(input || 0), so junk input makes NaN, and JSON.stringify puts NaN on the wire as null -- refusing it would break the existing client on the one input it already handles badly. But that means a junk keystroke still reaches storage as null, and the ONLY thing making that safe is that every reader now coerces. If a reader is added that does not, null is a hole I deliberately left. Check whether you agree the asymmetry between "500" refused and null accepted is the right line.

(3) I DID NOT HARDEN THE OTHER FIELDS ON THAT PAYLOAD. The branch still stores `status`, `issued` and anything else the caller sends, verbatim, in the jsonb blob. I guarded `amount` because that is the field the defect ran through. A reviewer who thinks a storage validator should validate the whole shape rather than the one field that bit us is making a fair point, and it is out of this change's scope rather than answered by it.

(4) THE THIRD TAX SURFACE IS THE PART I WOULD RE-CHECK. taxRender()'s invTotal had NO fallback at all -- the bare `s + i.amount` shape, not `s + (x || 0)` -- which truthy_sum_check cannot match by construction. I coerced it, but I did NOT widen the checker to that shape, so the next bare fold is as invisible as this one was. Recorded as planned-not-done in the register. If you think that widening belongs in this change rather than after it, say so.
